description:
The Code Enforcement Board was created by Ordinance No. 741 on June 16, 1981. The purpose of this Board is to review residential property infractions of the City Technical Codes, negotiate compliance and impose fines for failure to comply. The City utilizes a magistrate apart from the Code Board for code enforcement issues involving commercial properties. The Code Enforcement Board shall consist of seven (7) regular members and two (2) alternate members, all with three-year terms.
On June 2, 2026, the City Commission appointed one regular member and one alternate member to fill existing vacancies on the Board. However, both individuals resigned shortly after their appointments. As a result, the Board currently consists of six (6) regular members and no alternate members, with one (1) vacant regular member seat remaining. The vacant regular member seat has a term set to expire in June 2027.
An application has been submitted by Ali Elhajj, expressing interest in being appointed as a regular member of the Code Enforcement Board to fill the vacant seat and complete the term ending in June 2027. Currently, there are no other applications on file for this Board.
title: Approval of New Appointment to the Code Enforcement Board. (City Clerk Sibbitt)

description:
The Inspiration Planned Unit Development (PUD) was approved by the City Commission at its meeting on March 6, 2018. The PUD is located in District 3, directly south of the Florida Turnpike and west of Maguire Road. Access to the PUD is primarily from Heller Blvd, which was constructed as part of the development. The PUD encompasses 16.865 acres and features a mix of commercial and residential uses.
The commercial uses are distributed among four buildings with the following designated uses and maximum square footage:
Building 1 Pre-School (13,681 sq ft)
Building 2 Office/retail (12,600 sq ft)
Building 3 Office/retail (42,350 sq ft)
Building 4 Retail (3,300 sq ft)
The residential component of the PUD permits a maximum of 90 townhouses, resulting in a density of 5.4 dwelling units per acre. To date, eight of the ninety townhomes have been permitted and constructed. The original PUD plan also included a clubhouse with a pool, barbecue area, and picnic space. In total, the residential area comprises thirteen (13) buildings: twelve (12) townhome buildings and one (1) amenity center.
The applicant, DR Horton, Inc., acting on behalf of the property owner, has submitted a non-substantial amendment to the PUD Land Use Plan (LUP). The proposed amendment would modify the residential portion by revising the approved architectural style for ten of the twelve townhome buildings. Additionally, the proposed LUP would replace the previously approved residential amenity from a clubhouse with a pool, barbecue area, and picnic area to a gym with a smaller footprint in the same location. There are no other proposed changes to the PUD LUP.
The applicant has provided an amended PUD LUP, as well as elevations and renderings for the proposed townhomes and gymnasium amenity.
title: Approval of the Inspiration Planned Unit Development (PUD) Non-Substantial Amendment to PUD. (Community Development Administrator McFarlane)

description:
Finance staff continually evaluates industry best practices and emerging technologies to improve efficiency and compliance with public finance and government accounting standards. Following a review of available solutions, staff recommends contracting with Fifth Asset, Inc. for the DebtBook debt and cash management SaaS platform. The proposed solution provides unified debt, cash and investments in a single platform that centralizes data and streamlines critical workflows.
The DebtBook platform will enable staff to optimize cash flow and debt structures, ensuring resilient liquidity, stronger financial performance, and continued public trust. It will also assist in the preparation of note disclosures required in the City's annual comprehensive financial report (ACFR) to comply with Government Accounting Standards Board (GASB) pronouncements.
Under Fifth Asset, Inc.'s OMNIA cooperative purchasing contract (Region XIV Education Service Center as lead agency), DebtBook's proposal includes a three-year contract for FY2027 at a cost of $20,000; FY2028 at a cost of $21,000; and FY2029 at a cost of $22,060. The implementation phase of the software platform will take place during the current fiscal year.
title: Approval to Piggyback OMNIA's Contract with Fifth Asset Inc. for the DebtBook Debt and Cash Management Software as a Service (SaaS) Platform. (Finance Director Weber)

description:
The Ocoee WWTF Electrical Upgrade & Expansion - Rebid Project was approved to improve the existing Wastewater Treatment Facilities (WWTF) electrical capacity for the future improvement of the WWTF for the continued growth of the City and the expansion of the City’s Central Sewer System.
Utility staff have worked with the Contractor, Sawcross Incorporated, to compile all remaining instrumentation work, operational enhancements, and system integration necessary for the successful completion of this project. These systems were not included in the original scope; however, they are essential to fully implement the upgraded treatment processes, ensure operational continuity, and eliminate reliance on aging and outdated systems. The scope of these changes includes the following:WWTF Control Program Revision and Process Integration:
Comprehensive modification of the existing WWTF control program to incorporate new processes and equipment associated with the facility upgrades. This includes integration of additional aeration rotors, updates to process logic, restructuring of control sequences to support enhanced treatment operations, and alignment of programming with current industry standards.VFD Technology Integration:
Updates to the control system programming and operational logic to support the transition to Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) operation, improving energy efficiency and process responsiveness.RAS/WAS Station Optimization:
Fine-tuning and reconfiguration of programming for the Return Activated Sludge (RAS) and Waste Activated Sludge (WAS) station to improve process control, operational reliability, and treatment performance.Alarm System Enhancements:
Expansion and modernization of alarm functionalities to provide improved monitoring, early detection capabilities, and heightened operational awareness.
Removal of Obsolete Communication Equipment:
Decommissioning and removal of outdated plant and lift station communication devices that are incompatible with the updated control and monitoring systems.
Change Order No. 3 is necessary to ensure the complete integration of new processes, the modernization of the plant’s control infrastructure, and the long-term reliability of all upgraded systems. This change order will require a contract modification allowing the Contractor to provide these additional construction services, increasing the total project cost by $264,059.52.
title: Approval of Change Order No. 3 for ITB #24-008 Ocoee WWTF Electrical Upgrade & Expansion - Rebid Project. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The first reading of the ordinance was held on July 21, 2026.
On April 7, 2026, the City Commission approved continuing the City's hybrid model, with a Code Enforcement Board hearing code violations involving detached single-family residential properties and a Special Magistrate hearing all other cases. The City Commission also stated that they wanted to re-evaluate the Code Enforcement Board after 90 days. The 90-day evaluation was completed on July 7, 2026. Within this 90-day evaluation period, the board has met the quorum requirement for all meetings and imposed the recommended fines in all cases. As a result of the previous Code Board Attorney's retirement, a Code Board Attorney has been retained to provide legal guidance to the Code Board during hearings. There is still one vacancy on the Code Enforcement Board, and both alternate positions are currently vacant.
The proposed ordinance update states that, in the event of a conflict of interest or when the Special Magistrate is unavailable due to illness, disability, or death, the City Manager or his designee may appoint a Special Magistrate pro tem to perform the duties of a Magistrate. The proposed ordinance retains the City’s hybrid model while expressly authorizing the City Manager to assign cases to the Special Magistrate if the Code Board cannot achieve a quorum or the City Commission cannot promptly fill a vacancy on the seven-member board as required by State law.
The City Commission also asked staff to present updated fines for code violations. The proposed Ordinance increases: 1) potential fines not to exceed $1000.00 per day per violation. 2) potential fines not to exceed $5000.00 per day per violation for repeat violators. 3) potential fines not to exceed $15,000.00 per day per violation if the violation is irreplaceable or irreversible. These fines are in accordance with Florida Statutes 162.09 (2)(b) for municipalities with at least 50,000 residents, which states that the Magistrate or Code Board has discretion to impose code board fines up to the limit.
The proposed ordinance authorizes the Magistrate to hear all cases recommended by the Code Board for foreclosure. The Special Magistrate shall review and consider the application for reduction or release of lien, provide the violator with an opportunity to address the Special Magistrate regarding the application for reduction or release of lien, and take the testimony of other interested parties. The Special Magistrate shall render a written recommendation to the City Commission based on findings of fact and law. The proposed Ordinance establishes a formal procedure for lien reduction/elimination, providing for the Special Magistrate to make a recommendation to the City Commission, while retaining the City Manager’s right to compromise and settle code liens. The proposed Ordinance also establishes a Code Enforcement Recovery Fund. This fund will be a dedicated financial pool created to support the administration and operation of local code enforcement activities. It will be funded by revenues generated from fines, civil penalties, nuisance abatement recovery monies, and other costs or reimbursements collected through enforcement actions.

description:
On October 15, 2024, the City Commission adopted the candidate qualifying period for the offices of Mayor and City Commissioner, establishing the regular qualifying period as beginning at noon on the first Friday in December preceding the election and ending at noon on the second Friday in December preceding the election. The ordinance also authorizes the City Commission to establish, by resolution, an alternative five (5) business day qualifying period for a regular, special, or general election.
Section C-10 of the Charter of the City of Ocoee provides that the City Commission is responsible for determining the qualifications and eligibility of candidates for the offices of Mayor and City Commissioner, as well as the election and qualifications of its members and any grounds for forfeiture of office under the Charter. In addition, Section C-11 requires that candidates for Mayor or City Commissioner have resided within the City for one (1) year, furnish proof of meeting the residency requirement as prescribed by ordinance, and consent to a background check to verify their qualifications to hold office. These Charter provisions ensure that all candidates satisfy the eligibility requirements before being qualified for the election.
The Human Resources Director has advised that background checks may take up to four (4) business days to be completed after they are ordered. To allow sufficient time for staff to obtain and review the required background checks, and present the results to the City Commission prior to its regular meeting on December 15, 2026, staff recommends establishing an earlier qualifying period. The proposed qualifying period would begin at noon on Tuesday, December 1, 2026, and end at noon on Tuesday, December 8, 2026, for the March 2027 municipal election.
title: Approval of Resolution Establishing the Qualifying Period for the Election to be Held in March 2027. (City Attorney Geller)

description:
This item was considered at the July 3rd City Commission meeting and was not approved by a 2-2 vote. The applicant has requested that it be considered again.
V3 Capital Group, representing the owner of parcel ID 09-22-28-0000-00-060, has submitted a formal request for an access easement across City-owned property (parcel ID 09-22-28-0000-00-056). The subject properties are located in Commission District 4, north of A D Mims Road and east of Clarke Road. The attached image illustrates the location of the Silvestri property, the City property, and the approximate placement of the proposed easement (indicated by a red circle).
On April 22, 2025, V3 Capital Group, LLC, acting on behalf of Silvestri Investments of Florida, Inc., and City staff held a formal pre-application meeting to discuss a proposed 7-Eleven convenience store with a gas station and car wash on a 2-acre parcel located within the Prairie Lake PUD (Parcel ID 09-22-28-0000-00-060).
On July 10, 2025, the City held a community informational meeting regarding the proposed 7-Eleven with residents and V3 Capital Group LLC in attendance.
On July 16, 2025, City staff provided V3 Capital Group with a letter clarifying that the 2-acre parcel has a right to direct access to Clarke Road. This letter was provided after consulting with the City Attorney and reviewing the Agreement of Purchase and Sale between the City and Silvestri Investments of Florida. A copy of the letter and Agreement of Purchase and Sale has been included with this report.
Section 2 of the Purchase and Sale Agreement states: "...the parties [Silvestri and the City] have agreed (i) that the Retained Land will have frontage along and direct access to Clarke Road."
Since the initial submittal of the small-scale site plan application for the proposed 7-Eleven on November 11, 2025, City staff and representatives from V3 Capital Group have engaged in ongoing coordination regarding the facilitation of access to Clarke Road for the subject property. With the majority of staff comments on the site plan addressed, City staff are now presenting the proposed access easement for consideration and approval by the City Commission. The alignment of the easement is designed to provide clear and safe access for both the City-owned property and the proposed 7-Eleven development to Clarke Road. Additionally, the developer has indicated that installation of a traffic signal at the intersection of Clarke Road and Ocoee Vista Parkway would be beneficial to the project. City staff and the developer are collaboratively developing a mutually agreeable plan regarding the timing and construction of the traffic signal in conjunction with the proposed 7-Eleven development.
title: Approval of an Access Easement Agreement with Silvestri Investments of Florida, Inc. for the Market Store at Prairie Lake. CONTINUED FROM THE JULY 7, 2026, CITY COMMISSION MEETING. (Community Development Administrator McFarlane)

description:
The Ocoee Fire Department requests City Commission authorization to submit a grant application for funding to purchase and install vehicle exhaust capture systems on two fire apparatus: one E-ONE fire engine and one Sutphen 90-foot aerial platform. The requested action also authorizes the City to accept the grant, if awarded, provide the required 25% local matching funds, and purchase the two exhaust capturing systems.
Firefighters are routinely exposed to diesel exhaust emissions generated by emergency response apparatus. Diesel exhaust has been identified as a known human carcinogen and is associated with increased risks of cancer and respiratory disease. The NO SMOKE direct source diesel exhaust filtration system significantly reduces firefighter exposure by capturing and filtering diesel emissions directly at the source before they enter the fire station or surrounding work areas. All front line fire apparatus already have this system, except for the newly purchased fire engine and the aerial tower truck.
The proposed project will equip two frontline apparatus with onboard exhaust capture systems that comply with NFPA 1500 (2018) firefighter health and safety standards. Installation of these systems will improve station air quality, reduce occupational health risks, and further the Department's ongoing commitment to firefighter cancer prevention and workplace safety.
Approval of this item serves a valid public purpose by enhancing firefighter health and safety, reducing exposure to hazardous diesel exhaust emissions, improving workplace air quality within City fire stations, and ensuring emergency response apparatus are equipped with technology that supports nationally recognized firefighter safety standards. The project will help protect the City's emergency responders while improving the long-term reliability and safety of fire department operations.
The total estimated project cost, including equipment and installation for both apparatus, is $21,392.Total Project Cost: $21,392
Federal Grant Request (75%): $16,044

If the grant is awarded, the City's required matching funds will be provided through the Fire Department's approved budget.

description:
Effective June 24, 2026, Senate Bill 4-F revises the calculation for determining the maximum millage rate that a county, municipality, special district, or municipal service taxing unit may levy.
Section 2 of SB 4-F, amends subsection 200.065(5), Florida Statutes, to remove a calculation of the current year's maximum millage rate based on the prior year's taxes and maximum millage rate and removes the option to levy the adopted rate from the prior year, if higher. The amendment provides that the maximum millage rate that may be levied is the rolled-back rate computed under 200.065(1), F.S. A taxing authority may adopt a millage rate of up to 110 percent of the rolled-back rate by a two-thirds vote of the membership of the governing body. A taxing authority may adopt a millage rate exceeding 110 percent of the rolled-back rate by a unanimous vote of the membership of the governing body.
The City must consider setting a tentative millage rate to ensure financial stability amid rising costs and economic uncertainty. For Fiscal Year 2026/2027, the rolled-back millage rate is 4.8111 mills. This rate is lower than the current millage and would not generate enough revenue to sustain existing service levels. State statutes define the levels of approval required for adopting a millage rate and permit the governing body to approve a maximum rate of 5.2922 mills (110% of the rolled-back rate) with a two-thirds vote. This represents an increase from the current rate of 4.9500 mills.
From 2018 to 2025, the taxable value of all properties in the City increased by an average of 11.8% annually. For fiscal year 2027, the taxable values rose by only 8.6% to $5,859,466,089. To support the general fund, staff are proposing a tentative millage rate of 5.2922 mills, which is projected to generate approximately $31,009,466 in revenue.
title: Approval of Proposed Tentative Millage Rate for Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Budget. (Finance Director Weber)

description:

The inventory consists of aging mowers, trailers, sprayers, golf carts, and various miscellaneous maintenance equipment that are beyond their useful life and are no longer suitable for service.
These items have remained stored in the golf course maintenance yard, where they continue to deteriorate due to prolonged exposure to the elements. Staff has completed an evaluation of the equipment and determined that it is no longer economically feasible to repair or retain. Declaring these items as surplus and authorizing their disposal will improve the functionality and appearance of the maintenance yard, enhance operational efficiency, and support the City's ongoing efforts to improve and modernize Forest Lake Golf Club.

description:
The property located at 611 N. Lakewood Avenue, owned by Rental Home Holdings LLC, has been the subject of ongoing code enforcement proceedings regarding unsafe structural conditions and the accumulation of junk and debris. The violations were cited pursuant to Section 108-35 of the City Code, which addresses nuisance conditions or hazards impacting structures to the extent that repair, removal, securing, or demolition is necessary to protect public health, safety, and welfare.
On June 24, 2025, the Code Enforcement Board heard Case No. 2025-01222 regarding the unsafe structure and associated debris conditions at the property. During the hearing, Code Enforcement Officer Rodriguez advised the Board that the property remained noncompliant and requested an Order of Compliance requiring corrective action by August 23, 2025, or the imposition of a $100.00 per-day-per-violation fine thereafter. Additionally, the City indicated that if the property became vacant and remained non-compliant, it could proceed with abatement by demolition.
At that hearing, the owner’s representative, real estate broker Eric Spivey, informed the Board that contractors had been hired to address the violations and requested additional time to bring the property into compliance. Following the discussion, the Code Enforcement Board unanimously found the property in violation as of April 23, 2025, ordered compliance by August 23, 2025, imposed daily fines for continued noncompliance, and authorized the City to abate the property and assess the associated costs if it became vacant.
The property was subsequently brought back before the Code Enforcement Board on March 19, 2026. During that hearing, Code Enforcement Officer Loeffler advised the Board that the property remained non-compliant and continued to be an unsafe structure, with junk and debris littering the site. The Code Board and Staff are requesting authorization from the Commission to demolish the structure due to ongoing unsafe conditions and the property owner's failure to achieve compliance.
Following presentation of the case, the Code Enforcement Board unanimously approved a motion finding the property located at 611 N. Lakewood Avenue, Ocoee, Florida, to be in violation and authorizing the City to abate the property through demolition, with the costs of abatement to be assessed against the property.
Staff is seeking authorization to demolish the structure at 611 N. Lakewood Avenue, Ocoee, FL 34761. The cost of the demolition and the asbestos survey is expected to be less than $20,000. The property has remained in substantial non-compliance despite prior orders, extensions, and opportunities provided to the owner to correct the violations. The continued existence of the unsafe structure and associated debris presents an ongoing threat to the health, safety, and welfare of the surrounding community.
title: Approval of Demolition of 611 N. Lakewood Ave. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The 2017 Downtown Master Plan identified the lack of central sewer as a major barrier to redevelopment, and state-led Wekiva Basin studies identified septic tanks as a major contributor to nutrient loading in Starke Lake. To support downtown redevelopment and work towards meeting mandated state nutrient reduction requirements, the City has completed multiple central sewer projects downtown over the past several years.
In 2025, thirty‑nine properties using 41 septic tanks were found to have sewer service available but not yet connected to central sewer. A recently awarded Florida Springs Grant covers 100% of the on‑property construction costs needed to connect to sewer but does not fund the City’s one‑time sewer capital fee. To provide flexibility in paying this fee, the Commission approved three options on April 7, 2026:
Standard cash payment at time of connection
Interest free 24-month payment on the utility bill (statutorily required)
A 10-year non-ad valorem assessment under the City’s home rule authority and Section 197.3632, F.S.
The sewer capital fee is calculated based on the Equivalent Residential Unit (ERU) methodology as established in Chapter 173 City Code. The City Commission approved the sewer capital fee of $7,811/ERU. Document recording fees for financing totals $120. Two properties have already connected to the City’s sewer system. Fourteen property owners have chosen to pay the sewer capital fee using the one‑time payment option. Four property owners have chosen to use the interest‑free 24‑month payment plan on their utility bills.
The remaining nineteen properties will finance their capital fees through the 10‑year non‑ad valorem assessment at 3% interest.
title: Approval of Septic-To-Sewer Initial Assessment Resolution. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
On April 7, 2026, the City Commission approved continuing the City's hybrid model, with a Code Enforcement Board hearing code violations involving detached single-family residential properties and a Special Magistrate hearing all other cases. The City Commission also stated that they wanted to re-evaluate the Code Enforcement Board after 90 days. The 90-day evaluation was completed on July 7, 2026. Within this 90-day evaluation period, the board has met the quorum requirement for all meetings and imposed the recommended fines in all cases. As a result of the previous Code Board Attorney's retirement, a Code Board Attorney has been retained to provide legal guidance to the Code Board during hearings. There is still one vacancy on the Code Enforcement Board, and both alternate positions are currently vacant.
The proposed ordinance update states that, in the event of a conflict of interest or when the Special Magistrate is unavailable due to illness, disability, or death, the City Manager or his designee may appoint a Special Magistrate pro tem to perform the duties of a Magistrate. The proposed ordinance retains the City’s hybrid model while expressly authorizing the City Manager to assign cases to the Special Magistrate if the Board cannot achieve a quorum or the City Commission cannot promptly fill a vacancy on the seven-member board as required by State law.
The City Commission also asked staff to present updated fines for code violations. The proposed Ordinance increases: 1) potential fines from $250 per day per violation to $500 per day per violation, 2) for repeat violators, the proposed fines could range from $1,000 per day/ per violation to $5,000 per day/ per violation, and $15,000 per day/ per violation (single and repeat violations, and violations causing irreparable harm), as allowed by the Florida Statutes for municipalities with at least 50,000 residents.
The proposed ordinance authorizes the Magistrate to hear all cases recommended by the Code Board for foreclosure. The Special Magistrate shall review and consider the application for reduction or release of lien, provide the violator with an opportunity to address the Special Magistrate regarding the application for reduction or release of lien, and take the testimony of other interested parties. The Special Magistrate shall render a written recommendation to the City Commission based on findings of fact and law. The proposed Ordinance establishes a formal procedure for lien reduction/elimination, providing for the Special Magistrate to make a recommendation to the City Commission, while retaining the City Manager’s right to compromise and settle code liens. The proposed Ordinance also establishes a Code Enforcement Recovery Fund.
This fund will be a dedicated financial pool created to support the administration and operation of local code enforcement activities. It will be funded by revenues generated from fines, civil penalties, nuisance abatement recovery monies, and other costs or reimbursements collected through enforcement actions.

description:
The first reading of the ordinance was held on July 7, 2026.
The Charter Amendments
On March 11, 2024, the City of Ocoee voters approved amendments to Sections C-10 and C-11 of the City Charter. C-10 of the Charter now reads, “The City Commission shall be the judge of the qualifications and eligibility of candidates for the City Commission, the election and qualifications of its members, and the grounds for forfeiture of their office under this Charter.” C-10 further authorizes the City Commission “to censure, subpoena witnesses, administer oaths, require the production of evidence, and establish procedural rules for implementing this section and ensuring due process, including reasonable notice to affected parties.”
The proposed Ordinance would “establish procedural rules for implementing this section” consistent with due process.
Section C-10 works hand-in-hand with Section C-11 of the Charter, which establishes a one-year residency requirement for eligibility to run as a candidate for mayor or city commissioner and further requires candidates to “furnish such proof of meeting the one (1) year residency requirement as may be prescribed by ordinance” and “consent to a background check to verify the candidate’s qualifications to hold office.” C-11 further states, “No candidate shall be barred from running for office without notice, a hearing, and clear and convincing evidence that the candidate is not qualified to hold office.”
The City Clerk’s Limited Role
When a candidate submits qualifying papers to the City Clerk, the Clerk’s role as filing officer is ministerial in nature. She “may not determine whether the contents of the qualifying papers are accurate.” Mayfield v. Secretary of State, 402 So. 3d 1002, 1006 (Fla. 2025). Her ministerial function is “limited to assessing whether the required items have been properly and timely filed and whether each item is facially complete.” Id. Under the Section C-10 of the City Charter, the City Commission, not the Clerk, is the “judge of the qualifications and eligibility of candidates….”
Procedures for Candidate Challenges
Challenges to candidates should ordinarily be the exception and not the rule. Accordingly, the proposed Ordinance contemplates that the City Commission would approve of the slate of candidates on the Consent Agenda. To challenge a candidate's candidacy requires the City Commission to remove the candidate from the Consent Agenda under the Commission’s customary Rules and Procedures.
The City Commission would then “determine, based on reasonable cause, whether a quasi-judicial evidentiary hearing is necessary or appropriate to be scheduled to be able to make the determination as to such candidate, or to restore the candidate to the list of candidates on the consent agenda.” Reasonable cause could include the failure to satisfy the 1-year residency requirement, the failure to timely submit complete qualifying papers, conviction of a felony without the restoration of civil rights, or “any other disqualifying condition identified in the City Charter, City Code, Florida Statutes, or the Florida Constitution.”
As stated in the proposed Ordinance, “Upon a majority vote finding reasonable cause, an evidentiary hearing shall be scheduled before the City Commission. Otherwise, the candidate’s name shall be deemed restored to the list of candidates on the consent agenda and, upon approval of the consent agenda, shall appear on the ballot at the next municipal election.”
The City shall set the evidentiary hearing “under the procedures for emergency hearings or within such time as the candidate may request to prepare a defense, but no later than the next regularly scheduled city commission meeting or 30 days, whichever is later or within such time required to meet Orange County Supervisor of Elections deadlines.”
To enable the City Clerk to meet the deadline for preparing the Commission’s Agenda Packet while allowing some flexibility, “Any evidence to be presented to the City Commission shall be provided to the City Clerk at least three days before the hearing; provided, however, the Mayor shall have the authority to waive this requirement subject to being overruled by the City Commission.”
At the hearing, the candidate has the initial burden to establish that the qualifications and eligibility requirements are met. However, as stated in Section C-11, “A City Commission determination that a candidate does not meet the requirements to run for office must be based on clear and convincing evidence.” Florida law generally requires the “clear and convincing evidence standard” because a candidate who timely submits qualifying paperwork “has a clear legal right to appear on the…ballot.” Mayfield v. Secretary of State, 402 So. 3d 1002, 1006 (2025). It follows that clear and convincing evidence must prove otherwise.
An aggrieved party may appeal to the Circuit Court via a Petition for Writ of Certiorari based on the record before the City Commission. On first-tier certiorari review, the Circuit Court would ascertain whether the City afforded procedural due process, departed from the essential requirements of law, and whether Commission based its decision on “substantial competent evidence.” The Circuit Court is prohibited from re-weighing evidence.
The foregoing procedures would also apply to a forfeiture-of-office proceeding.
The City’s procedures are “in addition to any judicial process and remedies under the law and are not intended to limit the right of any person to seek an immediate hearing under section 102.168, Florida Statutes, or as otherwise authorized by the Florida Statutes, before or after any person assumes elective office.” This language is intended to avoid to possibility of having the Ordinance stricken as inconsistent with any rights under State law.

description:
The First Reading of the Ordinance was read at the July 7, 2026, City Commission meeting.
Senate Bill (SB) 954 was signed into law by the Governor with an effective date of July 1, 2025. The purpose of SB 954 was to require local governments to adopt an ordinance to formalize and streamline the process for applicants seeking reasonable accommodations under land use regulations for certified recovery residences. The proposed text amendment to the City's Land Development Code (LDC) would create section 4-13 to include language required by SB 954 regarding certified recovery residences. Specifically, this text amendment to the LDC would establish an application process with the City's Planning division, establish processing timelines, establish review criteria, and establish the process for the revocation and reinstatement of accommodations granted under this section of the Code. City staff is currently updating the City's Land Development Code. This text amendment would have been included in that substantial update to the City's LDC; however, SB 180 prevents any substantial updates to the City's LDC at this time. The language in SB 954 requires the City to update the LDC to include specific provisions regarding certified recovery residences.
Recovery residences are defined in Florida Statute as "...a residential dwelling unit, the community housing component of a licensed day or night treatment facility with community housing, or other form of group housing, which is offered or advertised through any means, including oral, written, electronic, or printed means, by any person or entity as a residence that provides a peer-supported, alcohol-free, and drug-free living environment."
Certified recovery residences are licensed through the Florida Department of Children and Families. According to the Florida Association of Recovery Residences (FARR), there are currently no Certified Recovery Residences within the City of Ocoee. Under the existing City of Ocoee Code, an applicant seeking to establish a certified recovery residence within the City would need to apply for and receive a Local Business Tax receipt. Further review and permitting by the City's Building Division and Fire Department may be required, depending on any proposed alterations to the building where the certified recovery residence is proposed to be located.

description:
The Ocoee Fire Department maintains a standardized uniform program to ensure professional appearance, employee safety, consistency, and compliance with departmental standards. The department requires a reliable vendor capable of providing uniform garments, alterations, embroidery services, insignia application, sizing, fitting, replacement garments, and ongoing support for all department personnel.
North America Fire Equipment Company (NAFECO), has served as the department’s uniform vendor and maintains an established relationship with the City for uniform ordering, sizing, embroidery, alterations, warranty support, and replacement services. NAFECO also maintains a local facility in Orlando, providing responsive customer service, product support, and expedited delivery for the department’s uniform needs.
SINGLE SOURCE JUSTIFICATION:
The Department has standardized its uniform program through NAFECO and has established operational processes associated with uniform procurement, sizing, ordering, alterations, embroidery, insignia application, and replacement services.
NAFECO is uniquely positioned to provide continuity of service because they:
• Maintain employee sizing records and ordering history.
• Provide department-approved uniform configurations and specifications.
• Coordinate embroidery, insignia, patches, rank insignia, and custom department markings.
• Provide warranty support and replacement services.
• Maintain local inventory access and regional support.
• Ensure consistency of appearance across all department personnel.
Changing vendors would require re-establishing sizing records, uniform specifications, embroidery standards, and inventory management processes, resulting in additional administrative costs, operational inefficiencies, and potential inconsistencies within the department’s uniform program.
In lieu of negotiating for a separate contract, the department would like permission to piggyback off of Lake County’s established contract.
LAKE COUNTY CONTRACT UTILIZATION JUSTIFICATION:
Lake County competitively solicited and awarded Contract No. 22-730I, Fire Equipment, Supplies, and Services, to NAFECO. The contract currently remains in effect through July 31, 2027. The City's Purchasing Ordinance permits the utilization of competitively awarded contracts from other governmental agencies when determined to be in the City's best interest.
To ensure continuity of service, staff is also requesting authorization to utilize any replacement, renewal, extension, or successor contracts awarded by Lake County to NAFECO for substantially similar uniforms, uniform-related products, and services, provided such contracts are competitively procured and determined by the City to be in the best interest of the municipality.
Staff recommends approving NAFECO as a single source vendor for Fire Department uniforms as budgeted each fiscal year, and utilizing the Lake County contract as a piggyback procurement vehicle to streamline purchasing, eliminate the need for a separate competitive solicitation, and secure favorable pricing that has already been competitively established.
title: Approval of Single Source Vendor and Piggyback Contract Utilization with North America Fire Equipment Company (NAFECO) for Fire Department Uniforms. (Deputy Fire Chief Van Camp)

description:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) administers the Resilient Florida Program to assist local governments in analyzing flood and climate-related risks and hazards, and in implementing projects that improve community resilience and mitigation capacity. To qualify for future implementation grant funding, a local government must first complete a Vulnerability Assessment that meets the requirements of Section 380.093, Florida Statutes.
The City of Ocoee applied for and received a Resilient Florida Vulnerability Assessment Planning Grant to complete this work. The Vulnerability Assessment will evaluate the City’s critical assets, infrastructure, and service areas under various flood and climate-related scenarios, using state standardized data and methodologies. Completion of this assessment is necessary to identify vulnerabilities, prioritize adaptation strategies, and comply with state resilience requirements. The cost for the Vulnerability Assessment is $177,000 and FDEP awarded 100% of the cost ($177,000) to complete the assessment.
Once the Vulnerability Assessment is completed and accepted by FDEP, the City will be eligible to apply for future Resilient Florida Implementation Grants. These grants can provide significant funding to design and construct projects that address the vulnerabilities identified in the assessment.

FIRST READING OF ORDINANCE

description:
The Charter Amendments
On March 11, 2024, the City of Ocoee voters approved amendments to Sections C-10 and C-11 of the City Charter. C-10 of the Charter now reads, “The City Commission shall be the judge of the qualifications and eligibility of candidates for the City Commission, the election and qualifications of its members, and the grounds for forfeiture of their office under this Charter.” C-10 further authorizes the City Commission “to censure, subpoena witnesses, administer oaths, require the production of evidence, and establish procedural rules for implementing this section and ensuring due process, including reasonable notice to affected parties.”
The proposed Ordinance would “establish procedural rules for implementing this section” consistent with due process.
Section C-10 works hand-in-hand with Section C-11 of the Charter, which establishes a one-year residency requirement for eligibility to run as a candidate for mayor or city commissioner and further requires candidates to “furnish such proof of meeting the one (1) year residency requirement as may be prescribed by ordinance” and “consent to a background check to verify the candidate’s qualifications to hold office.” C-11 further states, “No candidate shall be barred from running for office without notice, a hearing, and clear and convincing evidence that the candidate is not qualified to hold office.”
The City Clerk’s Limited Role
When a candidate submits qualifying papers to the City Clerk, the Clerk’s role as filing officer is ministerial in nature. She “may not determine whether the contents of the qualifying papers are accurate.” Mayfield v. Secretary of State, 402 So. 3d 1002, 1006 (Fla. 2025). Her ministerial function is “limited to assessing whether the required items have been properly and timely filed and whether each item is facially complete.” Id. Under the Section C-10 of the City Charter, the City Commission, not the Clerk, is the “judge of the qualifications and eligibility of candidates….”
Procedures for Candidate Challenges
Challenges to candidates should ordinarily be the exception and not the rule. Accordingly, the proposed Ordinance contemplates that the City Commission would approve of the slate of candidates on the Consent Agenda. To challenge a candidate's candidacy requires the City Commission to remove the candidate from the Consent Agenda under the Commission’s customary Rules and Procedures.
The City Commission would then “determine, based on reasonable cause, whether a quasi-judicial evidentiary hearing is necessary or appropriate to be scheduled to be able to make the determination as to such candidate, or to restore the candidate to the list of candidates on the consent agenda.” Reasonable cause could include the failure to satisfy the 1-year residency requirement, the failure to timely submit complete qualifying papers, conviction of a felony without the restoration of civil rights, or “any other disqualifying condition identified in the City Charter, City Code, Florida Statutes, or the Florida Constitution.”
As stated in the proposed Ordinance, “Upon a majority vote finding reasonable cause, an evidentiary hearing shall be scheduled before the City Commission. Otherwise, the candidate’s name shall be deemed restored to the list of candidates on the consent agenda and, upon approval of the consent agenda, shall appear on the ballot at the next municipal election.”
The City shall set the evidentiary hearing “under the procedures for emergency hearings or within such time as the candidate may request to prepare a defense, but no later than the next regularly scheduled city commission meeting or 30 days, whichever is later or within such time required to meet Orange County Supervisor of Elections deadlines.”
To enable the City Clerk to meet the deadline for preparing the Commission’s Agenda Packet while allowing some flexibility, “Any evidence to be presented to the City Commission shall be provided to the City Clerk at least three days before the hearing; provided, however, the Mayor shall have the authority to waive this requirement subject to being overruled by the City Commission.”
At the hearing, the candidate has the initial burden to establish that the qualifications and eligibility requirements are met. However, as stated in Section C-11, “A City Commission determination that a candidate does not meet the requirements to run for office must be based on clear and convincing evidence.” Florida law generally requires the “clear and convincing evidence standard” because a candidate who timely submits qualifying paperwork “has a clear legal right to appear on the…ballot.” Mayfield v. Secretary of State, 402 So. 3d 1002, 1006 (2025). It follows that clear and convincing evidence must prove otherwise.
An aggrieved party may appeal to the Circuit Court via a Petition for Writ of Certiorari based on the record before the City Commission. On first-tier certiorari review, the Circuit Court would ascertain whether the City afforded procedural due process, departed from the essential requirements of law, and whether Commission based its decision on “substantial competent evidence.” The Circuit Court is prohibited from re-weighing evidence.
The foregoing procedures would also apply to a forfeiture-of-office proceeding.
The City’s procedures are “in addition to any judicial process and remedies under the law and are not intended to limit the right of any person to seek an immediate hearing under section 102.168, Florida Statutes, or as otherwise authorized by the Florida Statutes, before or after any person assumes elective office.” This language is intended to avoid to possibility of having the Ordinance stricken as inconsistent with any rights under State law.
title: First Reading of an Ordinance Establishing Procedural Rules to Challenge Candidates to the City Commission under Section C-10 and Section C-11 of the City Charter. (City Attorney Geller)

description:
Senate Bill (SB) 954 was signed into law by the Governor with an effective date of July 1, 2025. The purpose of SB 954 was to require local governments to adopt an ordinance to formalize and streamline the process for applicants seeking reasonable accommodations under land use regulations for certified recovery residences. The proposed text amendment to the City's Land Development Code (LDC) would create section 4-13 to include language required by SB 954 regarding certified recovery residences. Specifically, this text amendment to the LDC would establish an application process with the City's Planning division, establish processing timelines, establish review criteria, and establish the process for the revocation and reinstatement of accommodations granted under this section of the Code. City staff is currently updating the City's Land Development Code. This text amendment would have been included in that substantial update to the City's LDC; however, SB 180 prevents any substantial updates to the City's LDC at this time. The language in SB 954 requires the City to update the LDC to include specific provisions regarding certified recovery residences.
Recovery residences are defined in Florida Statute as "...a residential dwelling unit, the community housing component of a licensed day or night treatment facility with community housing, or other form of group housing, which is offered or advertised through any means, including oral, written, electronic, or printed means, by any person or entity as a residence that provides a peer-supported, alcohol-free, and drug-free living environment."
Certified recovery residences are licensed through the Florida Department of Children and Families. According to the Florida Association of Recovery Residences (FARR), there are currently no Certified Recovery Residences within the City of Ocoee. Under the existing City of Ocoee Code, an applicant seeking to establish a certified recovery residence within the City would need to apply for and receive a Local Business Tax receipt. Further review and permitting by the City's Building Division and Fire Department may be required, depending on any proposed alterations to the building where the certified recovery residence is proposed to be located.
title: First Reading of Ordinance for the Text Amendment to the Land Development Code, Creating Section 4-13 to Establish Regulations and Procedures for Certified Recovery Residences. (Community Development Administrator McFarlane)

attachments.name: Ordinance Regulating Electric Bikes Micromobility Devices

description:
The first reading of the ordinance was held on June 16, 2026.
Micromobility vehicles (such as e-bikes, e-scooters, and motorized skateboards) have rapidly risen in popularity across Central Florida. Under current Florida law, F.S. 316.20655, which regulates e-bikes, no driver's license, registration, or insurance is required to ride a compliant e-bike. One can be operated wherever regular bikes go: roads, shoulders, bike lanes, and multi-use paths. Riders and passengers under 16 must wear a properly fitted helmet; it's optional but recommended for adults. Cities and counties can restrict e-bikes on sidewalks, beaches, dunes, and specific bike paths or trail networks.
The proposed micromobility ordinance will enable the City of Ocoee to establish a clear legal framework for managing the rapid rise in micromobility devices on its public streets and walkways. By passing local regulations, the city can cap riding speeds, mandate safety gear, address growing safety hazards, clarify enforcement laws, manage public spaces effectively, and reduce severe crashes and trauma-related injuries. Furthermore, enacting this ordinance aligns Ocoee with neighboring communities by empowering local law enforcement to regulate micromobility vehicles and enhance public safety.
Under current statewide law, F.S. 316.20655, which regulates e-bikes, no driver's license, registration, or insurance is required to ride or operate a compliant e-bike. These micromobility devices can generally be operated wherever regular bikes are allowed: on roadways, shoulders, bike lanes, and multi-use paths.Riders and passengers under 16 must wear a properly fitted helmet; it's optional, but highly recommended for adults.
section: SECOND READING OF ORDINANCE – PUBLIC HEARING
title: Second Reading of an Ordinance Regulating Micromobility Vehicles. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The first reading of the ordinance was held on June 16, 2026.
The 2017 Downtown Master Plan identified the lack of central sewer as a major barrier to redevelopment and the Wekiva Basin studies identified septic tanks as a major contributor to nutrient loading in Starke Lake. To meet mandated state nutrient reduction requirements and support downtown redevelopment, the City has extended sewer service through multiple projects over the past several years.Currently, thirty-nine downtown customers have sewer available but are not yet connected. State law (Section 381.00655(1)(a), Florida Statutes) and the 2016 Wastewater Revenue Bond, requires parcels with available sewer to connect. The recently awarded Florida Department of Environmental Protection, Florida Springs Grant, covers the on-property construction work needed to connect to sewer, but it does not cover the City’s required one-time sewer capital fee ($8,030.00).
To provide flexibility in paying this fee, the Commission approved three payment options on April 7, 2026:
1. Standard cash payment at time of connection
2. Interest free 24 month payment on the utility bill (statutorily required)
3. A 10-year non-ad valorem assessment under the City’s home rule authority and Section 197.3632, F.S.
Option 3 requires adoption of new Code provisions establishing the procedures for the special assessment. Although special assessments have historically been created on a project-by-project basis, the proposed ordinance creates a comprehensive and consistent framework for the imposition, administration, and collection of special assessments for services and capital improvements. This ordinance supports the sewer assessment and provides funding flexibility for future infrastructure projects, ensuring fair and reasonable cost apportionment to benefited properties.

The subject property is in Commission District 1 and is located at 10738 Clarcona Ocoee Road. It is zoned PUD-COMM (Planned Unit Development Commercial) and is within the Ocoee Village Center PUD. Although the property is within the Ocoee Village Center PUD, per the approved revised PUD/Land Use Plan for Ocoee Village Center, there is no waiver within the PUD pertaining to the City's Land Development Code Article VIII, "Signs." Due to this, the project to subject to the signage standards as set forth in the Land Development Code.
Per Article VIII, Section 8-6A of the Land Development Code, for a building up to 50,000 square feet, the maximum allowed sign area is 100 square feet, and the sign height is four (4) feet. On corner lot buildings, an additional one (1) square foot per lineal foot of building frontage facing the secondary street may be permitted at a maximum sign area of 100 square feet and a maximum height of four (4) feet. Article VIII, Section 8-6D. further establishes that the sign located under a canopy or awning shall not exceed six (6) inches in height or extend more than sixty (60) percent of the width of the awning or canopy. Although the code section only describes signs located under the canopy or awning, the requirement will also apply to signs installed on the canopy, as this section aligns most closely with that type of sign. This sign type, along with other signage, will be addressed with the Land Development Code (LDC) update.
The subject property is the recently approved Ocoee Village Center New Grocery and Fuel Station Large-Scale Final Site Plan. The applicant, Walmart Neighborhood Market, represented by Susie Stone, is requesting variances to Article VIII, Section 8-6A. and 8-6D. of the Land Development Code. Specifically, the applicant is requesting the following variances:
A sign height of 10'-4" in lieu of the maximum three (3) feet for the north sign elevation, representing a 158% increase, and
A sign height of 7'-9" in lieu of the maximum three (3) feet for the east sign elevation, representing a 94% increase, and
A sign area of 459.7 square feet in lieu of the maximum 100 square feet for the north sign elevation, representing a 360% increase, and
A sign area of 159.8 square feet in lieu of the maximum 100 square feet for the east sign elevation, representing a 60% increase.
A sign height of 1'-6" in lieu of the maximum six (6) inches for the north canopy, representing a 200% increase, and
A sign width of 22' in lieu of the maximum 21' for the north canopy, representing a 5% increase.
According to Article IV, Section 4- 9A, approval of a variance requires that the applicant demonstrate compliance with four (4) criteria, as follows:That special conditions and circumstances exist which are peculiar to the land, structures, or required subdivision improvements involved and which are not applicable to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements;
That a literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties with similar conditions;
That the special conditions and circumstances do not result from the actions of the applicant; and
That the granting of the variance requested will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by these regulations to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements under similar conditions.
Applicant's Response: The applicant's justification is as follows:
The request for a variance in the allowable square footage of wall signage is intended to provide the best possible customer experience. The proposed wall signage serves as a wayfinding tool to help customers know which services are offered and where.
Staff Analysis: Staff finds that the justification provided by the applicant does not support or sufficiently demonstrate compliance with the four (4) evaluation criteria. Staff's analysis is summarized below:
Criteria 1: Special Circumstances and Conditions: There are no special conditions or circumstances that exist that are peculiar to the land. There are various non-residential buildings in the city with previously permitted signage that were designed to comply with the city code sections. Staff identifies no special conditions or circumstances of the building that sufficiently justify the variance requests.
Criteria 2: Literal Interpretation of the Code: The literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would not deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties of similar conditions. Due to the proposed building's size of approximately 48,583 square feet, the building is permitted a wall sign area of 100 square feet and a height of four (4) feet. Additionally, because the property is a corner lot with frontage along Clarcona Ocoee Road and N Lakewood Avenue, the building is allotted an additional sign on the east elevation, with a sign area of 100 square feet and a height of four (4) feet. For the canopy sign, there is also no justification to increase the sign's height and width, as a 6 (six) inch tall, 21-foot-wide sign provides ample copy area to be legibly read by motorists. Staff finds that the literal interpretation of the code sections does not deprive the applicant but rather provides ample signage as allowed for both elevations.
Criteria 3: Actions of the Applicant: The circumstances of the variance request result from the applicant's request to increase the copy area and height of the various signs located on the north and east elevations of the building. There is no valid justification to rationalize the need for the significant increase in copy area, height, and width of the various signs, as the size of the letters and logos can be reduced.
Criteria 4: Conference of Special Privilege: Granting the requested variances would confer a special privilege to the applicant that is denied by these regulations to other non-residential properties under similar conditions, as other non-residential buildings are subject to the maximum allowed height and copy area of wall signage, as well as height and width of canopy signs. If the signs are constructed to meet the standards set in the respective code sections, the building will have a 100 square foot wall sign on the north and west elevation of the building and a six (6) inch tall, 21-foot wide canopy sign on the north elevation. Staff believes that the signs, with their copy, area, height, and design, are in conformance with the sign code sections and will provide sufficient signage for the building.
Staff does not support the requested variances, as there is insufficient code-based justification.

description:
V3 Capital Group, representing the owner of parcel ID 09-22-28-0000-00-060, has submitted a formal request for an access easement across City-owned property (parcel ID 09-22-28-0000-00-056). The subject properties are located in Commission District 4, north of A D Mims Road and east of Clarke Road. The attached image illustrates the location of the Silvestri property, the City property, and the approximate placement of the proposed easement (indicated by a red circle).
On April 22, 2025, V3 Capital Group, LLC, acting on behalf of Silvestri Investments of Florida, Inc., and City staff held a formal pre-application meeting to discuss a proposed 7-Eleven convenience store with a gas station and car wash on a 2-acre parcel located within the Prairie Lake PUD (Parcel ID 09-22-28-0000-00-060).
On July 10, 2025, the City held a community informational meeting regarding the proposed 7-Eleven with residents and V3 Capital Group LLC in attendance.
On July 16, 2025, City staff provided V3 Capital Group with a letter clarifying that the 2-acre parcel has a right to direct access to Clarke Road. This letter was provided after consulting with the City Attorney and reviewing the Agreement of Purchase and Sale between the City and Silvestri Investments of Florida. A copy of the letter and Agreement of Purchase and Sale has been included with this report.
Section 2 of the Purchase and Sale Agreement states: "...the parties [Silvestri and the City] have agreed (i) that the Retained Land will have frontage along and direct access to Clarke Road."
Since the initial submittal of the small-scale site plan application for the proposed 7-Eleven on November 11, 2025, City staff and representatives from V3 Capital Group have engaged in ongoing coordination regarding the facilitation of access to Clarke Road for the subject property. With the majority of staff comments on the site plan addressed, City staff are now presenting the proposed access easement for consideration and approval by the City Commission. The alignment of the easement is designed to provide clear and safe access for both the City-owned property and the proposed 7-Eleven development to Clarke Road. Additionally, the developer has indicated that installation of a traffic signal at the intersection of Clarke Road and Ocoee Vista Parkway would be beneficial to the project. City staff and the developer are collaboratively developing a mutually agreeable plan regarding the timing and construction of the traffic signal in conjunction with the proposed 7-Eleven development.

description:
Procurement staff continually evaluates industry best practices and emerging technologies to improve efficiency and compliance in public procurement. Following a comprehensive review of available solutions, staff recommends contracting with Vertosoft LLC for the OpenGov SaaS e-Procurement Platform. The proposed solution provides a fully integrated procurement process through its intake, solicitation, vendor management, evaluation, and contract management modules.
The OpenGov platform will enable staff to manage departmental procurement requests, develop and advertise solicitations, engage suppliers and departments, conduct evaluations and awards, and administer contracts throughout their lifecycle. Contract management features include change orders, renewals, electronic signatures, and insurance tracking. Implementation is scheduled for August 2026, allowing for a seamless transition from the City’s current solicitation platform before its expiration, with no disruption to bid solicitation activities.
OpenGov provides a no-cost platform for vendors, reducing barriers to participation and benefiting suppliers already familiar with the system through its use by numerous local governments, including Orange County, Orlando, Apopka, Winter Park, Clermont, Groveland, Leesburg, St. Cloud, Tampa, Gainesville, Volusia County, and Daytona Beach.
The City’s current agreement with Euna/Bonfire for solicitation services expires on September 30, 2026. After being notified of upcoming changes to the Bonfire platform, and in response to increasing solicitation and contract management demands, staff conducted a thorough evaluation of both the Euna/Bonfire and Vertosoft/OpenGov e-Procurement platforms. Based on functionality, ease of use, and overall value, staff recommends the Vertosoft/OpenGov solution.
Under Vertosoft LLC’s Sourcewell cooperative purchasing contract, OpenGov’s proposal includes a three-year contract that is prorated for FY 2026 at a cost of $17,231.04 and a FY 2027 first-year cost of $33,270.17, which includes professional implementation and training services. Following full implementation, annual software subscription costs decrease to $20,018.63 in FY 2028 and $21,019.57 in FY 2029. As reflected in the attached proposals, OpenGov’s pricing is lower than Euna/Bonfire’s proposed costs while providing a comprehensive e-Procurement solution for the city.
title: Approval to Piggyback Sourcewell's Contract with Vertosoft LLC. for the OpenGov E-Procurement Software as a Service (SaaS) Platform (Procurement Manager Tolbert)

description: Micromobility vehicles (such as e-bikes, e-scooters, and motorized skateboards) have rapidly risen in popularity across Central Florida. A micromobility ordinance will enable the City of Ocoee to establish a clear legal framework to manage the rapid rise of micromobility devices on its public streets and walkways. By passing local regulations, the city can cap riding speeds, mandate safety gear, address growing safety hazards, clarify enforcement laws, manage public spaces effectively, and reduce the number of severe crashes and trauma related injuries. Furthermore, enacting this ordinance aligns Ocoee with neighboring communities by empowering local law enforcement to regulate micromobility vehicles and enhance public safety.
title: First Reading of an Ordinance Regulating Micromobility Vehicles. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The 2017 Downtown Master Plan identified the lack of central sewer as a major barrier to redevelopment and the Wekiva Basin studies identified septic tanks as a major contributor to nutrient loading in Starke Lake. To meet mandated state nutrient reduction requirements and support downtown redevelopment, the City has extended sewer service through multiple projects over the past several years.
Currently, thirty-nine downtown customers have sewer available but are not yet connected. State law (Section 381.00655(1)(a), Florida Statutes) and the 2016 Wastewater Revenue Bond, requires parcels with available sewer to connect. The recently awarded Florida Department of Environmental Protection, Florida Springs Grant, covers the on-property construction work needed to connect to sewer, but it does not cover the City’s required one-time sewer capital fee ($8,030.00).
To provide flexibility in paying this fee, the Commission approved three payment options on April 7, 2026:
1. Standard cash payment at time of connection
2. Interest free 24 month payment on the utility bill (statutorily required)
3. A 10-year non-ad valorem assessment under the City’s home rule authority and Section 197.3632, F.S.
Option 3 requires adoption of new Code provisions establishing the procedures for the special assessment. Although special assessments have historically been created on a project-by-project basis, the proposed ordinance creates a comprehensive and consistent framework for the imposition, administration, and collection of special assessments for services and capital improvements. This ordinance supports the sewer assessment and provides funding flexibility for future infrastructure projects, ensuring fair and reasonable cost apportionment to benefited properties.
title: First Reading of An Ordinance To Create Chapter 105 Master Capital Project and Service Assessment. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The City entered into a seven (7) year Solid Waste Franchise contract that includes both commercial and residential services in 2020 with Waste Connections. The current Franchise period expires on April 6, 2027. The Franchise includes an optional three (3) year extension and requires Waste Connections to notify the City by July 1, 2026, of their intent to extend the contract. Waste Connections has notified the City they are not willing to extend the contract at the current rates which were established before the pandemic. Waste Connections has offered updated pricing to maintain the current service levels which are in line or below Central Florida market costs. Based on recent rate studies and bids in the immediate region, negotiating with Waste Connections on the offered pricing would avoid the increased costs of a new bid. In addition to determining if the City pursues negotiated or bid pricing, the subject of continuing curbside collection of recycling will need to be addressed.
Public Works Director Krug will present a summary of regional solid waste costs and review the proposed fees offered by Waste Connections. The City's current annual Non-ad-valorem residential fee is $344.42. Maintaining current service levels would require an $18.00 increase to $362.42 annually. Removing curbside recycling would allow the City to maintain the current $344.42 fee with an annual Consumer Price Index increase.

description:
On May 19, 2026, the City Commission was given a presentation on the Fire Service Assessment Fee Program, which was approved for just FY 26 with the option of selecting one of two new methodologies (Historical & Demand-Availability) and staff suggested an initial rate to cover approximately 40% of the Fire Departments Assessable budget. The City Commission voted 4-0 to authorize staff to update the City's Existing Fire Services Special Assessment Program from the Fire Protection Unit methodology to the Demand and Availability methodology and to set June 16, 2026, as the hearing date to adopt the initial assessment resolution.
Since that meeting date, the Florida Legislature has passed sweeping property tax reform legislation, and Florida voters are now scheduled to consider a proposed property tax overhaul this November. If approved, the measure would significantly expand homestead exemptions statewide, increasing the exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. Based on projections provided by the Orange County Property Appraiser’s Office, the City of Ocoee anticipates a reduction in ad valorem tax revenue of approximately $4.15 million in Fiscal Year 2027 as a result of the initial $150,000 homestead exemption. In Fiscal Year 2028, when the exemption increases to $250,000, the projected revenue loss nearly doubles to approximately $8.5 million. In anticipation of these potential revenue reductions, City staff has evaluated available strategies to address the resulting General Fund funding gap while continuing to meet rising public safety costs, with particular attention to maintaining fire protection services.
City staff, in coordination with the City's fire assessment consultant, Anser Advisory, has evaluated multiple funding scenarios under the Demand-Availability Methodology Fire Assessment Program approved by the City Commission on May 19, 2026. Under the current assessment structure, the City may establish a maximum assessable funding level, within which annual assessment rates may be adjusted through the annual TRIM notice process.Staff recommends that the City Commission formally adopt a maximum funding level equal to 70% of the five-year average assessable Fire Budget, which would authorize a maximum net revenue collection of approximately $13,139,397. Establishing this maximum funding level now will provide the Commission with flexibility to incrementally adjust annual assessment rates in response to the phased implementation of the proposed homestead exemption while avoiding the need to undertake a full assessment rate adoption process each fiscal year.
Proposed Fiscal Year 2027 Funding Level
In FY 2027, only the initial $150,000 additional homestead exemption is anticipated to be in effect, resulting in a projected ad valorem revenue reduction of approximately $4,151,856. Staff intends to recommend at the August 18, 2026, Rate Resolution Adoption public hearing that the City Commission adopt a FY 2027 Fire Service Assessment rate based on a 45% funding level. This funding level would generate approximately $4,561,637 in additional net assessment revenue, effectively offsetting the projected first-year revenue loss.At this funding level, the residential assessment rate would be approximately $383.90 per dwelling unit, representing a measured and proportional adjustment for Ocoee residents and businesses while helping maintain current fire protection service levels.
Proposed Fiscal Year 2028 Funding Level
In FY 2028, the homestead exemption is anticipated to increase to $250,000, resulting in a projected ad valorem revenue reduction of approximately $8.5 million. At a City Commission meeting in 2027, staff would recommend increasing the Fire Service Assessment rate to the 67% funding level, which is projected to generate approximately $8,989,891 in additional net assessment revenue—sufficient to offset the increased revenue shortfall. At this funding level, total net assessment revenue would be approximately $12,575,005, and the residential assessment rate would be approximately $571.57 per dwelling unit.Because the 67% funding level falls within the previously adopted 70% maximum funding ceiling, the annual assessment rate may be adjusted through the TRIM notice process without requiring a new maximum rate adoption. This approach would provide the City with flexibility to respond efficiently to the ongoing fiscal impacts of the proposed homestead exemption while maintaining a predictable funding mechanism for fire protection services.
For comparison purposes, the current Unincorporated Orange County Fire Rescue Municipal Service Taxing Unit (MSTU) millage rate of 2.84 mills would generate approximately $14,714,082 in revenue if applied to taxable property within the City of Ocoee.
A presentation regarding Fire Department costs, service demands, and available funding mechanisms will be provided to the City Commission.
title: Adoption of the Amended and Restated Initial Assessment Resolution for the FY 26-27 Fire Protection Assessments. (Assistant City Manager Rumer)

description:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) administers the Fire Prevention and Safety (FP&S) Grant Program to support projects that enhance community risk reduction, fire prevention, and public fire and life safety education initiatives. The Ocoee Fire Department is requesting authorization to apply for funding through the FP&S Grant Program for the purchase of an interactive fire safety educational robot known as “Freddie the Fire Truck.”
The proposed educational robot would be utilized as part of the department’s expanding Community Risk Reduction (CRR) and public education initiatives. Freddie the Fire Truck is a fully interactive educational platform capable of moving, speaking, listening, and engaging directly with children and participants during educational programs, school visits, community events, Fire Prevention Week activities, disaster preparedness outreach, and other public safety initiatives.
Through the department’s Community Risk Assessment and Standards of Cover process, the department identified the need for enhanced and more interactive educational tools capable of improving engagement and retention among school-aged children, younger audiences, and special needs populations. Traditional lecture-based educational methods have proven less effective in maintaining engagement among these demographics. The proposed robot would allow the department to deliver fire and life safety education in a more engaging, interactive, and accessible format.
The City of Ocoee contains approximately eleven (11) public schools and numerous daycare and childcare facilities serving thousands of children annually. A significant portion of the student population includes economically disadvantaged students, minority populations, and special needs individuals. The department believes the proposed robot would significantly enhance the effectiveness and reach of the department’s public education programming.
The robot would also be utilized during city events, festivals, open houses, and other outreach opportunities throughout the year. In addition, the equipment would support the department’s ongoing Community Risk Reduction efforts and help further FEMA’s mission of reducing fire-related injuries and deaths through prevention and education.
title: Approval to Apply for the FEMA Fire Prevention and Safety (FP&S) Grant Program for a Fire Safety Educational Robot. (Deputy Fire Chief Van Camp)

description:

Each SCBA system requested as part of the grant will include:
• One (1) SCBA air pack/frame assembly
• Two (2) SCBA cylinders/bottles
• One (1) PASS device
• One (1) regulator assembly
• One (1) heads-up display and integrated electronics package
• Associated straps, harnesses, hoses, and components required for a complete operational SCBA system.
title: Approval to Submit an Application for the FY 2025 Assistance to Firefighters Grant (AFG) Program for Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) Replacement Equipment. (Deputy Fire Chief Van Camp)

description:
The Utilities Department is responsible for the operation and maintenance of approximately 387 miles of potable water, reclaimed water, and sanitary sewer lines throughout the City of Ocoee. When underground utility repairs occur beneath or adjacent to sidewalks, small sections of concrete must be removed to access the infrastructure and replaced once the work is completed.These sidewalk replacements are typically small, intermittent jobs. Due to their size, most large concrete contractors cannot perform the work quickly or cost effectively. To minimize safety concerns and reduce delays in sidewalk restoration, the Utilities Department has utilized Jc & J Contractors, a local concrete firm specializing in small-area concrete repairs.
During the current fiscal year, Jc & J Contractors has completed multiple sidewalk replacements associated with utilities repairs. As a result, cumulative expenditures with this vendor now exceed $50,000. Any additional work will surpass the City Manager’s purchasing authority, requiring City Commission approval to proceed.
