description:
Reserve at Lake Meadow Subdivision is located in Commission District 1 and is made up of 46 lots, the development of detached single-family homes. The parent parcel was addressed at 2149 Lauren Beth Ave. and assigned parcel ID number 04-22-28-0000-00-024. The development site is approximately 1,130 feet south of Lake Meadow Rd., which is 2,720 feet south of the intersection of Lake Meadow Rd./Ingram Rd and Clarcona Ocoee Rd. The developer has completed construction of the infrastructure improvements for the subdivision and has requested a Certificate of Completion. The infrastructure improvements include potable water, sanitary sewer, reclaimed water, utilities, roadways, stormwater collection system, and perimeter wall/fencing. Required installation of street trees and lot trees will occur as each lot is permitted and developed with a single-family residence. All other identified punch list repairs have been completed, and the developer is ready to start the two-year warranty period for the public improvements, excluding trees and landscaping.
As a requirement of the Land Development Code, the developer is required to furnish the City with a Surety to cover any possible damages discovered during the next two years. Should the developer not choose to make those repairs, Park Square Enterprises, LLC, has provided the City with a Letter of Credit in the amount of $297,694.50, which is 10% of the constructed improvements. The attached Maintenance, Materials, and Workmanship Agreement (Form 8 of the Land Development Code) acts as the executable document between the developer and the City. The Surety will be returned to the developer upon completion of the two-year warranty period and following the repair of any damages caused or occurring over those two years.
Additionally, the developer has furnished the City with a separate Surety in the amount of $166,866.84, to cover the construction cost of adding the second lift of asphalt to all the public streets of the subdivision. This arrangement will ensure that the final road surface is not worn or scarred during the construction of the homes. The attached Maintenance, Materials, and Workmanship Agreement for Asphalt acts as the executable document between the developer and the City in the event the developer fails to provide the second lift of asphalt within two years of the issuance of the Certificate of Completion or when 80% of the homes have received Certificates of Occupancy. The Surety will be returned to the developer upon completion of the warranty period and following the repair of any damages caused or occurring over that period.
title: Approval of a Two-Year Warranty Surety and Maintenance, Materials, and Workmanship Agreement for Infrastructure Improvements and Surety and Maintenance, Materials, and Workmanship Agreement for Asphalt for Reserve at Lake Meadow. (Development Engineer Keaton)

description:
The Ocoee Music Festival has consistently showcased national talent over the past two decades, earning a reputation as one of the region's premier music events. Each year, the festival draws acclaimed artists from across the country, offering attendees unforgettable performances spanning various genres. This long-standing tradition of featuring top-tier talent has helped the festival grow in popularity and prestige, making it a highly anticipated event for music lovers both locally and beyond. In addition to its cultural value, the festival has a significant impact on the local economy, bringing in thousands of visitors who support nearby restaurants, hotels, shops, and small businesses, contributing to the community's economic growth and vitality. This year, the festival is part of the already successful series of events specifically planned as part of the City's centennial year.
Despite rising costs in many areas, the festival remains committed to offering cost-friendly entertainment for the community. This year’s event is made possible in part by careful budgeting and strategic partnerships, allowing the city to deliver a high-quality experience without placing additional financial strain on the city or attendees, or reliance on sponsorship. One such partnership is with Cox Media Group. Cox Media Group, one of the largest multimedia companies in the world, is able to bring in entertainers at lower pricing than current national published rates, and they also bring enhanced marketing capabilities. This year's Ocoee Music Festival looks to continue the long tradition of showcasing national talent on November 14th and 15th, and in accordance with the City of Ocoee Purchasing Rules and Regulations, the contract for entertainment with Cox Media Group exceeds the City Manager's approval, requiring approval from the City Commission.
title: Approval of Contract for the 2025 Ocoee Centennial Music Festival Entertainment. (Parks and Leisure Services Director Johnson)

description: The Police Department is requesting to use residual, unexpended, capital funds from this fiscal year's budget to purchase two (2) new unmarked vehicles for the Police Department fleet. This purchase will also provide the opportunity to obtain the vehicles at this year's cost before any future price increase, and thereby reducing the number of vehicles requested in next year's proposed budget. Existing contracts are indicated on each estimate. The vehicles are available for immediate delivery. All upfitting costs are included. The cost of the vehicles, including the upfitting, is $91,791.
title: Approval to Purchase Two (2) Police Vehicles. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description: The Ocoee Police Department is requesting the installation of a screened-in patio at the station to address ongoing concerns related to insects and small animals entering the building. Staff have reported frequent issues with frogs, mosquitoes, and other pests entering the building when exterior doors are opened, creating an uncomfortable and unsanitary work environment. A screened-in enclosure would serve as a barrier to mitigate this problem while also providing a secure, shaded space for officers and staff to hold informal meetings. To support this initiative, the department is requesting a transfer of funds from GL# 317-521-00-6400 (Capital Equipment) in the amount of $6,000.00 to GL #317-521-00-6302 (Capital Improvement) to cover the cost of materials and installation. This improvement is a practical and proactive step toward enhancing workplace conditions and supporting staff wellness.
title: Approval to Transfer Funds for Installation of a Screened Enclosure at the Ocoee Police Department. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description: The Institute of Police Technology is awarding the City of Ocoee Police Department $7,014.71 in grant funding to support Florida's Bicycle and Pedestrian Focused Initiative on Communication and High Visibility Enforcement. These funds aim to use law enforcement to reinforce safe pedestrian, bicyclist, and driver behaviors in priority counties in Florida. The goal of this effort is to reduce traffic crashes resulting in severe and fatal injuries to pedestrians and bicyclists through high-visibility education and enforcement detail. The grant will fund overtime high-visibility education and enforcement operations through May 08, 2026.
title: Approval of Pedestrian and Bicycle Safety High Visibility Enforcement and Support Program. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The Ocoee Police Department has historically donated State Forfeiture Funds to support programs or organizations that partner with the Department in its crime prevention/public safety mission and wishes to continue doing so. The services these organizations provide to the Ocoee Police Department and the community cannot be duplicated within the Department. The Ocoee Police Department recommends donating funds to the following programs: Crimeline ($2,000.00) provides crime-solving to the law enforcement agencies within Central Florida and provides rewards for members of the public.
Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) ($2,000.00), whose mission is to end drunk driving and support victims of these crimes and prevent underage drinking.
Aspire Behavioral Health Care ($2,500.00) (also known as Central Florida Crisis Intervention Team) trains members of law enforcement on how to deal with people in mental health crises.
Children’s Safety Village ($1,000.00) aims to make Central Florida the safest community for children by providing various safety programs, including car seat check-ups, safety workshops, and sports clinics.
These donations comply with Florida State Statute 932.7055, which states that “Such funds may be used only for school resource officers, crime prevention, safe neighborhood, drug abuse education, or drug prevention programs or such other law enforcement purposes as the board of county commissioners or governing body of the municipality deems appropriate.”
title: Approval to Donate State Forfeiture Funds to Organizations Supporting Law Enforcement. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The Ocoee Police Department would like approval to transition from the current handgun (Glock 45 MOS) to the Glock 45 COA handgun. The Glock 45 COA model will have factory-installed red dot optics. By transitioning to these handguns, the officers have a better tactical and operational advantage in low-light conditions and high-stress scenarios. The red dot optic will enhance target acquisition, accuracy, and situational awareness, ultimately improving officer safety and effectiveness. Installing these optics on the current model handgun would require additional mounting plates and the replacement of factory iron sights with suppressor-height versions to ensure co-witnessing (the alignment of iron sights with a red dot sight on a firearm, ensuring consistent aiming). This multistep retrofit process places a significant demand on department resources, especially the armorer, and introduces potential failure points due to the added mounting components. The Glock 45 COA will address these limitations. This handgun comes factory-equipped with a red dot optic (Aimpoint ACRO) and suppressor-height iron sights, eliminating the need for mounting plates and aftermarket sight replacement. This streamlined design ensures greater reliability, durability, and consistency.
The Police Department has obtained two pricing options:
Option #1: Purchase 100 red dot optics and 100 sets of suppressor-height iron sights for installation on the current Glock 45 MOS handguns. This will cost the Ocoee Police Department $37,400.00.
Option #2: Trade in the current 100 Glock 45 MOS handguns and purchase 100 Glock 45 COA model handguns with factory-installed optics and sights, and receive trade-in credit for the existing Glock 45 MOS inventory. This will cost the Ocoee Police Department $39,200.00.
Option #2 delivers significant operational and logistical benefits, such as: Eliminates the need for armorer labor and installation downtime
Reduces potential failure points associated with mounting plates
Improves long-term reliability and equipment standardization
Offers a cleaner transition path with fewer aftermarket modifications
The Police Department would like the City Commission to consider option #2. This option ensures a streamlined, durable, and cost-effective solution for the department’s handgun modernization initiative. The vendor, Lawmen's & Shooters, provided us with a quote of $73,200.00 for the Glock 45 COA model handguns. However, Lawmen's & Shooters Supply has also provided us with a quote that entails trading in the current Glock 45 MOS handguns for $34,000.00, which would bring the price for the purchase of the Glock 45 COA to $39,200.00. The price difference between the two options is $1,800.00.
title: Approval to Upgrade to Glock Model Handguns with Factory-Installed Optics and Sights. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description: On April 19, 2022, the City Commission awarded RFP #22-003 Auditing Services and entered into a continuing-term contract with Purvis Gray & Company LLP for these services. The term of the current contract is for three (3) fiscal years (FY's 22-24) with two (2) one-year optional renewal extensions. This optional renewal is to perform the Fiscal Year 2025 Audit. Upon approval, this contract will have one more optional renewal for the Fiscal Year 2026 Audit.
title: Approval of the One-Year Optional Renewal for Fiscal Year 2025 with Purvis Gray & Company for RFP #22-003 Auditing Services. (Procurement Manager Tolbert)

description: The City Commission awarded a Continuing Professional Architectural Services Contract, RFQ #25-004, to JL2 Architecture on April 1, 2025. The first Task Order under the contract was listed as the design of the new Fire Station No. 38 to be located on City property at the southwest corner of North Lakewood Avenue and 2nd Ave. A scope of services meeting was held with JL2, ZHA (City's Owners Representative) and City staff to develop a Task Order proposal. JL2's proposal of $470,000.00 for the design services has been reviewed by both ZHA and City staff and found to be in line with industry standards. A preliminary design of the Station was provided by JL2 at the scope of services meeting and a notice to proceed will be issued following authorization of this Task Order. While design is underway, ZHA and City staff are working to advertise a Construction Manager At Risk (CMAR) contract to secure the services of a building contractor prior to the completion of the design, which will include constructability reviews to control costs and accelerate the overall completion schedule of the station. The design of the new station is adequately funded in the current budget. Public Works recommends Commission authorization of the Task Order for Fire Station No. 38.
title: Authorization of Task Order to JL2 Architecture for Design of Fire Station No. 38 Under Continuing Professional Architectural Services Contract RFQ #25-004. (Public Works Director Krug)

description:
At the June 4, 2013, City Commission meeting, the Commission approved the Public Works Team’s utilization of Cintas for uniform, shop rag, fender cover and carpet service. Pricing was based on a Hartford County Public Schools, Maryland, Master Agreement. This agreement has expired and was updated to a new Master Agreement with the University of Nebraska. Ocoee is a member of Omnia Partners, which is a government cooperative that allows the City to take advantage of competitively bid contracts from other public agencies. The University of Nebraska has provided a cooperative agreement for the City to utilize uniform, shop rag, fender cover and carpet service, providing significant savings. Public Works will save approximately $1,500 annually for the services compared to the current expired contract.
Public Works recommends awarding the uniform, shop rag, fender cover and carpet service to Cintas through the Omnia Partners Master Agreement by and between The University of Nebraska and Cintas, Contract #210198220.

description: The Utilities Department maintains approximately 387 miles of potable water, reclaimed water and sewage lines located throughout the City of Ocoee. When maintenance or repairs to these lines are needed beneath or near sidewalks, small sections of sidewalk must be removed for the repair and replaced after the repair is completed. Due to the small scope of these repairs, the City’s regular sidewalk contractors are unable to respond in an expedited and cost-effective manner. Staff contacted Florida Concrete Enterprises (FCE), a Central Florida company that specializes in small-scale concrete repairs, for sidewalk replacement needed as the result of utilities repairs. FCE recently completed the installation of a concrete pad at the wastewater treatment plant and expedited sidewalk repairs in (17) different areas of the City, resulting in a cumulative expenditure of $50,000.00 to date. Any additional work by FCE will cause the cumulative total to exceed the City Manager’s approval level of $50,000.00.
title: Approval of Florida Concrete Enterprises as a Single Source Vendor for Miscellaneous Utilities Concrete Repairs. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
Under the Wekiwa and Rock Springs Basin Management Action Plan, the City is required to complete numerous projects to comply with the state-mandated nutrient reduction requirements, including but not limited to “septic to sewer” projects.
The City has completed six septic to sewer projects in and around the downtown area, and 41 properties within these project areas remain unconnected to the City sewer system. When connecting to City sewer service, the cost to abandon a septic tank and connect to the existing sewer system, as well as the sewer capital fee, are the responsibility of the property owner. In 2024, the Utilities Department submitted a grant application to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to include the “Downtown Sewer Connections Project” in the FY2024-25 Springs Restoration Grant Program to cover the customer's construction costs to connect. In March 2025, FDEP announced that the City of Ocoee was awarded up to $700,000.00 for connection to existing sewer cleanouts located at the right of way (gravity or private grinder station), proper abandonment of the septic systems, and any necessary restoration associated with the connection.
This grant offers a unique opportunity to assist 41 properties currently eligible for connection to sewer by providing construction funding for the sewer connection.
title: Approval of the Florida Springs Grant Agreement SR005 from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection for the City of Ocoee "Downtown Sewer Connections Project". (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The Orange County Utilities (OCU)/City of Ocoee reclaimed water agreement provides for the transfer of 1.0 million gallons per day (MGD) of reclaimed water into the City’s Primary Reclaimed Water Service Area (south of Clarcona Road). This additional reclaimed water supply is a critical component of the City’s St Johns River Water Management District Consumptive Use Permit as it reduces the City’s groundwater demand and mitigates negative environmental impacts that may result from groundwater withdrawals. The storage tank, pump station, and transmission main are currently under construction and are funded using ARPA and the utilities fund.
In 2024, the Utilities Department submitted a grant application to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) for cost-share funding for the reclaimed water transmission main “interconnect”, which includes the piping and appurtenances to connect the new reclaimed water storage tank and pump station to the Orange County reclaimed water system. In March 2025, FDEP announced that the City of Ocoee was awarded 60% cost share funding (up to $1,532,500.00) for the reclaimed water interconnect. The reimbursement applies to the portion of the project funded by the utilities fund.
title: Approval of Alternate Water Supply Grant Agreement WS112 from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection for the City of Ocoee Transmission Main Interconnect to OCU Project. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description: The City of Ocoee budgets funds annually for the delivery and supply of sodium hypochlorite, which is the disinfectant used for the treatment of both water and wastewater. Odyssey Manufacturing currently supplies the City with sodium hypochlorite under a piggyback contract with the City of Tarpon Springs, which expired on May 26, 2025. Odyssey Manufacturing has agreed to supply sodium hypochlorite to the City under a new piggyback contract with the Clay County Utility Authority. The new contract will expire on March 7, 2026, and has two additional one-year renewals remaining. As the City’s main supplier of sodium hypochlorite, Odyssey Manufacturing has proven to be a reliable vendor and has served the City well in both regular and emergency circumstances.
title: Approval to Piggyback the Clay County Utility Authority Contract with Odyssey Manufacturing for the Supply of Sodium Hypochlorite. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The City’s Consumptive Use Permit requires that the City maintain a High Water User Program to target high potable water users. This program is continuously evolving to encourage customer engagement and water savings using proven technologies.
Residential landscape irrigation accounts for over 50% of household water use and the reduction in this use provides significant savings to both the City and our customers. In July 2025, the Utilities Department submitted an application to the St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) Water Conservation Rebate Program for 50% cost-share funding to support the new Ocoee Smart Irrigation Controller Program. Smart irrigation controllers are WI-FI enabled and automatically adjust watering schedules based on real-time weather data, type of landscaping, and seasonal conditions. By adapting landscape watering to local conditions, the new smart irrigation controllers help conserve water, reduce City and resident utility costs, and support the City’s long-term sustainability goals.
SJRWMD has approved the City's application and will reimburse 50% of the cost for each smart controller installed by September 30, 2025. Eligible recipients must be high water users using potable water for irrigation.
title: Approval of Water Conservation Rebate Cost Share Agreement 41440 between the St. Johns River Water Management District and the City of Ocoee. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The property is located at 1561 Dusty Pine Drive, assigned parcel ID number 05-22-28-2853-02-700. It is Lot 270 of the Forest Lake Estates Phase 2 subdivision. Per the subdivision plat and property survey, there are 5-foot drainage and utility easements on both side yards and a 5-foot wall and 10-foot distribution easements in the rear yard of the property.
The property owners want to install and retain a paver patio and walkways on both side yards and concrete and pavers in the rear yard that encroach on these easement areas. Specifically:
Installation of pavers for the side porch, and
Installation of paver walkways along the side yards, and
Installation of paver walkways in the rear yard, and
Installation of a paver fire pit in the rear yard, and
Installation of a paver area around a tree in the rear yard, and
Installation of a concrete slab (basketball court) in the rear yard.
Section 5-1 of Article V of the Land Development Code (LDC) states that the City cannot interfere with, abrogate, or annul any lawful easements and, therefore, cannot issue permits for the construction of improvements within an easement. For that reason, the property owners are seeking City approval to vacate the 5-foot drainage and utility easements along both side yards and the 5-foot wall and 10-foot distribution easements in the rear yard of the property. Attached is the survey indicating the easements requested to be vacated.
Letters were sent to the utility providers and the Forest Lake Estates Homeowners Association board, and no objections to the requested vacation have been received.
title: Public Hearing for 1561 Dusty Pine Drive - Fermaint Property Easement Vacate Request; Project No: VAC-25-038. TO BE CONTINUED BY THE CITY TO A DATE TO BE DETERMINED. (Planner I Belizaire)

description:
The property is in Commission District 1 and is located at 1561 Dusty Pine Drive. It is zoned PUD-LD (Planned Unit Development-Low Density), and is within the Forest Lake Estates PUD. The property is assigned parcel ID 05-22-28-2853-02-700. The applicants are requesting a variance to the Forest Lake Estates 2015 Preliminary/Final Subdivision Plan to exceed the maximum allowed 65 percent impervious surface area (ISA) and to Section 5-4D of Article V of the Land Development Code (LDC) to encroach into the 2-foot side and rear property line setback for impervious materials.
Per the Forest Lake Estates 2015 Preliminary/Final Subdivision Plan, the maximum allowed ISA for a single-family lot is 65 percent. With the subject property containing 6,011 square feet (SF) of land, the maximum allowed ISA is 3,907 SF. The applicants are requesting a total ISA of 4,168 (or 69 percent of the lot), representing a 6.7 percent variance to the Forest Lake Estates 2015 Preliminary/ Final Subdivision Plan. This causes the lot to exceed the maximum allowable ISA by four (4) percent (approximately 261 SF).
Per Section 5-4D of Article V of the LDC, any pedestrian walkway, path, patio, driveway, parking space, or other vehicle circulation area shall be set back at least 2 feet from the side and rear property lines. As impervious materials have been installed (without a permit) 1.5 feet from the side property lines and right along the rear property line, the applicants are also requesting a variance to encroach into the side and rear setbacks for impervious materials by 0.5 feet for a proposed ISA setback of 1.5 feet on side and rear yards.
The property has a 5-foot drainage and utility easement along the side property lines, a 5-foot wall easement along the rear property line, and a 10-foot distribution easement also along the rear property line. Concurrently with this variance application, the applicants have submitted a request to vacate all side and rear yard easements on the property. Per Section 5-1 of Article 5 of the LDC, the City cannot interfere with, abrogate, or annul any lawful easement and, therefore, cannot issue permits for the construction of improvements within any easement area. Due to impervious materials being installed without permits within the 5-foot-wide drainage and utility easements along both side yards and the 10-foot distribution easement (which would also encompass the 5-foot wall easement), both the easement vacation and a reduction in the impervious material setback would be needed in order for the existing impervious materials to remain.
Because the easement vacation request follows a separate process, this item only reflects the applicant's two (2) variances, as follows: (1) a variance to Section 5-4D of Article V of the LDC to encroach into the minimum 2-foot side and rear setback for impervious materials by 0.5 feet for a proposed ISA setback of 1.5 feet and (2) a variance to the Forest Lake Estates 2015 Preliminary/ Final Subdivision Plan to exceed the maximum allowed 65 percent ISA by four (4) percent (approximately 261 SF), which is the minimum additional ISA needed to keep the proposed 69 percent ISA if the requested easement vacations were also approved. The requested variances are for the purpose of installing and retaining a paver patio and walkways on both side yards and concrete and pavers in the rear yard, specifically:
Installation of pavers for the side porch, and
Installation of paver walkways along the side yards, and
Installation of paver walkways in the rear yard, and
Installation of a concrete patio in the rear yard, and
Installation of a paver fire pit in the rear yard, and
Installation of a paver area around a tree in the rear yard, and
Installation of a concrete slab (basketball court) in the rear yard.
According to Section 4- 9A of Article IV of the LDC, approval of a variance requires that the applicant demonstrate compliance with four (4) criteria, as follows:
That special conditions and circumstances exist which are peculiar to the land, structures, or required subdivision improvements involved and which are not applicable to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements;
That a literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties with similar conditions;
That the special conditions and circumstances do not result from the actions of the applicant; and
That the granting of the variance requested will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by these regulations to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements under similar conditions.
Applicant Response: The applicants' justifications are as follows:
Rain and water erosion caused damage to the home’s foundation. Soil was weathered away, and the erosion began to expose the foundation walls. The home’s structural integrity would have been compromised and led to future costly repairs had this damage not been corrected with the placement of the side pavers and repairs to the foundation.
The pavers already exist along with other requests that need permit approval. The current impervious surface area is 67.65 percent. The maximum surface area is 65 percent, and we are requesting to exceed that due to the current surface area total.
Staff Analysis: Staff finds that the justifications provided by the applicants do not support and are not sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the four (4) evaluation criteria. Staff's analysis is summarized below:
Criteria 1: Special Circumstances & Conditions: No special conditions and circumstances exist that are peculiar to the land in that the subject lot is of similar dimensions, shape, and size as other lots in this block of the subdivision. The lot is rectangular and, like other lots in the subdivision, has a 5-foot drainage and utility easement along the side lot lines. Additionally, for lots 267 through 278, there is a distribution easement in the rear of the property. For all side and rear easements, impervious materials are not permitted. In the instance of the easement vacations being approved, there is a minimum 2-foot setback requirement for impervious materials.
Criteria 2: Literal Interpretation of the Code: The literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would not deprive the applicants of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties with similar conditions. Construction of the residence, including the entry, driveway, walkway, AC pad, and rear stoop, yielded an ISA of approximately 32 percent, leaving 33 percent (or approximately 1,984 SF) of ISA available for use by the property owner. Staff finds that the remaining 33 percent ISA (1,984 SF) is ample square footage for the property owners to construct a reasonably sized patio, accessory structures, or any other improvements on the property and still remain compliant with the LDC. Staff finds that prohibiting the installation of buildings or structures in easements and requiring a 2-foot side and rear setback for impervious materials would not place an undue burden or hardship on this lot.
Criteria 3: Actions of the Applicant: The circumstances of this variance are the result of the actions of the applicants, as the impervious materials were installed without permits. If the applicants sought a permit prior to work being completed, staff would have informed them of the requirements. The property was cited by Code Enforcement for having unpermitted pavers in the front and side yards. In an effort to be compliant with Code Enforcement, the applicants/property owners applied for a building permit. During the course of staff review of the building permit, staff found that there were additional unpermitted improvements in the rear of the property that were not indicated on the survey or accounted for in the impervious area calculation sheet (refer to the attached surveys).
Criteria 4: Conference of Special Privilege: Granting the requested variance would confer a special privilege to the applicants that is denied by these regulations to other lands or required subdivision improvements under similar conditions, as other properties are also not permitted to exceed the maximum allowed ISA, install impervious materials within 2-feet of side and rear property lines or install impervious materials within easements.
Outcomes Based on Application Approvals and Denials: As previously discussed, the variance application is being reviewed concurrently with a separate easement vacation application. Depending on the approval and denial of each of the applications, the following revisions are required for the current building permit in order for it to be approved.
Approval of the Easement Vacation and Variance Requests: If the easement vacation and variance requests are approved, (1) the impervious materials may remain within all easement areas, (2) all impervious materials will have a 1.5 feet setback from the side and rear property lines, and (3) the impervious surface area of the lot can be exceeded by four (4) percent for a total ISA of 69 percent.
Denial of the Easement Vacation and Variance Requests: If the easement vacation and variance requests are denied, all impervious materials within the side and rear easement areas, representing approximately 856 SF or 14 percent ISA, must be removed. With this, the lot will be compliant with the Code as there will be no impervious materials within the side and rear easements, and the ISA of the lot would be reduced to 55 percent, and no longer exceed the maximum allowed ISA.
Approval of the Easement Vacation and Denial of the Variance Requests: If the easement vacation is approved and the variance requests are denied, impervious material within the 2-foot side and rear setback for impervious materials, representing approximately 156 SF, must be removed, as well as an additional 105 SF of impervious material on the property to reduce the ISA of the lot by a total of 261 SF to reduce the ISA of the lot to the maximum allowed 65 percent.
Denial of the Easement Vacation and Approval of the Variance Requests: If the easement vacation is denied and the variance requests are approved, all impervious material within the side and rear easement areas, representing approximately 856 SF, must be removed. In this instance, the variance requests are not necessary as impervious materials are not allowed in the easement areas regardless of the impervious material setback, and the ISA of the lot will be reduced to 55 percent.
Since the start of the permit application (April 2024), staff have had several in-person conversations at City Hall, email correspondences, and a site visit with the applicants related to the exceeded ISA and the installation of impervious materials within easements. Based on what has been presented for review to this point, staff does not support the requested variance as there is insufficient, code-based justification to support the variance.

description:
The Solid Waste Fund has reported a negative net position for several years. City staff have conducted a thorough historical evaluation of the issue and developed a comprehensive plan to restore the fund’s financial stability. The plan includes a one-time $1.3 million transfer from the General Fund to address the deficit, along with a rate adjustment to meet ongoing obligations and support the long-term sustainability of the fund.
The City Commission approved Resolution No. 2023-005 on April 18, 2023, to establish the current rate for solid waste/residential curbside services for garbage, recycling and yard & bulk waste collection. Public Works is requesting the City Commission approve an increase in order to adequately cover the actual cost of administering this contracted service and a transfer from the General Fund of $1,300,000.00 to restore the financial stability of Solid Waste Fund. Public Works worked with Finance to determine the long-term sustainability of this fund requires an additional increase of $42.00 annually per service household. The current rate is $298.24 annually. The new rate will include the 1.4% annual increase at $302.42, plus the additional $42.00 annual fee, to provide a new annual fee of $344.42 (approximately $28.71 monthly). Approval of a Resolution will adopt the new rate which provides an increase of $584,024.00 from the current year. Certification of the Non-Ad Valorem Assessment Roll for Solid Waste Inclusion on the Orange County Tax Roll for FY 2025/2026 will be brought before the City Commission for approval at the August 19th meeting.
title: Public Hearing for Adoption of Resolution Increasing Rates for Solid Waste/Residential Service. (Public Works Director Krug)

description:
On March 5th, 2024, the City Commission approved a proposal for the development of the Lake Apopka Nature Park Master Plan through Kimley-Horn. This proposal was split into two (2) phases, with Phase 1 being the development of a Master Plan and Phase 2 being the development of the design and engineering documents. Since last year, staff from Development Services, Parks & Leisure Services, and Public Works have been working with Kimley-Horn to develop the Master Plan (see Lake Apopka Nature Park Master Plan).
With the Master Plan being finalized, the next step for this project is to move forward with the design, engineering, and construction documents based on the Master Plan. Kimley-Horn has submitted an amendment to their original proposal to proceed with 60% design plans with services such as grant research, civil design plans, a stormwater design plan, a tree mitigation plan, a landscape plan, an irrigation plan, a hardscape plan, environmental work, a topographic survey, geotechnical work, and structural engineering (see Lake Apopka Nature Park Master Plan Proposal Amendment (Phase 2)).
The total cost for Phase 2 is $202,800, and funding is available utilizing the remainder of the funds contributed by Mattamy Homes in 2016. A preliminary Opinion of Probable Cost (OPC) for the full development of the park has been provided by Kimley-Horn, and the preliminary total is $4,937,000 (see Lake Apopka Nature Park Master Plan OPC). As part of Phase 2, Kimley-Horn will research grant opportunities that could help offset the costs of the park. As the project proceeds into the following steps after 60% design plans, it will be brought back to the City Commission for input and funding. Additionally, staff will continue to work with Kimley-Horn to identify potential grant opportunities.
Staff is requesting authorization to proceed with the amendment to the proposal for 60% design plans, which is the next step in the full development of this park.
title: Approval of the Design & Engineering Services for the Lake Apopka Nature Park with Kimley-Horn & Associates in the Amount of $202,800. (Concurrency and Commitment Coordinator McFarlane)

description:
Senate Bill (SB) 784, which was signed by the Governor on June 20, 2025, and incorporated into Chapter 2025-164 Laws of Florida on June 23, 2025, went into effect on July 1, 2025. SB 784 amended Section 177.071, Florida Statutes, to stipulate that a plat or replat must be administratively approved and that no further action by the governing body of a local government is required if the plat or replat complies with the requirements of Section 177.091, Florida Statutes. SB 784 also amended Section 177.071, Florida Statutes, to require local governments to designate, by ordinance or resolution, an administrative authority to receive, review, and process the plat or replat submittals, including the designation of an administrative official responsible for approving, approving with conditions, or denying the proposed plat or replat.
Although SB 784 also contains provisions for a sufficiency review process and timeline as well as other provisions, this Resolution is intended to comply with the provisions of Section 177.071(1)(a) and (b), Florida Statutes, in that it designates the Development Services Department as the administrative authority for receiving, reviewing, and processing plats and replats and the City Manager as the administrative official authorized to approve, approve with conditions, or deny plat and replat submittals in accordance with Sections 177.071 and 177.091, Florida Statutes.
title: Approval of Resolution Designating Administrative Official Authorized to Approve Plats and Replats. (Deputy Development Services Director Whitfield)

The millage rate may be reduced during the September budget hearings, a practice the City has traditionally followed.

description:
The City’s current continuing contracts for Emergency-Disaster Debris Monitoring services will expire on December 2, 2025. However, execution of contracts for this RFP #25-007 will supersede and cause early termination of the current contracts. In compliance with State and Federal Regulations and Chapter 21 of the City’s Code of Ordinances, the City solicited proposals for pre-event emergency-disaster debris monitoring services from qualified firms to perform the required services. The Contractor(s) will be required to enter into a contract with the City along the terms and conditions included in the RFP, including the RFP Exhibits and Federal Requirements, for the initial period of three (3) years with two (2) separate automatic one (1) year renewal terms; the contract may be optionally renewed for an additional one-year period at the option of the City after the completion of the automatic renewal terms.
This pre-event contract is subject to the provisions of 2 C.F.R. Part 200 and the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. The RFP describes and defines the services required for the execution of paper and electronic debris removal monitoring, including grant (reimbursement) management, for the City following a natural disaster. Activities include, but are not limited to, monitoring the following - field operations regarding all storm generated debris; debris pickup, debris hauling, debris staging and reduction, temporary debris storage site management, debris management, and final disposal of debris to an approved facility. The debris monitoring Contractor shall provide all management, supervision, labor, transportation, and equipment necessary for the monitoring of all aspects of disaster debris collection, processing and disposal operations on behalf of the City, ensuring compliance with the FEMA Public Assistance Debris Monitoring Guide and other Federal requirements (including, but not limited to FHWA & OSHA) and the City’s applicant debris management plans as related to contractor operation, oversight, truck measurements/certification, accurate load tracking (ticket or electronic) preparation and issuing, monitoring (including GPS and photograph documentation), report preparation, project administration, and grant (reimbursement) management.
The RFP was advertised on April 27, 2025, and was publicly opened on June 3, 2025. A total of three (3) proposals were received; however, after review, one (1) Respondent was deemed non-responsive for failure to submit the required bid security and for failure to provide the required surety letter of intent as specified in the RFP Documents. Attached are the two (2) responsive proposals; copies of all proposals are available in the Finance Department for your review.
The two (2) responsive proposals were evaluated by the RFP Evaluation Committee appointed by the City Manager, which consisted of five (5) members: Stephen Krug, Public Works Director; Hseth Burch, Staff Engineer; Felicia Sanders, Accountant II; Kiel Gajadhar, Assistant Public Works Director; and Milen Womack, City Engineer. The public RFP Evaluation Committee meeting was held on July 8, 2025, at 10:00 a.m. with the Evaluation Committee evaluating and shortlisting the firms on specific evaluation criteria. Please see the attached shortlist/evaluation form. The evaluation committee short-listed the following firms in ranked order, and recommends contracting with the top-ranked firm, Thompson Consulting Services, LLC; and with the second-ranked firm, DebrisTech, LLC, as an alternate/secondary term contract, per the attached award recommendation from Stephen Krug, Public Works Director.

section: SECOND READING OF ORDINANCE – PUBLIC HEARING
title: SECOND READING OF ORDINANCE – PUBLIC HEARING

description:
The First Reading Transmittal and Public Hearing of an Ordinance was held on April 15, 2025. The Transmittal Packet was electronically transmitted on April 24, 2025, to state and regional agencies, Orange County Public Schools, Orange County, and the City of Winter Garden.
Chapter 163, Part II, Florida Statutes, requires local governments to adopt a comprehensive plan that establishes principles, guidelines, standards, and strategies for the City's orderly and balanced economic, social, physical, environmental, and fiscal development. Section 163.3177(5)(a), F.S., requires that the Comprehensive Plan include at least two planning periods: one covering at least the first 10-year period occurring after the plan’s adoption and the other covering at least a 20-year period.
The current Comprehensive Plan, adopted on October 1, 2002, has reached its long-term planning horizon of 2022. Therefore, "The Comprehensive Plan must be updated to include the statutorily required ten-year and twenty-year planning horizons." In accordance with Section 163.3177(6), F.S., the Comprehensive Plan is based on relevant and appropriate data and analysis including, but not be limited to, surveys, studies, and other data available at the time of the preparation of the plan, as well as data prepared by the City, all of which are included within a Data, Inventory, and Analysis (DIA) document. Ocoee's DIA document contains an evaluation of historical growth and development trends. It also includes the City's 2045 population projections based on several methodologies (including those listed in Florida Statutes), an evaluation of anticipated demands, and an assessment of the City's ability to accommodate these demands on public infrastructure and municipal services, including completion of the 10-Year Water Supply Plan.
Thus, in accordance with Chapter 163, Part II, Florida Statutes, the City developed a Vision Statement and prepared an updated Comprehensive Plan, entitled "Envision 2045 Ocoee Comprehensive Plan" ("Envision 2045"), which consists of two (2) volumes.
Volume one is the Envision 2045 Ocoee Comprehensive Plan policy document, which is Exhibit A of the ordinance proposed for adoption. The policy document will be the governing framework that directs growth and development in the city over the next 10-year and 20-year planning horizons. The Envision 2045 policy document includes a Vision Statement, Goals, Objectives, and Policies to achieve its vision of Ocoee becoming “a vibrant, attractive, and economically sustainable community where businesses thrive and neighborhoods flourish through diverse, compact, and complementary land uses that produce quality developments, enhanced and active public realms, and safe and efficient mobility systems while simultaneously preserving environmental systems and creating parks, trails, and open spaces to promote social engagement, community health, and overall well-being of the City".
Volume two is the Data, Inventory, and Analysis document, which serves as supporting documentation for Volume One and is not included for adoption.
Envision 2045 and the supporting DIA document were prepared in-house by a multidisciplinary and multi-department Comprehensive Planning Team comprised of technical staff from the Development Services, Public Works, Utilities, and Parks and Leisure Services Departments, with technical assistance from the City's transportation consultant firm regarding the Transportation Element (which has been renamed the Mobility Element). It reflects the City Commission's direction and public feedback received during the preparation of the City's Evaluation and Appraisal Report (EAR) and Special Area Plans, including the Downtown Master Plan and the SR 429 Overlay District, along with its three Character Area Plans, which the City Commission has adopted within the past 10 years. This Plan update also recognizes the changing trends in the market and development community.
Because this update is a repeal and replacement of the expired 2002 Comprehensive Plan, the goals, objectives, and policies within the proposed Envision 2045 policy document are not presented in strike-through/underline format. Some existing policies were kept but were reworded, combined, or reorganized into updated Objectives. Additionally, the 2002 Comprehensive Plan was organized by Elements, but with this Update, the Elements within the Plan are proposed to be organized by topic-oriented Chapters, as presented below:
Envision 2045 Chapters1Introduction2Vibrant, Attractive & Inclusive CommunityFuture Land Use ElementHousing (Revitalization & Neighborhood Preservation) ElementRecreation & Open Space Element3Efficient, Reliable, and Well-Maintained InfrastructureInfrastructure ElementUtility Sub-ElementDrainage Sub-Element4Safe & Convenient Mobility Mobility Element5Environment-Friendly, Resilient & Sustainable CommunityConservation Element6Responsible, Accessible & Open Governance Public Schools Facilities ElementIntergovernmental Coordination ElementCapital Improvements ElementPrivate Property Rights ElementAppendix
Supporting ResourcesAcronymsPlaceholder [5-Year Capital Improvements Plan][Placeholder Water Supply Plan]
A summary of the major changes in each element is provided below.
Future Land Use Element (FLUE): Creation of two (2) new land use categories: Low Medium Density Residential (LMDR) with a density range of 5 to 8 dwelling units per acre and Mixed Use (MU) with a density of up to 20 units per acre and intensity of up to 3.0 floor area ratio (similar to the FAR for the current Commercial and Industrial categories). Bonus dwelling units per acre may be available to enhance architectural and public realm improvements.
Creation of policies that provide specific locational requirements for the application of the Mixed Use category, as well as urban (site) and architectural requirements for developments within the Mixed Use category.
Adjustments to the density ranges within the current residential land use categories to (1) accommodate projected population growth, (2) improve the City's competitiveness in the market, and (3) increase flexibility in development patterns, specifically:Low Density Residential from "up to 4 units per acre" to "up to 5 units per acre",
Medium Density Residential from "4 to less than 8 units per acre" to "8 to 15 units per acre" (NOTE: The starting density for MDR aligns with the ending density for the proposed new LMDR category.)
High Density Residential from "8 to 16 units per acre" to "15 to 20 units per acre", and
Allowing residential density within the Commercial and Industrial categories under certain, specific but limited, circumstances.
Creation of policy and specific criteria for approval of amendments to the Future Land Use Map (FLUM).
Creation of policies that clearly define the meanings of density and intensity, as well as the calculation method for maximum development potential (transition from gross to net land area) when an application for a FLUM amendment is proposed.
Creation of new objectives related to managing growth and development patterns that enhance the quality of life, prioritize a safe and connected built environment to promote community health and wellness, and adopt sustainable and innovative development practices. This includes prioritizing projects and strategies that foster economic sustainability and vitality.
Identification and mapping of the Downtown District and the Community Redevelopment Area (CRA) District on the Future Land Use Map and amending the Future Land Use Map to apply the new Mixed Use category to the Downtown District and the CRA District.
Removal of duplicate language from the FLUE that exists in other Elements.
Housing Element:Reorganizing and rewording existing priorities within the current Objectives and placing those policies under clear new objectives.
Creation of a "Housing For All" program to ensure housing choices for current and future residents through all stages of life.
Creation of a "Live Here/Grow Here" initiative (developed by staff and not associated with the Live Local Act) that prioritizes the coordination of land use planning, housing, and transportation planning to ensure that the built environment and development patterns within the city create a community environment where people want to move to or stay in Ocoee and thrive.
Strengthening policies to protect and help ensure housing availability for the elderly and other special populations.
Creation of policies to guide the preservation, maintenance, and restoration of historically significant properties and resources.
Recreation and Open Space Element:Update the level of service for parks from 4 acres of parks and open space per 1,000 residents to 8 acres of parkland and civic open space per 1,000.
Inclusion of policies geared towards achieving a goal of one (1) park per 2,346 residents.
Establishing a goal to achieve the National Recreation and Parks Association (NRPA) median level of service, which is 10.2 acres of parkland and civic open space per 1,000 residents, by 2045.
Reiteration and strengthening of the City's goal of creating a coordinated, comprehensive, diverse, accessible, sustainable, and inclusive parks system to create a healthy and active community for all ages and abilities through neighborhood, community, regional, and nature parks and specialty facilities. A key concept in park performance is creating the 10-minute walk to parks, which translates to a half (1/2) mile distance that most people are willing to walk to reach a destination.
Objectives and policies regarding park facilities planning, park funding, resource management, sustainability, and stewardship.
Infrastructure Element:Updates to the level of service standards for potable water and wastewater.
Creation of a level of service for drainage and stormwater systems and facilities.
Strengthening objectives and policies related to water conservation and water quality protection, including protection of surface waters and the aquifer.
Policies to strengthen flood resiliency.
Mobility Element: Development of objectives and policies that shift transportation planning and design from the traditional auto-oriented mode to a context-oriented (or context classification-based) mode.
Prioritizing safe pedestrian and bicycle travel and mode choices through the creation of a level of service standard for pedestrian and bicycle facilities, as measured by the "level of traffic stress" (LTS)(from 1 to 4). LTS gauges the comfort levels experienced by pedestrians and bicyclists traveling on roadways (the lower the number, the greater the comfort level).
Inclusion of objectives and policies to direct greater coordination between land use, transportation planning, and housing, and to reduce pressure to widen roadways at a great expense through identifying opportunities for parallel or interconnected roadways and gridded streets, whenever possible.
Conservation Element:Strengthening, clarifying, and reorganizing objectives and policies to protect wetlands to meet or exceed Federal, State, and County requirements.
Strengthening objectives and policies for floodplain protection that exceed the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) requirements, thereby increasing the City’s classification within the Community Rating System (CRS) to ensure residents are eligible for insurance discounts.
Establishing objectives and policies that require sustainable and low-impact development, including provisions that encourage: Expansion of an EV infrastructure within the City,
Protection and expansion of the City’s Urban Tree Canopy,
Implementation of a Vegetative Roof Ordinance, and
Implementation of policies that protect community access to the night sky by reducing light pollution.
Capital Improvements Element:Updates were relative to updating the level of service standards as provided in each of the above relevant elements,
Combined policies regarding the prioritization of capital projects into a single section, and
Removed duplicate language and tables from the Public School Facilities 10-Year Capital Outlay Plan and other date-specific revenue sources, revenue expenditures, and other financial commitments that have now passed.
Generally, no changes were proposed within the Public School Facilities Element, the Intergovernmental Coordination Element, or the Private Property Rights Element. The only changes are related to reorganizing existing policies, removing outdated or no longer applicable references to the Florida Administrative Code, and policy commitments that have already been fulfilled within the past 20-year planning horizon.
As the City awaited agency review comments, we took the opportunity to engage the community by hosting a Community Outreach Meeting on Wednesday, May 28, 2025. This event provided residents and property owners a valuable chance to review the proposed Plan in detail, ask questions, and share feedback directly with technical staff. The meeting began with a 30-minute presentation and Q&A session, followed by an open house-style forum that encouraged one-on-one conversations. Fourteen community members attended, not including elected officials and staff. We are grateful for the thoughtful participation and are especially appreciative of the positive feedback received—attendees were highly complimentary of the proposed Plan and expressed appreciation for the dedication and hard work of City staff in advancing the Plan Update. A summary of comments and questions is provided below:Plans for future parks and recreation facilities and resources and where they live relative to the parks,
Transportation comments:Why the timing of Franklin Street/Silver Star Road capacity improvements in 2045 not being planned sooner (which is a state project)
Signal timing on State Road 50,
Roadway and construction noise complaints and a request for sound walls in the northeast quadrant of SR 429 and Plant Street,
Positive comments on proposed trail connectivity and questions on the timing of them,
Correction needed on map relative to existing sidewalk segment on Silver Star Road (Map is in the process of being corrected),
Questions regarding flooding and flood prevention,
Questions on how the City interacts with other local governments and agencies, including which schools served the City's population, school capacity and any planned schools and school enrollment (which would be directed to Orange County Public Schools),
Some interest in the expansion of the City's central wastewater system and connecting to City wastewater service,
Questions on City's plan to comply with recent state laws banning certain additives (i.e. fluoride) in the drinking water supply,
Interest in bringing a water main down Pine Street, and
Questions on the status of Palm Drive roadway improvements.
State reviewing agency comments were due on June 9, 2025 (45 days from electronic transmittal to all agencies). No state or regional agency identified comments, concerns, or objections that would be used to form the basis of a challenge. The absence of comments from the State’s review underscores the quality and completeness of the submitted documents, reflecting the professionalism, diligence, and expertise of both City staff and the consulting team in preparing a thorough and statutory compliant submittal. However, several agencies provided technical assistance comments, which are summarized below.

2. Septic System Conversion to Central Sanitary Sewer System Service: Section 163.3177(6)(c)3, F.S., requires that, by July 1, 2024, the Infrastructure Element must be updated to consider the feasibility of providing sanitary sewer services to any development of more than 50 residential lots, whether built or inbuilt, with more than one onsite sewage treatment and disposal system (OSTDS) per one acre within a 10-year planning horizon, and to identify the wastewater facility (capacity, projected flows for the next 20 years, and timeline for construction of the sanitary sewer system) that could receive the sanitary sewer flows after connection and as needed thereafter to account for the future applicable developments. The proposed Comprehensive Plan does not include the information required by this section of F.S.
3. 5-Year CIP: The proposed Comprehensive Plan Update does not include the Five-Year Capital Improvements Plan (CIP) and instead references the CIP as part of the City's budget. This is not consistent with Section 163.3177(3)(a)4, F.S.Response to TA Comment 1: FLU Figures 1 and 3, and REC Figures 1 and 5, as well as MOB Figure 11, have been updated to include/state the "2045" timeframe.
Response to TA Comment 2: UTL Policy 7.9 has been added to consider the feasibility of providing sanitary sewer services within a 10-year planning horizon to any development within the City’s jurisdiction of more than 50 built or unbuilt residential lots with a density of more than one OSTDS per acre.

Staff also explained the City's procedures for applications, including transportation capacity analyses and transportation operations analyses, depending upon the context of the proposed development or application. FDOT expressed its appreciation of the explanation and requested that the City continue coordination and collaborate with the Department as a resource.

description:
The City currently charges fire protection service assessments within its incorporated boundaries pursuant to a methodology established in a study conducted by Anser Advisory, formerly known as Government Services Group (GSG), dated August 2013. Section 2.08 of the City’s Fire Protection Assessment Ordinance, adopted as Ordinance No. 2013-010 on August 6, 2013, sets forth the procedure for determining the Fire Protection Assessment for each subsequent fiscal year.
Since 2014, an annual fire protection assessment has been imposed pursuant to Ordinance No. 2014-008 at a rate of $69.50 per fire protection unit. For Fiscal Year 2025, the $69.50 rate generated approximately $2.1 million for fire protection services. These revenues account for approximately 17.97% of the Fire Department’s total adopted budget of $13,197,529 for the fiscal year. It should be noted that fire protection assessments are applied exclusively to fire protection services, including capital expenditures, and do not include emergency medical services (EMS) or ambulatory transport operations.
To ensure the Fire Protection Assessment program remains current, equitable, and legally defensible, the City has retained Anser Advisory to assist with an update of the program for Fiscal Year 2025–2026. As part of this effort, Anser Advisory has prepared a new City of Ocoee Fire Assessment Memorandum, which includes the following components:
A general description of the fire protection services, facilities, and programs to be provided;
The Fire Protection Assessed Cost for FY 2026, representing the portion of the Fire Department’s budget eligible portion of the Fire Department’s budget eligible to be funded through the assessment.
The proposed assessment rates for the upcoming fiscal year.
The primary objectives of this update are to:
Develop pro forma budgets and corresponding assessment rates for FY 2025–26; and
Ensure the program’s continued compliance with current legislative requirements and applicable case law governing the legal enforceability of non-ad valorem assessments.
As part of the update, Anser Advisory has calculated revised assessment rates and classifications necessary to fully fund the assessable costs associated with providing fire protection services within the City. Notably, while the analysis identifies the funding needed to fully support these services, the City retains discretion—based on policy direction—to fund all or only a portion of these costs through fire assessments.
Additionally, the memorandum outlines the methodology used to identify the total assessable cost of providing fire protection services (net of other revenue sources), and to allocate those costs to the properties that receive a special benefit from such services.
Finally, the updated assessment study establishes a proposed new maximum rate of $386.75 per fire protection assessment unit, which represents the full funding level required to support the Fire Department’s total projected expenditures for FY 2026.
On May 20, 2025, the City Commission approved Resolution 2025-05, which set the initial maximum rate at $139.23 per fire protection unit—representing approximately 36% of the funding for fire protection services. The actual rate will be established with the adoption of this resolution. The Commission can lower the rate to any amount under $139.23; However, the Commission cannot raise the rate above the published rate.
Staff recommends the Commission adopt the Amended and Restated Final Assessment Resolution for Fire Assessments at a maximum rate at $139.23 per fire protection unit. This document serves as the Amended and Restated Final Assessment Resolution as defined in Section 77-1 of the Code of Ordinances. This increase would generate an estimated additional $2–$2.1 million in revenue for FY 2026. Even with this proposed increase, the assessment remains modest in light of projected Fire Department expenditures, which are expected to rise to $15.5–$16 million in each of the next five years.
This projection reflects:
Continued growth in personnel-related costs,
Scheduled vehicle replacements and station construction and upgrades, and
Inflationary pressure on operational line items.
Maintaining current funding levels and relying primarily on ad valorem (property) taxes to cover assessable fire protection expenditures is becoming increasingly unpredictable due to changes in traditional state revenue sources. Most recently, Florida voters approved Amendment 5 in the November 2024 election, which provides for an annual inflation-based adjustment to the second $25,000 homestead exemption for non-school property taxes. As this exemption grows with the Consumer Price Index (CPI), it reduces the City's ability to generate consistent revenue from property taxes—particularly during periods of high inflation—while the cost of providing essential services such as fire protection continues to rise.
Given these constraints, adopting a more stable, transparent, and equitable funding mechanism—such as an updated and legally defensible fire assessment—ensures that all property owners who benefit from fire protection services contribute fairly to their cost. Unlike property taxes, fire assessments are based on the benefit received, not property value, meaning every parcel pays a share that reflects its service demand.
Key benefits of updating the fire assessment now include:
Predictable Revenue: A fire assessment provides a dedicated and stable source of funding, reducing dependency on fluctuating tax revenues and state aid.
Transparency: The revenue generated is reported in the City Auditor's Annual Financial Report submitted to the State of Florida Department of Financial Services as a line item.
Fair Cost Distribution: Assessments are applied uniformly to all properties based on the level of service provided, ensuring equity across the city.
Strategic Fiscal Planning: Establishing appropriate assessment rates today reduces the risk of larger, more burdensome increases in the future as service demands and costs grow.
title: Adoption of the Amended and Restated Final Resolution Pertaining to Fire Protection Assessments for Fiscal Year 2025–2026. (Assistant City Manager Rumer)

description:
Under the Wekiwa and Rock Springs Basin Management Action Plan, the City is required to complete numerous projects to comply with the state-mandated nutrient reduction requirements, including but not limited to “septic to sewer” projects. The City has completed six central sewer projects in and around the downtown area, and 41 parcels remain unconnected. When connecting to City sewer service, the cost of abandoning a septic tank and connecting to an existing sewer system, as well as the sewer capital fee, are the responsibility of the property owner.
In 2024, the Utilities Department submitted a grant application to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to include the Downtown Sewer Connections Project in the FY2024-25 Springs Restoration Grant Program. In March 2025, FDEP announced that the City of Ocoee was awarded up to $700,000.00 for sewer-eligible buildings to connect to existing sewer cleanouts located at the right of way (gravity or private grinder station), proper abandonment of their septic system and any necessary restoration associated with central sewer connection and septic tank abandonment.
This grant offers a unique opportunity to assist 41 properties currently eligible for connection to sewer by providing construction funding for the sewer connection.

description:
The Code Enforcement Board was created by Ordinance No. 741 on June 16, 1981. The purpose of this Board is to review residential property infractions of the City Technical Codes, negotiate compliance and impose fines for failure to comply. The City utilizes a magistrate apart from the Code Board for code enforcement issues involving commercial properties. The Code Enforcement Board shall consist of seven (7) regular members and two (2) alternate members, all with three-year terms. Currently, the Board has seven (7) regular members and no alternate members.
There are three (3) regular member seats with terms set to expire June 2025. Staff reached out to the three (3) regular members whose terms are set to expire in June 2025 to confirm their interest in reappointment and requested updated applications. The three-year terms of Members Joe Bandur, William Mann, and Laini Schultz will conclude in June 2025. Members Bandur and Schultz have expressed interest in being considered for reappointment and have submitted updated applications, which are attached. Member Mann has not responded regarding his interest in reappointment; therefore, his seat will be considered vacant at the end of the month. In 2024, Member Bandur, who currently serves as Chair, attended all scheduled meetings. In 2024, Member Schultz attended eight (8) of nine (9) meetings.
At the Regular City Commission Meeting held on May 20, 2025, the Police Department requested that the City Commission reconsider the current use of the Code Enforcement Board and proposed that all code enforcement cases, both residential and commercial, be referred to a Special Magistrate instead. Following discussion, the City Commission voted to maintain the seven-member Code Enforcement Board and to begin accepting new applications in an effort to secure future quorums. Additionally, questions were raised about the cancellation of the Board’s November and December meetings. Since no information was available at the time, a Commissioner later contacted staff to follow up on the cancellation reasons and requested a solution. Upon reviewing past meeting minutes, staff determined that the Board began canceling its December meetings in 1993 through a memorandum from the Chair, with subsequent cancellations continued by Board motions in the following years. Since September 2021, the Board has also voted to cancel its November meetings following discussion. If the City Commission prefers that the November and December meetings continue as scheduled, staff recommends considering a change in the meeting day to the third Thursday of each month to help avoid conflicts with holiday weeks.
title: Approval of Code Enforcement Board Reappointments and Discussion on Changing Meeting Day. (City Clerk Sibbitt)

description:
This report is submitted in response to concerns raised during the May 6, 2025, City Commission Meeting, during which the Commission highlighted the need to strengthen deterrents against motorists who disregard “No Parking” signage and fail to comply with existing traffic enforcement measures. In response, City Manager Shadrix advised that addressing this issue would necessitate amendments to the City Code and committed to bringing forward policy options for the Commission’s consideration.
Since that time, Police Chief Ogburn, in collaboration with city staff, has conducted a review of best management practices and developed a comprehensive set of policy and enforcement recommendations. These recommendations are designed to enhance parking compliance and improve the overall effectiveness of code enforcement efforts. Given the interrelated nature of parking and code violations, deficiencies in one area often compromise the efficacy of the other.
To implement these improvements, amendments to Chapter 168 of the City Ordinance (Parking Violations and Enforcement) will be required. The proposed revisions include provisions for escalating penalties, enhanced tracking mechanisms, and strengthened enforcement procedures.
Under the current ordinance, initial enforcement action for parking violations involves the placement of a warning sticker on the vehicle, which must remain for a minimum of 48 hours in accordance with §165-6 of the City Code. In alignment with previous Commission discussions, staff is now presenting a set of follow-up recommendations and enforcement options to be considered as next steps beyond the initial warning phase.
1. Implement Escalating Penalties for Repeat Parking Offenders
Increase citation fines for recurring violations within 12 months:First citation: $40 (Currently in the code)
The City Code would be amended to create:Second citation: $75
Third citation: $100
Fourth citation: $250, includes towing or immobilization of the vehicle at the owner’s expense.
2. Authorize Vehicle Immobilization or Towing After Notice Period
Provide for the placement of a 48-hour notice on vehicles parked in violation. If the vehicle remains in violation after 48 hours:Option A: Issue a violation, and if unaddressed, immobilize or tow the vehicle.
Option B: Proceed directly to immobilization or towing without an additional citation, at the owner's expense.
3. Improve Violation Tracking Capabilities
Currently, the city does not possess software that tracks the number of parking violations issued to a single vehicle. Staff recommends authorizing the Police Department to research and procure software that can track and monitor parking offenses to manage habitual violators better.
4. Increase Visibility and Efficiency in EnforcementImprove signage visibility in problem areas to deter violations.
Streamline enforcement procedures to ensure consistent application of penalties and notices.
Staff is presenting these recommendations to the commission for consideration, and they are designed to reduce habitual violations, promote public compliance with posted regulations, and enhance overall traffic safety within the City of Ocoee.
title: Discussion and Direction on Planned Actions in Reference to Code Enforcement and Parking Concerns. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
Since 2022, the City of Ocoee has held an Ocoee Remembers event on the first Saturday in November to honor and pay tribute to the descendants of the African Americans who were victims of the 1920 Ocoee Election Day Massacre. This observance recognizes the historical injustices that occurred and seeks to provide a space for reflection and remembrance while continuing to move forward in unity. This year, the city’s remembrance event is planned for Saturday, November 1, 2025. Staff is seeking the Commission’s authorization to proceed with the event as planned below.
Without prior coordination, the Alliance for Truth and Justice (ATJ) organization recently informed city staff that they plan to host their own remembrance events for the descendants on November 1st. The ATJ has partnered with the Orlando Museum of Art to invite the descendants and the public to a video presentation to be held at the museum. After the museum presentation, the ATJ in collaboration with the Ocoee Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), will host a service at the church for the descendants. The church service will also be open to the public. Historical note: during the tragic events on November 2, 1920, the Ocoee Christian Church provided a safe haven for African Americans fleeing the mob violence. The ATJ has reached out to ask about partnering with the City.
Unless authorized by the City Commission, staff is moving forward with the City's event as usual with the 2025 Ocoee Remembers event program outlined below:
Memorial Wall Remembrance Ceremony at Unity Park– Open to the Public
4:30 p.m. – 5:30 p.m.
Invocation – Pastor Keith Tower, HighPoint Church
Opening Remarks/Recognition of Elected Officials – Mayor
Presentation of white roses to descendants, who will be invited to lay them on the Memorial Wall, which bears the names of the 263 African Americans known to have lived in Ocoee in 1920
Remarks - Descendants
Poem shared in honor of the victims and survivors
Dove release to symbolically honor the memory of those who once called Ocoee home
Reception at the Ocoee Lakeshore Center – Invitation Only
6 p.m. – 7 p.m.Heavy hors d'oeuvres
Ocoee High School Jazz Band (TBD)
Photos of previous Ocoee Remembers events shown on television monitors
Caricature Artists
Memory Jars
Keepsake gift for the descendants
title: Approval of Ocoee Remembers Event - November 1, 2025. (Parks and Leisure Services Deputy Director Gaines)

description:
The Code Enforcement Board was created by Ordinance No. 741 on June 16, 1981. The purpose of this Board is to review residential property infractions of the City Technical Codes, negotiate compliance and impose fines for failure to comply. The City utilizes a magistrate apart from the Code Board for code enforcement issues involving commercial properties. The Code Enforcement Board shall consist of seven (7) regular members and two (2) alternate members, all with three-year terms. Currently, the Board has six (6) regular members and no alternate members. There are three (3) regular member seats with terms set to expire June 2025, one (1) vacant regular member seat with a term set to expire June 2027, and two (2) vacant alternate member seats.
At the Regular City Commission Meeting held on May 20, 2025, the Police Department requested that the City Commission reconsider the current use of the Code Enforcement Board and proposed that all code enforcement cases, both residential and commercial, be referred to a Special Magistrate instead. This request stemmed from the Board’s inability to meet since October 2024 due to a lack of quorum. The Commission discussed the potential of utilizing a Special Magistrate as well as the option of restructuring and maintaining a citizen-based Board. Ultimately, the City Commission voted to retain the existing seven-member Code Enforcement Board and to begin accepting applications to help ensure future quorums.
An application has been submitted by Ravi Bickram, expressing interest in being appointed as a regular member of the Code Enforcement Board to fill the term ending in June 2027.
