description:
Pursuant to the direction provided by the City Commission during its April 2, 2024, meeting—at which the Commission unanimously reached a consensus for staff to proceed with an another formal request to the United States Postal Service (USPS) to consolidate the City’s existing six (6) ZIP Codes into one (1) unique ZIP Code for the entire Ocoee community. This request was sent to the Postmaster General and copied to all relevant state and federal elected officials. On August 23, 2024, the City received an acknowledgment via email confirming that the USPS had received the request. However, despite multiple follow-up inquiries seeking a status update, no additional response has been received to date.
Subsequently, H.R. 672 was introduced in the current 119th Congress by Representative Mario Diaz-Balart and co-sponsored by Representative Daniel Webster, which would require the USPS to designate a single, unique ZIP Code for each of fourteen (14) specified communities, including the City of Ocoee and the following 13 communities:
Eastvale, California
Scotland, Connecticut
Castle Pines, Colorado
Silver Cliff, Colorado
Hollywood, Florida
Miami Lakes, Florida
Urbandale, Iowa
Franklin, Wisconsin
Greenfield, Wisconsin
Village of Caledonia, Wisconsin
Village of Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin
Village of Somers, Wisconsin
Mills, Wyoming
H.R. 672 passed the House Oversight Committee 41-1 and is on its way to the House Floor for consideration next month. Based on the information received and the comments that were shared at the Oversight Committee meeting, it is recommended each municipality adopt a resolution or issue a formal letter supporting the bill.
title: Approval of Resolution for City Commission Support for H.R. 672 (Representative Mario Diaz-Balart) to Direct the United States Postal Service to Designate Single, Unique ZIP Codes for Certain Communities, including Ocoee. (Assistant City Manager Rumer)

description:
The approved Ocoee American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) project list includes funds to construct a new reclaimed storage tank and pump station at the City’s Wastewater Treatment Plant. This project is intended to provide the infrastructure necessary to accept, store, and re-pump 1.0 million gallons per day (MGD) of reclaimed water from Orange County into the City’s reclaim distribution system. However, following the completion of the project design, Orange County implemented new rate classification requirements that necessitate modifications to the original design.
The City is taking steps to qualify for lower rates under the updated rate classifications, the first of which is to revise the design for this project by increasing pump capacity, modifying onsite piping, and increasing the storage tank capacity to 1.5 million gallons. This change requires a contract modification, increasing the total project cost by $737,076.33.

description:
The property is in Commission District 1 and is located at 1561 Dusty Pine Drive. It is zoned PUD-LD (Planned Unit Development-Low Density), and is within the Forest Lake Estates PUD. The property is assigned parcel ID 32-22-28-9285-00-740. The applicant is requesting a variance to the Forest Lake 2015 Preliminary/Final Subdivision Plan to exceed the maximum allowed 65 percent impervious surface area (ISA) and to Section 5-4D of Article V of the Land Development Code to encroach into the 2-foot side and rear property line setback for impervious materials.
Per the Forest Lake Estates 2015 Preliminary/Final Subdivision Plan, the maximum allowed ISA for a single-family lot is 65 percent. With the subject property containing 6,011 square feet (SF) of land, the maximum allowed ISA is 3,907 SF. The applicant is requesting a total ISA of 4,168 (or 69 percent of the lot), representing a 6.7 percent variance to the Forest Lake Estates 2015 Preliminary/ Final Subdivision Plan. This causes the lot to exceed the maximum allowable ISA by four (4) percent (approximately 261 SF).
Per Section 5-4D of Article V of the Land Development Code, any pedestrian walkway, path, patio, driveway, parking space, or other vehicle circulation area shall be set back at least 2 feet from the side and rear property lines. As impervious materials have been installed (without a permit) 1.5 feet from the side property lines and right along the rear property line, the applicant is also requesting a variance to encroach into the side and rear setbacks for impervious materials by 0.5 feet for a proposed ISA setback of 1.5 feet on side and rear yards.
The property has a 5-foot drainage and utility easement along the side property lines, a 5-foot wall easement along the rear property line, and a 10-foot distribution easement also along the rear property line. Concurrent with this variance application, the applicant has submitted a request to vacate all side and rear yard easements on the property. Per Section 5-1 of Article 5, the City cannot interfere with, abrogate, or annul any lawful easement and, therefore, cannot issue permits for the construction of improvements within any easement area. Due to impervious materials being installed without permits within the 5-foot-wide drainage and utility easements along both side yards as well as the 10-foot distribution easement (which would also encompass the 5-foot wall easement), both the easement vacation and a reduction in the impervious material setback would be needed in order for the existing impervious materials to remain.
Because the easement vacation request follows a separate process, this item only reflects the applicant's two (2) variances, as follows: (1) a variance to Article V Section 5-4D of the Land Development Code to encroach into the minimum 2-foot side and rear setback for impervious materials 0.5 feet for a proposed ISA setback of 1.5 feet and (2) a variance to the Forest Lake Estates Planned Unit Development (PUD) Preliminary/ Final Subdivision Plan to exceed the maximum allowed 65 percent impervious surface area (ISA) by four (4) percent (approximately 261 SF), which is the minimum additional ISA needed to keep the proposed 69 percent ISA if the requested easement vacations, which are currently under review, were also approved. The requested variances are for the purpose of installing and retaining paver walkways on both side yards and concrete and pavers in the rear yard, specifically: Installation of pavers for the side porch, and
Installation of paver walkways along the side yards, and
Installation of paver walkways in the rear yard, and
Installation of a concrete patio in the rear yard, and
Installation of a paver fire pit in the rear yard, and
Installation of a paver area around a tree in the rear yard, and
Installation of a concrete slab (basketball court) in the rear yard.
According to Article IV, Section 4- 9A, approval of a variance requires that the applicant demonstrate compliance with four (4) criteria, as follows:That special conditions and circumstances exist which are peculiar to the land, structures, or required subdivision improvements involved and which are not applicable to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements;
That a literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties with similar conditions;
That the special conditions and circumstances do not result from the actions of the applicant; and
That the granting of the variance requested will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by these regulations to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements under similar conditions.
Applicant Response: The applicant's justifications are as follows:Rain and water erosion caused damage to the home’s foundation. Soil was weathered away, and the erosion began to expose the foundation walls. The home’s structural integrity would have been compromised and led to future costly repairs had this damage not been corrected with the placement of the side pavers and repairs to the foundation.
The pavers already exist along with other requests that need permit approval. The current impervious surface area is 67.65 percent. The maximum surface area is 65 percent, and we are requesting to exceed that due to the current surface area total.
Staff Analysis:Staff finds that the justifications provided by the applicant do not support and are not sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the four (4) evaluation criteria. Staff's analysis is summarized below:Criteria 1: Special Circumstances & Conditions: No special conditions and circumstances exist that are peculiar to the land in that the subject lot is of similar dimensions, shape, and size as other lots in this block of the subdivision. The lot is rectangular and, similarly to other lots in the subdivision, has a 5-foot drainage and utility easement along the side lot lines. Additionally, for lots 267 through 278, there is also a distribution easement in the rear of the property. For all side and rear easements, impervious materials are not permitted. In the instance of the easement vacations being approved, there is a minimum 2-foot setback requirement for impervious materials.
Criteria 2: Literal Interpretation of the Code: The literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would not deprive the property owners of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties with similar conditions. Construction of the residence, including the entry, driveway, walkway, AC pad, and rear stoop, yielded an ISA of approximately 32 percent, leaving 33 percent (or approximately 1,984 SF) of ISA available for use by the property owner. Staff finds that the remaining 33 percent ISA (1,984 SF) is ample square footage for the property owners to construct a reasonably sized patio, accessory structures, or any other improvements on the property and still remain compliant with the Code. Staff finds that prohibiting the installation of buildings or structures in easements and requiring a 2-foot side and rear setback for impervious materials would not place an undue burden or hardship on this lot. The Forest Lake Estates Phase 2 Plat Note 12 further reinforces this requirement for lots 267 through 278 (subject lot number 270) by prohibiting buildings, structures, or obstacles (except fences) from being located, constructed, excavated, or created within the distribution easement area.
Criteria 3: Actions of the Applicant: The circumstances of this variance are the result of the actions of the applicant/property owners, as the impervious materials were installed without permits. If they had sought a permit prior to work being completed, staff would have informed them of the requirements. The property was cited by Code Enforcement for having unpermitted pavers in the front and side yards. In an effort to be compliant with Code Enforcement, the applicant/property owners applied for a building permit. During the course of staff review of the building permit, staff found that there were additional unpermitted improvements in the rear of the property that were not indicated on the survey or accounted for in the impervious area calculation sheet (refer to the attached surveys).
Criteria 4: Conference of Special Privilege: Granting the requested variance would confer a special privilege to the applicant/property owners that is denied by these regulations to other lands or required subdivision improvements under similar conditions, as other properties are also not permitted to exceed the maximum allowed ISA, install impervious materials within 2-feet of side and rear property lines or install impervious materials within easements.
Outcomes Based on Application Approvals and Denials: As previously discussed, the variance application is being reviewed concurrently with a separate easement vacation application. Depending on the approval and denial of each of the applications, the following revisions are required for the current building permit in order for it to be approved.Approval of the Easement Vacation and Variance Requests: If the easement vacation and variance requests are approved, (1) the impervious materials may remain within all easement areas, (2) all impervious materials will have a 1.5 feet setback from the side and rear property lines, and (3) the impervious surface area of the lot can be exceeded by four (4) percent for a total ISA of 69 percent.
Denial of the Easement Vacation and Variance Requests: If the easement vacation and variance requests are denied, all impervious materials within the side and rear easement areas, representing approximately 856 SF or 14 percent ISA, must be removed. With this, the lot will be compliant with the Code as there will be no impervious materials within the side and rear easements and the ISA of the lot would be reduced to 55 percent, and no longer exceed the maximum allowed ISA.
Approval of the Easement Vacation and Denial of the Variance Requests: If the easement vacation is approved and the variance requests are denied, impervious material within the 2-foot side and rear setback for impervious materials, representing approximately 156 SF, must be removed, as well as an additional 105 SF of impervious material on the property to reduce the ISA of the lot by a total of 261 SF to reduce the ISA of the lot to the maximum allowed 65 percent.
Denial of the Easement Vacation and Approval of the Variance Requests: If the easement vacation is denied and the variance requests are approved, all impervious material within the side and rear easement areas, representing approximately 856 SF, must be removed. In this instance, the variance requests are not necessary as the impervious material is not allowed in the easement areas regardless of the impervious material setback and the ISA of the lot will be reduced to 55 percent.
Since the start of the permit application (April 2024), staff have had several in-person conversations at City Hall, email correspondences, and a site visit with the property owners related to the exceeded ISA and the installation of impervious materials within easements. Based on what has been presented for review to this point, staff does not support the requested variance as there is insufficient, code-based justification to support the variance.

description:
The Ocoee City Commission approved the implementation of the new Ocoee Neighborhood Matching Grant Program at their meeting on October 15, 2019. The grant program was formerly known as the Most Valuable Partnership Awards (MVP). Staff revamped the MVP to simplify and improve the application process and criteria.
The Neighborhood Matching Grant Program is held annually. This year’s grant cycle opened on February 11, 2025. Applications were due on March 14, 2025. Per City Commission approval, the deadline was extended to April 25, 2025. The neighborhood grant program is for homeowner associations (HOA) and neighborhoods that do not have a structured HOA. The goal of the grant program is to assist residents with making improvements to their neighborhoods. The maximum matching grant award is $2,000. Applicants pay for their improvement projects, and then get a portion back, up to a maximum of $2,000. Given the nature of the grant program, which is to improve city neighborhoods, the Development Services Department conducted the primary review of applications.
Nine (9) Homeowner Associations submitted grant applications for this grant cycle. One HOA’s grant application, Forest Lake Estates’ application, is in question because the applicant finished their project before it was approved. Forest Ridge’s original application was not recommended due to zoning concerns. Forest Ridge was given the opportunity to change their project, which staff now recommends. The total amount requested by the nine neighborhood associations is $17,500.00.

The Magnolia Reserve Townhome Subdivision is located in Commission District 1, on the south side of Desert Candle Drive, east of Renaissance Charter School and West Orange Trail, and generally adjacent to the Greens at Forest Lake Townhome Subdivision.
At the builder's request, the abandonment and vacation request is for the vacation of the front 34-foot portions of the 5-foot utility easements located on the side yards of eight (8) corner lots (specifically Lots 1, 12, 13, 24, 25, 36, 37, and 48) of the Magnolia Reserve Townhomes Subdivision. The request is to vacate an approximately 170 square foot area per lot, which equates to a total of 1,360 square feet of easement area for all eight (8) lots. The specific easement areas to be vacated for the 8 corner lots are all located on the external side yards of the properties and are all 5 feet wide and run 34 feet from the front of the property line towards the rear.
The purpose of the partial vacate is to resolve an issue resulting from the construction of walkways and front porch columns for these 8 lots within the 5-foot utility easement area. For purposes of clarity and accuracy, the full legal descriptions and sketches for the easement areas to be vacated within all 8 lots have been included as exhibits to the proposed Resolution. However, to summarize, Figure 1 shows an example where walkway and part of the townhouse structure encroach into the easement. Staff notes that these easements are not shown on the stamped final subdivision plans (approved October 2023) but are shown on the recorded plat (approved May 2024). Figure 2 depicts the locations (not-to-scale) where the partial vacates for the 8 lots are requested.
As part of the review process, staff sent letters to the standard list of utility providers for their determination of whether they had any concerns and would release their interests in the utility easements. Following receipt of no concerns or objections from the applicable utility providers, staff supports the applicants request for the partial easement vacations on these 8 listed corner lots and has advanced the vacation request to the City Commission for consideration and approval.

description:
The Code Enforcement Board last convened in October 2024. No meetings were held in November or December 2024 due to the meeting date coinciding with a holiday. Furthermore, quorum issues prevented meetings from taking place in January, February, and March 2025. As a result, more than 20 cases have remained unresolved since October 2024. According to the City Code of Ordinances (Chapter 7 - Enforcement of Code), Section 7-5(D), "If a Board member fails to attend two of three successive Board meetings without cause and without prior approval from the Board Chair, the Board will declare the member’s office vacant and report the vacancy to the City Commission, which will promptly fill the vacancy. " Appointments to fill the vacancy will be for the remainder of the unexpired term." The Board Chair did not notify the Code Board Clerk of any excused absences as required by the code, nor did the Board Chair approve any of the absences. There are several concerns related to the lack of quorum: (1) it delays the resolution of cases, leaving violations unresolved and potentially allowing non-compliance to persist; (2) it contributes to a decline in community standards; and (3) it causes inconvenience for the public, who must rearrange their schedules only to discover that meetings have been canceled.
To ensure these code cases move forward, the City Manager has temporarily appointed the Code Enforcement Magistrate to hear these cases, in accordance with Chapter 7, Article 7-3(C) of the City Code of Ordinances. This will provide citizens issued residential code enforcement violations with the opportunity to have their case heard and come into compliance, while also eliminating the burden of case cancelations due to quorum issues. It should be noted that the Special Magistrate currently fills the role of Attorney for the Code Enforcement Board.
City staff now request that the City Commission make a more permanent decision going forward. Several options for the Commission to consider include: (1) appointing alternate members to the board, establishing a pool of individuals who can step in when regular members are absent, ensuring the board can function even with some members missing; or (2) transitioning residential Code Enforcement cases to a special magistrate—a licensed attorney or retired judge—who would handle these cases, streamlining enforcement, reducing delays, and ensuring legal expertise in decision-making.
The Ocoee Police Department recommends reconsidering the Code Enforcement Board and proposes assigning all code enforcement violation cases (both residential and commercial) to the special magistrate to handle. Currently, Red Light Camera Hearings and non-residential Code Enforcement cases are heard by the magistrate, with the agreement set to expire in September 2025. The Special Magistrate will also be required to hear all school zone speed camera enforcement violation hearings. The Police Department's aim is to streamline the adjudication process and enhance efficiency. Additionally, staff recommends approval to proceed with a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) process to hire a new magistrate, as the current agreement is set to expire in September 2025.
title: Discussion on Issues Related to the Code Enforcement Board and Direction to Seek Alternatives to Include Using a Special Magistrate. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The City currently imposes fire assessments within its incorporated area based on a study conducted by Anser Advisory f.k.a. Government Services Group (GSG) in August 2013. Section 2.08 of the City's Fire Protection Assessment Ordinance, adopted as Ordinance No. 2013-010 on August 6, 2013, established the process for determining the Fire Protection Assessment in each subsequent fiscal year.
From Fiscal Year 2014 through Fiscal Year 2025, the annual Fire Assessment rate was set at $69.50 per fire protection unit. For FY 2025, this assessment rate generated approximately $2,425,000 in revenue, covering 17.97% of the Fire Department's total budgeted expenditures of $13,197,529. It is important to note that fire assessment fees cover fire protection services only and do not include EMS-related transport services.
To ensure the Fire Assessment program remains current and legally defensible, Anser Advisory has been contracted to assist the City in updating the program for Fiscal Year 2025–26. Anser Advisory has provided a new City of Ocoee Fire Assessment Memorandum, which includes:A brief and general description of the fire protection services, facilities, or programs to be provided;
The Fire Protection Assessed Cost to be collected for the upcoming fiscal year (this is the total amount of the fire protection budget that will be funded by the assessment);
The proposed new assessment rate for the upcoming fiscal year.
The purpose of this update is to:
1. Develop pro forma budgets and assessment rates for FY 2025–26; and
2. Ensure compliance with recent legislation and case law impacting the legal defensibility of non-ad valorem assessments.
This update involves calculating assessment rates and classifications needed to fully fund the identified assessable costs to provide fire services within the City for Fiscal Year 2025-26. However, the City has the choice of funding all or only a portion of the assessable costs based on policy direction. In addition, the work effort recorded in this Assessment Memorandum requires the identification of the full costs of assessable fire services (minus all revenues) and the allocation of those costs to properties that specially benefit from the provision of such fire services.
Additionally, attached is an Amended and Restated Initial Assessment Resolution for Fire Assessments prepared by consulting attorneys Nabors, Giblin & Nickerson- who previously represented the City on similar matters. This document serves as the Amended and Restated Initial Assessment Resolution as defined in Section 77-1 of the Ordinance. It establishes:
The date, time, and location of a public hearing (July 15, 2025) at which the City Commission will consider adoption of the Amended and Restated Annual Rate Resolution for the upcoming fiscal year; and
Direct the City Manager to update the Assessment Roll and provide required notice via publication and first-class mail to affected property owners.
As stated earlier, the current assessment rate of $69.50 per fire protection unit reflects a 17.97% funding level. Based on Anser Advisory’s updated analysis, the City could impose a maximum rate of $386.75 per unit to fully fund the fire protection budget. However, staff is recommending a rate increase to $139.23 per unit—representing approximately 36% of the funding requirement. This increase would generate an estimated additional $2–$2.1 million in revenue for FY 2025–26.
Even with this proposed increase, the assessment remains modest in light of projected Fire Department expenditures, which are expected to rise to $15.5–$16 million in each of the next five years. This projection reflects:
Continued growth in personnel-related costs,
Scheduled vehicle replacements and station construction and upgrades, and
Inflationary pressure on operational line items.
Maintaining current funding levels and relying on ad valorem taxes to cover the remaining assessable expenditures is becoming increasingly unpredictable with traditional state funding sources. Recently, Florida voters approved Amendment 5 which passed in November 2024, and provides for an annual adjustment to the second $25,000 homestead exemption, which applies to non-school property taxes. The adjustment is tied to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), meaning the exemption will increase if inflation rises. Therefore, a more stable and equitable funding mechanism—such as an updated and legally defensible fire assessment—would provide the City with a predictable and reliable revenue source. By making this change now, we reduce the risk of a larger, more burdensome assessment in the future.
title: Adoption of the Amended and Restated Initial Assessment Resolution for the FY 25-26 Fire Protection Assessments. (Assistant City Manager Rumer)

description:
The Human Relations Diversity Board (HRDB) was established by resolution on September 16, 2003. Subsequent amendments to the resolution followed, with the most recent amendment providing for changes to membership and clarifying requirements as adopted by Resolution 2023-01 on January 17, 2023. The HRDB's general mission is to promote understanding, respect, goodwill, and equality among all citizens and businesses of the City of Ocoee. The board consists of seven (7) voting members: five (5) members are appointed by the City Commissioners, with each Commissioner selecting one member from their respective district, and the Mayor appointing one member from any district. Additionally, two (2) at-large members are chosen by the City Commissioners from a pool of eligible applicants who have submitted an application to serve on City Boards.
In accordance with the by-laws, effective January 1, 2023, the members from District 1, District 3, and the first of the two at-large members were appointed to serve two-year terms, set to expire in May 2025. At the City Commission Meeting held on May 6, 2025, Member Hemraj (Vinny) Singh, representing District 1, and at-large Member Kellie Beck were reappointed. Commissioners Firstner and Oliver were asked to present applicants for consideration at the May 20th Regular Commission Meeting to fill the District 3 seat and the vacant District 4 seat. Commissioner Firstner requested that the City Clerk's Department reach out to the current District 3 member to confirm his interest in reappointment; however, the member expressed uncertainty about continuing to serve. To date, the City Clerk's Department has not received any applications for the District 3 seat. Commissioner Oliver has stated that the sole application, submitted by Robert Henderson of District 4, is his consideration for appointment to the vacant District 4 seat, which has a term expiring in May 2026.
title: Appointment of District 4 Member to the Human Relations Diversity Board (HRDB). (City Clerk Sibbitt)

Florida Statute Section 1006.12, Florida Statutes, entitled "Safe-School officers at each public school", requires each District School Board and School District Superintendent to partner with law enforcement agencies to establish or assign one or more safe-school officers at each school facility within the District by implementing a security option which best meets the needs of the school district. The School Board has suggested that Charter Schools, which are designated as Florida public schools in Section 1002.33, Florida Statutes, should contract for and obtain school resource officers individually with law enforcement agencies.
Innovation Montessori Charter School desires to continue contracting with the Ocoee Police Department for a School Resource Officer for their Ocoee campuses located at 1475 E. Silver Star Road, Ocoee, FL 34761, and 1610 N. Lakewood Avenue, Ocoee, FL 34761. The Ocoee Police Department will provide one (1) School Resource Officer to each Innovation Montessori Charter School campus. Agreements between the City of Ocoee and the Charter Schools are required for the Police Department to understand officer responsibilities and for the City of Ocoee to be reimbursed by the Charter School's Board of Directors. The Charter Schools will be charged a fee for School Resource Officer services based on the 10-month school year. The agreement is effective for a two-year term beginning July 1, 2025, and ending June 30, 2027.

description:
The Florida Legislature has amended Section 1006.12, Florida Statutes, entitled “Safe-School officers at each public school,” requiring each District School Board and Superintendent to partner with law enforcement agencies to establish or assign one or more safe-school officers at each school facility within the district by implementing a security option that best meets the district's needs. The Florida Legislature further amended the laws relating to school safety through the Implementation of Legislative Recommendations of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Commission, which was signed by the Governor on May 8, 2019 and went into effect on October 1, 2019. The School Board of Orange County (SBOC) has elected to comply with Section 1006.12, Florida Statutes, by establishing a School Resource Officer program as defined in Section 1006.12(1). The SBOC has identified those schools within each agency’s jurisdiction that require the assignment of an SRO in order to comply with Section 1006.12, Florida Statutes.
The Ocoee Police Department provides Orange County Public Schools with nine officers and one supervisor. There are five (5) School Resource Officers for the five elementary schools, two (2) School Resource Officers for one middle school, and two (2) School Resource Officers for one high school, all located within the City of Ocoee. An agreement between the City of Ocoee and the School Board of Orange County is required for the Ocoee Police Department to delineate officers' responsibilities and for the City of Ocoee to be reimbursed by the School Board of Orange County for a portion of the officers and a supervisor’s salaries.
This will be a two-year agreement that begins on July 1, 2025, and terminates on June 30, 2027. The agreement commits the School Board of Orange County to reimburse the City of Ocoee $73,000.00 for one supervisor and $73,000.00 per School Resource Officer for the 2025/2026 school year. This agreement also commits the School Board of Orange County to reimburse the City of Ocoee $75,000.00 per supervisor and $75,000.00 per School Resource Officer for the 2026/2027 school year.
title: Approval of a Two-Year School Resource Officer Agreement with the School Board of Orange County. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The Ocoee Police Department is seeking authorization to execute a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Orange County Sheriff’s Office regarding participation in the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network (NIBIN). This agreement will allow a certified Crime Scene Investigator (CSI) from the Ocoee Police Department to conduct firearms testing related to cases that occur within the City of Ocoee and to enter fired cartridge cases into NIBIN. This national network supports ballistic evaluations and generates actionable investigative leads in firearms-related cases.
Firearms testing will be conducted in a controlled environment at the Orange County Sheriff’s Office. The certification and direct access to NIBIN will significantly streamline the investigative process, allowing for quicker turnaround times on ballistic evidence. This will reduce the department’s reliance on the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE), whose backlogs can delay results for weeks or even months.
With this partnership, the Ocoee Police Department anticipates receiving ballistic results within the same week, enabling detectives to develop leads more rapidly and bring cases to resolution more efficiently. Additionally, it will provide greater control over firearms evidence, minimizing chain-of-custody concerns.
Approving this MOU will enhance the department’s ability to solve firearms-related cases promptly and will support the efforts of our detectives, evidence and property personnel, and the State Attorney’s Office in achieving timely case closures.
title: Authorization to execute a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network (NIBIN) with the Orange County Sheriff's Office. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The City Commission approved funding in the current budget to perform contracted sidewalk repairs. Public Works is requesting Commission authorization to piggyback on the existing competitively bid City of Kissimmee contract IFB2022-002, Alternative Paving Methods, awarded to APEC, LLC, which includes sidewalk replacement items. APEC is one of the City of Ocoee's continuing contractors for small construction services providers (RFQ22-005). description: As part of the approved City of Ocoee Budget for Fiscal Year 2023-2024, the Water Facilities Repair & Replacement (R&R) budget includes $65,000.00 to inspect and make necessary repairs to Well #2 at the South Water Plant (SWP). A purchase order in the amount of $14,372.50 was issued to Locke Well & Pump to pull and inspect the pump and 12" flanged pipe, as well as provide a video inspection of the well while the pump was out. After the pump was removed and inspected, it was determined that it would be more cost-effective to replace the pump. In addition, the video inspection of Well #2 revealed damage to the motor shaft assembly and the concrete riser. Locke Well & Pump provided a quote of $62,587.16 to replace the pump and make the necessary structural repairs, bringing the combined cost of this project to $76,959.66. Although this is over the budgeted amount of $65,000.00, the Water Facilities R&R budget has adequate funds available for this project.
title: Approval of the Purchase of a New Pump for Well #2 at the South Water Plant. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description: On Monday, December 16, 2024, the liner in Manhole #4543 (N Lakewood Ave & Security Cir) suffered a catastrophic failure during bypass pumping operations at Lift Station #63 (Security Circle). The failed manhole liner allowed sewage to seep between the layers of the road at the intersection of N Lakewood Avenue & Security Circle, causing the surface of the road to upheave. Staff contacted Cathcart Construction, an approved contractor for construction projects under $500,000.00, who was able to provide immediate assistance by supplying MOT, sewage cleanup, and repaving the damaged section of road after the manhole liner was replaced. Staff notified the City Manager of the damage caused by the failed manhole and received approval to make any repairs necessary in order to open the road as quickly and safely as possible.
title: Notification of an Emergency Purchase with Cathcart Construction Company for Repairs to the Intersection of N Lakewood Avenue and Security Circle in accordance with Section 21.6 of the City of Ocoee Code of Ordinances. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The City of Ocoee is a member of Florida’s Water/Wastewater Agency Response Network (FlaWARN), a formalized system of “utilities helping utilities” during man-made and natural disasters. FlaWARN was established in 2005 after the devastating impacts of 2004’s hurricanes. It is a formalized mutual aid response network of utilities willing to provide critical resources to member utilities during man-made or natural disasters, and is a support entity to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) in partnership with the University of Florida.
Being a member of FlaWARN provides the City access to a database of available resources. However, to receive aid and provide aid to other utilities during and after disasters requires that the City enter into a FlaWARN Mutual Aid Agreement (MMA) for Water/Wastewater. The MMA expedites the rapid emergency response between FlaWARN member utilities by codifying how the City and other utilities share resources such as personnel teams, facilities, equipment, and supplies during recovery efforts. The MMA establishes the terms under which one party provides resources to another party and how reimbursement is fulfilled upfront. Personnel fees are reimbursed for all direct and indirect payroll costs and expenses incurred during the period of assistance, including, but not limited to, employee pensions and benefits. Equipment reimbursement is based on FEMA’s schedule of equipment rates.
FlaWARN provides an extra layer of protection in emergency situations where service restoration is critical. The MMA outlines terms and conditions of reimbursement prior to any member requesting and receiving assistance to ensure both rapid response and reimbursement. Participation in disaster recovery under the MMA is at the City’s discretion.
title: Approval of FlaWARN Mutual Aid Agreement for Water/Wastewater. (Utilities Director Bolling)

The Human Relations Diversity Board (HRDB) was established by resolution on September 16, 2003. Subsequent amendments to the resolution followed, with the most recent amendment providing for changes to membership and clarifying requirements as adopted by Resolution 2023-01 on January 17, 2023. The HRDB's general mission is to promote understanding, respect, goodwill, and equality among all citizens and businesses of the City of Ocoee. The board consists of seven (7) voting members: five (5) members are appointed by the City Commissioners, with each Commissioner selecting one member from their respective district, and the Mayor appointing one member from any district. Additionally, two (2) at-large members are chosen by the City Commissioners from a pool of eligible applicants who have submitted an application to serve on City Boards.
In accordance with the by-laws, effective January 1, 2023, the member appointed from District 1, the member appointed from District 3, and the first of the two (2) at-large members shall serve a two (2) year term. Those terms will expire in May 2025. Additionally, there is also a vacancy in District 4, as that member resigned. At the May 6, 2025, City Commission Meeting, the Commissioners for Districts 1 and 3 may either reappoint the current members or select new individuals who have expressed interest and submitted applications to the City Clerk's Office. These appointments will serve 3-year terms, expiring in May 2028. The City Commission will appoint one (1) at-large member from a list of eligible applicants to serve a 3-year term, also set to expire in May 2028. The District 4 Commissioner will fill the vacant seat for that district, with a new appointment to complete the current 3-year term, which will expire in May 2026. As of April 8, 2025, the City Clerk's Office has received two applications from current members seeking reappointment: Hemraj (Vinny) Singh, who is the current member for the District 1 seat and Kellie Beck, who is the current member for the first of the two at-large seats.
title: Notification of Initial Two-Year Term Ending for Two (2) District Members, One (1) At-Large Member, and One (1) Vacancy on the Human Relations Diversity Board. (Deputy City Clerk Parks)

description:
On April 1, 2025, the City Commission selected SSS Down To Earth OPCO LLC (DTE), to take over the Forest Lake Golf Course Interim operations. DTE was selected from three (3) qualified local vendors to take over the Golf Course's interim operations from May 1, 2025, to November 3, 2025. This interim management plan implements an interim operator that is tasked with creating a first-class maintenance program for the Golf Club, which will result in optimum agronomic, turf and playing conditions on a year-round basis, taking into consideration an Operating Plan approved by the City.
Additional items of interest are:
Restaurant / Food and Beverage Operations. Manager shall perform all the food and beverage operations at the Golf Club, including banquet/catering services.
Resident Rate. Manager shall implement a discounted greens fee rate for all Ocoee Residents, subject to additional terms, conditions, and restrictions from Owner.
Golf Shop. Manager will provide operations in the Golf Shop consistent with the Golf Club Quality Standard
Driving Range. The driving range shall be open from dawn to dusk every day that the Golf Course is open for play.
Manager shall comply with all requirements of any Permits and with all Laws applicable to the Effluent System permit.
As reviewed and approved by the Commission at the April 1, City Commission meeting, the Management Fee for DTE is based on the following:Base Management Fee. Manager shall be paid a base management fee in the amount of Five Thousand and No/00 Dollars ($5,000.00) per month. The Base Management Fee shall be comprehensive of all of Manager’s expenses, and except as expressly set forth herein and/or in the Operating Plan, or as otherwise approved, in writing, by Owner, no administrative expenses or additional overhead or other direct or indirect costs of Manager shall be billed directly or indirectly to Owner.
Incentive Fee. Manager shall share any Net Income received by Owner, reconciled on a monthly basis, in a ratio of seventy percent (70%) to Owner and thirty percent (30%) to the Manager, provided that the Incentive Fee shall not exceed Four Thousand Dollars ($4,000.00) per month.
Management Fee Cap. The Management Fee shall not exceed Nine Thousand Dollars ($9,000.00) in any calendar month during the Term.
title: Approval of a Management Agreement with SSS Down To Earth OPCO LLC, for Interim Operator of Forest Lake Golf Course. (Assistant City Manager Rumer)

description:
The 409 Business Park, 409 Ocoee Apopka Rd. property is in Commission District 3, about 725 feet north of the intersection of Ocoee Apopka Rd. and West Silver Star Rd. The developer has completed construction of the subdivision's infrastructure improvements and requested a Certificate of Completion. The infrastructure improvements include potable water, sanitary sewer, reclaimed water, utilities, roadways, stormwater collection system, perimeter wall/fencing, and associated landscaping. All identified punch list repairs have been completed, and the developer is ready to start the two-year warranty period for the public improvements.
As a requirement of the Land Development Code, the developer must furnish the City with a Surety to cover any possible damage discovered during the next two years. Should the developer not choose to make those repairs, SFG Ocoee Owner, LP has provided the City with a Warranty Bond in the amount of 10% of the constructed improvements cost. The attached Maintenance, Materials, and Workmanship Agreement (Form 8 from the Land Development Code) acts as the executable document between the developer and the City. The Surety will be returned to the developer upon completion of the two-year warranty period and the repair of any damages caused over those two years.
title: Approval of a Two-Year Warranty Surety Bond and Maintenance, Materials, and Workmanship Agreement for SFG Ocoee Owner, LP for the 409 Business Park, 409 Ocoee Apopka Rd. (Development Engineer Keaton)

description:
On January 16, 2024, the City executed the agreement with Kimley-Horn & Associates (KHA) to provide professional services for the City of Ocoee’s Land Development Code (LDC) Update. Following the kickoff meeting, the consultant held numerous meetings with city staff, as well as reviewed the City's regulations and pertinent planning studies. KHA delivered their first draft LDC on December 31, 2024. On January 22, 2025, staff notified the firm that they had found the first draft of the LDC to be unacceptable due to a multitude of issues, omissions, and inconsistencies. Between January and mid-February, staff from both the City and KHA met multiple times to review the outline and content. On February 18, KHA submitted a revised first draft of the LDC. Following its submission, staff continued discussions with KHA regarding the updated draft. Upon reviewing the document, staff noted that while the reorganization generally aligned with the outline they had provided, there remain significant issues and apparent misunderstandings between what staff intended to convey and what KHA delivered.
Therefore, after much discussion among City staff, including the City Manager’s Office, a consensus was reached to terminate the KHA contract. On April 1, 2025, KHA was notified that City staff would request the City Commission to terminate the KHA contract on April 15, 2025. KHA was instructed to stop work immediately by the Development Services Director, except for the time required to package and forward their work effort to date to the City. Following KHA's final invoice, it is estimated that $56,000 will not be expended by KHA.
As a reminder, the City Commission has approved a resolution adopting the Pending Legislation Doctrine (also referred to as the Pending Ordinance Doctrine) in relation to Envision 2045 and the updated Land Development Code. This resolution serves to notify the public and all relevant parties that the City is actively in the process of finalizing its new governing policy framework, as outlined in Envision 2045 and the updated Land Development Code. Consequently, any land development applications submitted after the expiration of the processing moratorium on March 17, 2025, will be subject to the provisions set forth in Envision 2045 and the new Land Development Code.
With the Comprehensive Plan draft now complete, and pursuant to the provisions of the Pending Ordinance Doctrine, staff have the necessary authority and time to finalize the Land Development Code. Staff remain committed to meeting the target completion date for the LDC by August 2025.
title: Approval to Terminate Contract #23-010 with Kimley-Horn & Associates to Update the City's Land Development Code. (Development Services Director Ginger)

description: During an inventory of the Police Department’s armory, it was confirmed that several unused and outdated firearms remained in storage. These weapons are no longer in active service and are incompatible with the department’s current operational standards. The cache of weapons consists of various models phased out over time. The following firearms have been identified: (6) Mossberg 12-gauge shotguns, (2) 37mm gas launchers, (2) Springfield Armory M1 Garand rifles, (2) Glock 45 handguns, (9) Glock 19 handguns, (1) Winchester Model 94 .30-.30 rifle, (2) Colt AR-15 .223 carbine rifles, (1) Colt Law Enforcement Carbine 5.56 rifle, (1) Ruger AR-556 5.56mm rifle. SSD International has offered the Ocoee Police Department a trade-in credit of $10,251.00 for these firearms. In exchange, the Ocoee Police Department would use this credit towards purchasing (9) new FN short-barreled rifles, increasing the number of issuable weapons by nine (9) and helping ensure that the department’s equipment remains modern and operationally consistent. In addition, exchanging these unused and outdated weapons will free up critical storage space within the armory. This transaction will be completed at no cost to the City of Ocoee or the Police Department.
title: Approval to Trade in Older Firearms for Credit Towards the Purchase of New Rifles. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
In compliance with the City of Ocoee (City) Purchasing code, Ch. 21, sealed proposals were solicited from qualified firms to provide pest control and fertilization services for the control of lawn pests, weeds, and vegetation at the City of Ocoee's athletic fields as needed.
The request for proposals was publicly advertised on January 26, 2025, and publicly opened on March 11, 2025. A total of four (4) proposals were received at the bid opening, with one proposal deemed non-responsive and rejected for failure to provide the required bid security. The term contract is for an initial three (3) years with two (2) automatic one-year renewals, and one (1) optional renewal at the City’s discretion. Prices remain firm for the initial three (3) year term, with price adjustments considered during the renewal terms.
The three responsive proposals were reviewed by the Finance Department and provided to the RFP Evaluation Committee. The Evaluation Committee comprised of five members: Dan Abdo, Parks and Leisure Services Operations Manager; Toren Hogan, Parks and Leisure Services Operations Manager; Doug Gaines, Parks and Leisure Services Assistant Director; Chris Hines, Parks and Leisure Services Supervisor; and Trent Hopper, Assistant Director Utilities Department. The public RFP Evaluation Committee meeting was held on March 25, 2025, with the Evaluation Committee evaluating and shortlisting the firms on specific evaluation criteria as shown in the attached shortlist and evaluation forms. The evaluation committee recommends award to the top-ranked firm, Lake Jem Farms, per the attached award recommendation from Dan Abdo, Parks and Leisure Services Operations Manager.
The City denied a bid protest received from TruGreen. A copy of the protest is attached along with the City's response, which was reviewed by the City Attorney.

description:
The approved Facilities Maintenance Division capital budget includes the replacement of generators at three (3) of the City's fire stations. The current generators have come to the end of their service life, with frequent costly repairs due to low parts availability. The City traditionally purchases equipment through various competitively bid annual contracts. Public Works has researched pricing and has found the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office provides competitively bid pricing for equipment utilizing competitively bid contracts. Their contract document requirements included a Request For Proposal (RFP), an award letter, and a response.
Public Works would like to piggyback off of Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office's term contract for the three (3) fire station generator replacements, utilizing IPS Power Systems (parent company of TAW Power Systems, Inc.) as the contractor. IPS Power Systems was also responsible for the installation of the generator in the New City Hall building, as well as maintenance of generators city-wide. The replacement of the fire station generators is proposed at the following prices:
Fire Station 25: 563 S. Bluford Ave. - $95,820.26
Fire Station 26: 1500 N. Clarke Rd. - $58,076.25
Fire Station 39: 2515 Maguire Rd. - $58,076.25
Public Works recommends issuing purchase orders to IPS Power Systems for the above amounts, as they will be primarily utilized for maintaining the equipment. Public Works would also like approval to designate the old generators as surplus to be auctioned through the City's annual surplus process.
title: Approval to Surplus and Replace Stand-by Generators for Ocoee Fire Stations. (Assistant Public Works Director Gajadhar)

A Shared Access Easement Agreement was established on June 15, 2004, between the City and the previous owner of the FC 429 Property (Daryl M. Carter). On December 11, 2024, the City Commission approved the City's annual operating budget. After the budget was adopted, the City faced unexpected demands that have created a need for a budget amendment. These unexpected needs include new program opportunities, particularly within Parks & Leisure Services, as well as additional funding requirements for essential services such as the General Fund and Water/Wastewater Fund. Additionally, rising costs related to the City's health insurance program became evident, further necessitating the need for a budget amendment for the cumulative costs of the health insurance program across all funds.
The total adopted General Fund budget was $75,835,480. However, the General Fund requires an additional expense of $5,835,797 for the following:

Police Operations require $80,902 for an unanticipated increase in the contractual services and legal expenses.
In relation to this requirement, the Finance Department has identified $529,611 that can be returned to the General Fund reserves out of the remaining funds from Capital Fund completed projects. This lowers the total Fund requirement from the General Fund Balance to $5,306,186.
The Recreation Program fund budget adopted was $141,554. The Recreation Program Fund requires the accounting of additional revenues and expenses since the City Commission approved the takeover of Ocoee Little League operations. Operational control began on February 8, 2025. The City received revenue from this program in addition to the $12,000 check issued by the Ocoee Little League Board as a revenue source.

Additionally, the Water/Wastewater fund will receive a supplemental appropriation of Loan from the General fund implementing the Seventh Amendment to the Lease Agreement for Forest Lake Golf Club in the amount of $4,500,000.
The Stormwater fund adopted a budget of $4,243,000. The Stormwater fund requires an additional appropriation of $43,323 for:

description:
Chapter 163, Part II, Florida Statutes, requires local governments to adopt a comprehensive plan that establishes principles, guidelines, standards, and strategies for the City's orderly and balanced economic, social, physical, environmental, and fiscal development. Section 163.3177(5)(a), F.S., requires that the Comprehensive Plan include at least two planning periods: one covering at least the first 10-year period occurring after the plan’s adoption and the other covering at least a 20-year period.
The current Comprehensive Plan, adopted on October 1, 2002, has reached its long-term planning horizon of 2022. Therefore, "The Comprehensive Plan must be updated to include the statutorily required ten-year and twenty-year planning horizons." In accordance with Section 163.3177(6), F.S., the Comprehensive Plan is based on relevant and appropriate data and analysis including, but not be limited to, surveys, studies, and other data available at the time of the preparation of the plan, as well as data prepared by the City, all of which are included within a Data, Inventory, and Analysis (DIA) document. Ocoee's DIA document contains an evaluation of historical growth and development trends. It also includes the City's 2045 population projections based on several methodologies (including those listed in Florida Statutes), an evaluation of anticipated demands, and an assessment of the City's ability to accommodate these demands on public infrastructure and municipal services, including completion of the 10-Year Water Supply Plan.
Thus, in accordance with Chapter 163, Part II, Florida Statutes, the City developed a Vision Statement and prepared an updated Comprehensive Plan, entitled "Envision 2045 Ocoee Comprehensive Plan" ("Envision 2045"), which consists of two (2) volumes.
Volume one is the Envision 2045 Ocoee Comprehensive Plan policy document, which is Exhibit A of the ordinance proposed for adoption. The policy document will be the governing framework that directs growth and development in the city over the next 10-year and 20-year planning horizons. The Envision 2045 policy document includes a Vision Statement, Goals, Objectives, and Policies to achieve its vision of Ocoee becoming “a vibrant, attractive, and economically sustainable community where businesses thrive and neighborhoods flourish through diverse, compact, and complementary land uses that produce quality developments, enhanced and active public realms, and safe and efficient mobility systems while simultaneously preserving environmental systems and creating parks, trails, and open spaces to promote social engagement, community health, and overall well-being of the City".
Volume two is the Data, Inventory, and Analysis document, which serves as supporting documentation to volume one and which is not proposed for adoption.
Envision 2045 and the supporting DIA document were prepared in-house by a multidisciplinary and multi-department Comprehensive Planning Team comprised of technical staff from the Development Services, Public Works, Utilities, and Parks and Leisure Services Departments, with technical assistance from the City's transportation consultant firm regarding the Transportation Element (which has been renamed the Mobility Element). It reflects the City Commission's direction and public feedback received during the preparation of the City's Evaluation and Appraisal Report (EAR) and Special Area Plans, including the Downtown Master Plan and the SR 429 Overlay District, along with its three Character Area Plans, which the City Commission has adopted within the past 10 years. This Plan update also recognizes the changing trends in the market and development community.
Because this update is a repeal and replacement of the expired 2002 Comprehensive Plan, the goals, objectives, and policies within the proposed Envision 2045 policy document are not presented in strike-through/underline format. Some existing policies were kept but were reworded, combined, or reorganized into updated Objectives. Additionally, the 2002 Comprehensive Plan was organized by Elements, but with this Update, the Elements within the Plan are proposed to be organized by topic-oriented Chapters, as presented below:
Envision 2045 Chapters1Introduction2Vibrant, Attractive & Inclusive Community
Future Land Use ElementHousing (Revitalization & Neighborhood Preservation) ElementRecreation & Open Space Element3Efficient, Reliable, and Well-Maintained Infrastructure
Infrastructure ElementUtility Sub-ElementDrainage Sub-Element4Safe & Convenient Mobility
Mobility Element5Environment-Friendly, Resilient & Sustainable Community
Conservation Element6Responsible, Accessible & Open Governance
Public Schools Facilities ElementIntergovernmental Coordination ElementCapital Improvements ElementPrivate Property Rights ElementAppendix
Supporting Resources
AcronymsPlaceholder [5-Year Capital Improvements Plan][Placeholder Water Supply Plan]
A summary of the major changes in each element is provided below.
Future Land Use Element (FLUE): Creation of two (2) new land use categories: Low Medium Density Residential (LMDR) with a density range of 5 to 8 dwelling units per acre and Mixed Use (MU) with a density of up to 20 units per acre and intensity of up to 3.0 floor area ratio (similar to the FAR for the current Commercial and Industrial categories). Bonus dwelling units per acre may be available to enhance architectural and public realm improvements.
Creation of policies that provide specific locational requirements for the application of the Mixed Use category, as well as urban (site) and architectural requirements for developments within the Mixed Use category.
Adjustments to the density ranges within the current residential land use categories to (1) accommodate projected population growth, (2) improve the City's competitiveness in the market, and (3) increase flexibility in development patterns, specifically:Low Density Residential from "up to 4 units per acre" to "up to 5 units per acre",
Medium Density Residential from "4 to less than 8 units per acre" to "8 to 15 units per acre" (NOTE: The starting density for MDR aligns with the ending density for the proposed new LMDR category.)
High Density Residential from "8 to 16 units per acre" to "15 to 20 units per acre", and
Allowing residential density within the Commercial and Industrial categories under certain, specific but limited, circumstances.
Creation of policy and specific criteria for approval of amendments to the Future Land Use Map (FLUM).
Creation of policies that clearly define the meanings of density and intensity, as well as the calculation method for maximum development potential (transition from gross to net land area) when an application for a FLUM amendment is proposed.
Creation of new objectives related to managing growth and development patterns that enhance the quality of life, prioritize a safe and connected built environment to promote community health and wellness, and adopt sustainable and innovative development practices. This includes prioritizing projects and strategies that foster economic sustainability and vitality.
Identification and mapping of the Downtown District and the Community Redevelopment Area (CRA) District on the Future Land Use Map and amending the Future Land Use Map to apply the new Mixed Use category to the Downtown District and the CRA District.
Removal of duplicate language from the FLUE that exists in other Elements.
Housing Element:Reorganizing and rewording existing priorities within the current Objectives and placing those policies under clear new objectives.
Creation of a "Housing For All" program to ensure housing choices for current and future residents through all stages of life.
Creation of a "Live Here/Grow Here" initiative (developed by staff and not associated with the Live Local Act) that prioritizes the coordination of land use planning, housing, and transportation planning to ensure that the built environment and development patterns within the city create a community environment where people want to move to or stay in Ocoee and thrive.
Strengthening policies to protect and help ensure housing availability for the elderly and other special populations.
Creation of policies to guide the preservation, maintenance, and restoration of historically significant properties and resources.
Recreation and Open Space Element:Update the level of service for parks from 4 acres of parks and open space per 1,000 residents to 8 acres of parkland and civic open space per 1,000.
Inclusion of policies geared towards achieving a goal of one (1) park per 2,346 residents.
Establishing a goal to achieve the National Recreation and Parks Association (NRPA) median level of service, which is 10.2 acres of parkland and civic open space per 1,000 residents, by 2045.
Reiteration and strengthening of the City's goal of creating a coordinated, comprehensive, diverse, accessible, sustainable, and inclusive parks system to create a healthy and active community for all ages and abilities through neighborhood, community, regional, and nature parks and specialty facilities. A key concept in park performance is creating the 10-minute walk to parks, which translates to a half (1/2) mile distance that most people are willing to walk to reach a destination.
Objectives and policies regarding park facilities planning, park funding, resource management, sustainability, and stewardship.
Infrastructure Element:Updates to the level of service standards for potable water and wastewater.
Creation of a level of service for drainage and stormwater systems and facilities.
Strengthening objectives and policies related to water conservation and water quality protection, including protection of surface waters and the aquifer.
Policies to strengthen flood resiliency.
Mobility Element: Development of objectives and policies that shift transportation planning and design from the traditional auto-oriented mode to a context-oriented (or context classification-based) mode.
Prioritizing safe pedestrian and bicycle travel and mode choices through the creation of a level of service standard for pedestrian and bicycle facilities, as measured by the "level of traffic stress" (from 1 to 4). LTS gauges the comfort levels experienced by pedestrians and bicyclists traveling on roadways (the lower the number, the greater the comfort level).
Inclusion of objectives and policies to direct greater coordination between land use, transportation planning, and housing, and to reduce pressure to widen roadways at a great expense through identifying opportunities for parallel or interconnected roadways and gridded streets, whenever possible.
Conservation Element:Strengthening, clarifying, and reorganizing objectives and policies to protect wetlands to meet or exceed Federal, State, and County requirements.
Strengthening objectives and policies for floodplain protection that exceed the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) requirements, thereby increasing the City’s classification within the Community Rating System (CRS) to ensure residents are eligible for insurance discounts.
Establishing objectives and policies that require sustainable and low-impact development, including provisions that encourage: Expansion of an EV infrastructure within the City,
Protection and expansion of the City’s Urban Tree Canopy,
Implementation of a Vegetative Roof Ordinance, and
Implementation of policies that protect community access to the night sky by reducing light pollution.
Capital Improvements Element:Updates were relative to updating the level of service standards as provided in each of the above relevant Elements,
Combined policies regarding the prioritization of capital projects into a single section, and
Removed duplicate language and tables from the Public School Facilities 10-Year Capital Outlay Plan and other date-specific revenue sources, revenue expenditures, and other financial commitments that have now passed.
Generally, no changes were proposed within the Public School Facilities Element, the Intergovernmental Coordination Element, or the Private Property Rights Element. The only changes are related to reorganizing existing policies, removing outdated or no longer applicable references to the Florida Administrative Code, and policy commitments that have already been fulfilled within the past 20-year planning horizon.
Based on current tracking, the completion of Envision 2045 Comprehensive Plan is as follows:Planning and Zoning Commission Hearing - April 8, 2025
City Commission 1st Reading Transmittal - April 15, 2025
Transmit to State Agencies for their Commenting Period of up to 45 days - May 30, 2025
City Commission 2nd Reading/Adoption - June 17, 2025

description:
Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPRs) have become valuable tools in modern law enforcement, aiding in the identification of stolen vehicles, missing persons, and suspects involved in criminal activities. Flock Safety, a prominent provider of ALPR technology, offers solutions designed to improve public safety through advanced data collection and analysis. The City has the opportunity to increase its current inventory of FLOCK ALPRS from ten to fifteen units through a partnership with the Orange County Sheriff’s Office (OCSO), which serves as the Grant Stakeholder for the Urban Area Security Initiative (UASI) Grant. For five years, OCSO assumes all financial responsibility for the hardware, software, and Professional Services associated with the cameras, which the UASI 23 Grant will fund. At the end of the five-year cycle, the City has the option to assume financial responsibility for continuing the contract with FLOCK Safety, which would involve a 24-month agreement for approximately $35,000.
The only initial requirement is for the City to install a breakaway pole on the right-of-way at the intersection of Franklin Street and State Road 429, at a cost of $600. The camera locations will be at the following intersections: Clarcona Ocoee Road & North Lakewood Avenue, Clarcona Ocoee Road & Clarke Road, Maguire Road & Tomyn Road, Maguire Road & Old Winter Garden Road, and Franklin Street & State Road 429.
title: Approval for Additional Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR) within the City. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
In compliance with the Consultants’ Competitive Negotiations Act (CCNA), § 287.055, Florida Statutes, the Federal Procurement Standards set forth in the Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR 200.317 through 2 CFR 200.327, as applicable, and Chapter 21 of the City of Ocoee's (City) Code of Ordinances, the City solicited statements of qualifications from licensed professional architectural firms that are interested in providing general professional architectural services for various planning and design, and development review projects. The work may consist of, but will not necessarily be limited to: design, planning, inspection, and assessment; conceptual design; construction plan preparation; and construction management for public projects by the City. The firms selected by the City will provide architectural services to the City on an as-needed basis, which will be assigned using task orders/service authorizations issued by the City under the continuing contracts. Projects may also include those funded through federal grants.
The City intends to award continuing contracts to the top two (2) ranked firms, deemed to be the most highly qualified to perform the required services, with the top-ranked firm initially chosen to undertake Task Order 1, the Fire Station Architectural Design Project. description:
The approved W. Oakland Avenue Reconstruction Project includes improvements to the potable water and gravity sewer systems. description:
The City of Ocoee has appropriated $28,000 for the Neighborhood Matching Grants this fiscal year. The application is located on the City's website. The original due date was March 14, 2025. A press release was distributed, and the information was also posted on the City's website, Facebook page, and via a flyer in the City Hall lobby. Additionally, an article covering this information was published in the Orange Observer. Staff initially received only two (2) applications; therefore, staff extended the deadline by two weeks, to March 28, 2025. Staff then issued a second press release, sent an email directly to all the City's HOAs, and posted an additional update on the City's Facebook page. Despite these efforts, staff has not received any additional applications, which is highly unusual as this program typically brings in a minimum of ten (10). As a result, staff has extended the deadline again, to April 7, 2025, and asked the Mayor and Commissioners to contact HOAs in their districts to gauge interest. Currently, staff has two (2) complete applications and one pending submission. Additionally, staff was contacted by an HOA recipient who received funding last fiscal year and expressed interest in applying during this program cycle after being contacted by their District Commissioner.
At the October 15, 2019, City Commission Meeting, the implementation of the criteria for administering neighborhood grants was approved. That criteria included the following clause: "regardless if the neighborhood has an HOA or not, subdivisions may only apply for grant funds every other year". Given the low number of applications received this year, staff is asking the City Commission to discuss accepting applications from last year's recipients, for this year only.
title: Discussion and Direction Regarding the 2025 Neighborhood Matching Grant Program. (Parks and Leisure Services Deputy Director Gaines)

Section C-9 of the Ocoee City Charter states: … “The Mayor pro tem shall be elected from among the Commissioners by the City Commission but shall continue to represent the district in which such Commissioner resides. The Mayor pro tem shall be elected at the first City Commission meeting following the swearing in of the candidates elected at each general city election … and shall serve as Mayor pro tem until the successor is elected.”
On March 20, 2007, the City Commission established a policy to annually select the Mayor pro tem, even during non-election years. Then, on April 6, 2021, the City Commission agreed to rotate the Mayor pro tem annually based on districts. In 2023, Commissioner Wilsen (District 2) was selected to serve as Mayor pro tem due to the vacancy in the District 4 seat, followed by Commissioner Kennedy (District 1) in 2024. To maintain the annual rotation based on districts, Commissioner Wilsen (District 2) should be elected as Mayor pro tem for the 2025-2026 term.

description:
Recently, around 700,000 administrative (civil) arrest warrants (Form I-205) issued by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) were entered into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database. As a result, officers engaged in everyday policing activities may encounter individuals for whom ICE has issued an administrative arrest warrant. However, officers who are not 287(g) deputized by the Department of Homeland Security are not authorized to serve or make arrests based on these administrative warrants, even if they appear in NCIC records. Only federal agents or officers with immigration authority, or state or local officers/deputies who are 287(g) deputized, have the authority to make arrests on these warrants.
ICE is currently updating its virtual immigration enforcement training to enable law enforcement officers to become 287(g) deputized. The training spans 40 hours, and it must be completed within 60-days. The Ocoee Police Department is looking to have one sworn officer become 287(g) deputized to comply with the 287 (g) Task Force Model Memorandum of Agreement (MOA). According to ICE, the 287(g) program allows the delegation of certain immigration officer functions to state and local law enforcement under ICE's direction and oversight. The Task Force Model acts as a force multiplier for law enforcement agencies, granting limited immigration authority under ICE supervision during routine police duties. This MOA outlines the terms and conditions under which selected law enforcement agency (LEA) personnel will be nominated, trained, and approved by ICE to carry out specific immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and supervision within the LEA’s jurisdiction. It also details the scope of immigration officer duties that DHS authorizes participating LEA personnel to perform.
title: Approval of Memorandum of Agreement 287 (g) Task Force Model Between the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the City of Ocoee. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description: This West Orange Narcotics Task Force Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into by and between the City of Winter Garden (“Winter Garden”), the City of Apopka (“Apopka”), the City of Ocoee (“Ocoee”), and John W. Mina, as Sheriff of Orange County, Florida (“Sheriff”) (“Parties”). The Parties desire to continue operating the joint West Orange Narcotics Task Force (“WONTF”) to combat illegal narcotics and related criminal activity in or near Winter Garden, Apopka, and Ocoee and the unincorporated areas of Orange County. Winter Garden, Apopka, and Ocoee wish to continue providing sworn law enforcement officers to staff the WONTF, and the Parties benefit from their joint efforts to combat illegal narcotics and related criminal activities, which often cross jurisdictional lines. Winter Garden, Apopka, and Ocoee each have an Operational Assistance and Voluntary Cooperation Agreement with the Sheriff, which requires requests for mutual aid to be in writing for specific events unless certain circumstances present themselves. description:
Attached is a departmental listing of items requested to be declared as surplus property. A tentative listing was given to all departments, allowing an opportunity to request any items meeting their departmental needs. All transfer requests are removed from the surplus list, and any capital transfer requests will come before the City Commission for approval at a later date. The Police Department’s unclaimed evidence and abandoned property have been transferred to the City, per the attached memorandum. The fire equipment items on the surplus list identified as ID Code “D” will be donated to the First Response Training Group-Fire Academy, per the attached request.
Staff requests the approval of the City Commission to contract with George Gideon Auctioneers, Inc., Zellwood, Florida for the public sale of the City’s surplus property. These items are identified on the list as ID Code “G”. Due to market demand, Gideon Auctioneers performs online auctions only. Gideon Auctioneers will continue to act as the dealer in transferring all titles and collecting sales tax, collecting payments, removing city markings and preparing items for sale, taking auction pictures and listing each item, which includes answering questions and showing the items to the public. This action will present the City with the opportunity for a larger coverage area with more convenience for the public and would alleviate the overtime costs and auctioneer fees incurred in conducting the auction in-house. The City successfully utilized Gideon Auctioneers for previous surplus sales, and found the proceeds received for items sold by Gideon Auctioneers to be comparable to those sold directly by the City or by other online auction platforms.
Gideon Auctioneers has contracted with numerous other governmental agencies, and the City would be piggybacking on the School District of Osceola County’s Online Auction Services Contract, competitively solicited RFP #SDOC-25-P-007-LV, Contract #C-25-0393-LV, which expires January 25, 2028, and may be extended by the School District. Gideon Auctioneers receives a 9% buyer paid premium for all titled items (vehicles/on-road equipment), an 18% buyer paid premium for miscellaneous items, and a 2% buyer paid online bid processing fee, which is common for this industry. There is no commission charge to the City.
Any items that do not sell will be listed again, or other selling options will be explored by staff and brought back to the City Commission for approval. A detailed report of all items sold and their respective amounts will be forwarded to the City along with payment within fourteen (14) business days of the end of the auction. The surplus property will be transported to the Gideon Auctioneers property located at 2753 N. Hwy. 441, Zellwood, FL 32798. The public inspection of items at the auction site is during business hours from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., 3:00 p.m. for deliveries. A link to the City’s surplus auctions on Gideon Auctioneer’s auction site will be placed on the City’s website. In compliance with Florida Statute §274, the public notice of auction will be advertised in the Orlando Sentinel, the West Orange Times, and the City’s website.

description:
The approved Fleet Maintenance Division capital budget includes the replacement of fuel dispensers at the four (4) fueling locations throughout the City. The current dispensers are the originally installed units which have come to the end of their service life, with frequent costly repairs due to low parts availability.
