attachments.name: Ordinance for FY 2026 Year-End Budget Amendment

description:
Annually, the City is required to reconcile its budget at the close of each fiscal year. On September 17, 2025, the City Commission approved Ordinance 2025-20, adopting the budget for fiscal year 2026. Pursuant to Florida Statute 166.241(8), the governing body of a municipality may amend the budget for a prior fiscal year at any time during that year or within 60 days following its conclusion. In accordance with this provision, the City Commission adopted mid-year budget amendments through Ordinance 2026-07 on June 2, 2026, and Ordinance 2026-15 on August 4, 2026.
Following a review of fund activities through September 30, 2026, there is a need for a budget amendment to address additional appropriations of revenue and expenditures for the General Fund; the Stormwater Fund; the Police Impact Fund; the Police Trust Fund; the Police Training Fund; The Spring Conservation Fund; the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) Fund; the Debt Service Fund; The Water and Wastewater Fund; the Water Capital Fund; the Wastewater Capital Fund; the Forest Lake Golf Course Fund; and the Health Insurance Fund prior to the fiscal-year close. This amendment will not raise the City’s millage rate and will have no impact on the overall financial position of the funds.
Details of the General Fund Budget Adjustment:Received an additional $72,365 related to the half-cent sales tax.
Refund of previous year’s transfer to the Spring Conservation Fund.
General government operations require $27,290 for FEMA reimbursement to other funds for costs related to Hurricane Ian.
An additional $66,834 in expenditures related to workers' compensation claim liability from prior years. Allocated as follows:
$56,992 to the Police Department.
$9,842 to the Fire Department.
The Stormwater Fund requires an additional appropriation of $2,854 in reserves for FEMA reimbursement of costs related to Hurricane Ian.
The Police Impact Fund requires an additional appropriation of $2,680 in reserves for FEMA reimbursement of costs related to Hurricane Ian.
The Police Trust and Training funds accounting to reflect increases in both revenue and expenses related to the confiscated property activity and police education program:$10,000 for confiscated property activity.
$8,700 for the police education program.
The Police Community Programs Fund requires a transfer from the General Fund to cover additional community program costs.
The Spring Conservation fund requires an adjustment to reflect the refund of a prior year transfer from the General Fund.
The Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) Fund requires an additional appropriation of $199 in reserves for FEMA reimbursement of costs related to Hurricane Ian.
The Debt Service fund requires additional revenue to cover the agent fee related to annual debt service payments.
The General Government Capital Fund requires a budget true-up to show additional transfers from the Police Department budget to cover the cost of replacing police vehicles in excess of insurance proceeds received.
The Water and Wastewater Fund requires an additional appropriation of $21,557 in reserves for FEMA reimbursement of costs related to Hurricane Ian.
The Water and Wastewater Capital funds require a budget true-up to show additional capital charges revenue as well as amounts refunded after construction was completed, and the final capacity provided was known.
The Forest Lake Golf Course fund requires a budget true-up to reflect additional course revenue and expenditures to match actual results for the year.
The Health Insurance Fund requires a budget true-up to reflect additional workers' compensation premiums from the General Fund and additional workers' compensation claim liability from prior years. An adjustment is also needed to show actual payroll contributions (City and employees), as well as the actual health claims and related costs incurred in the fiscal year. The total increase in both revenue and expense is $1,600,403.

The City decommissioned the Jamela Storage Building, formerly a water storage tank located at 1107 Wurst Rd., in the early 2000s and subsequently repurposed the facility for storage. Recently, the building’s air-conditioning units failed, and the roof developed multiple leaks. Due to the structure’s age and overall condition, repairing these issues is not financially practical. All necessary stored materials have already been relocated by a hazardous material contractor. Staff therefore recommends approval to demolish the structure in order to eliminate ongoing City liability. Adjacent property owners will be notified prior to the start of work, and appropriate precautions will be taken due to the structure’s proximity to surrounding residential buildings.
The Public Works Department recommends utilizing the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Term Contract for Demolition Services, Contract Agreement BEI37, and selecting Cross Construction Services as the contractor. The proposed cost for demolition is $49,742.50. In addition, the State requires an asbestos survey prior to demolition, which Cross Construction Services will also perform at a cost of $2,570. Public Works recommends approval of this award.
title: Approval for Demolition of Structure at 1107 Wurst Rd. (CIP Administrator Gajadhar)

description:
The Healthy West Orange Trails Connection (HWOTC) is an organization consisting of a collaborative inter-jurisdictional committee to implement the ideas of the Healthy West Orange Trails Initiative. The Initiative was created in 2021, with the mission of "bring[ing] together partners in the shared goal of promoting and activating the trail system to create opportunities for physical activity, social engagement, prosperity, and happiness."
The City has been a partner since HWOTC's inception and has been working closely with the other partner agencies, including the Towns of Windermere and Oakland, the City of Winter Garden, the Gotha Rural Settlement, and the Foundation for a Healthier West Orange as well as other supporting agencies, to plan and implement various trail-related programs and projects. From 2022 to 2026, programs and projects have included trail enhancement projects, trail safety audits, future trail corridor evaluations, community events, and the creation of the Trail Side Development Design & Policy Guidelines.
Also, since the inception of the HWOTC collaborative effort, Bike/Walk Central Florida (BWCF) has provided program facilitation services in accordance with Program Services Scopes prepared on an annual basis. Thus, for the upcoming year, a new Scope of Program Services is needed to guide activities, programs, and services for fiscal year 2027 (FY27). Pursuant to this need, BWCF has prepared the attached Scope of Program Services and Cost-Sharing Schedule, which includes the total cost of the scope of services for FY27 and the funding contribution needed from each partner.

description:
City staff applied for a matching grant with the Foundation for a Healthier West Orange (FHWO) in the amount of $100,000 to begin Phase 1 construction of the Ocoee Downtown Rail Trail. The Rail Trail will run along Kissimmee Avenue from W. Oakland Avenue south to Ohio Street and will provide Ocoee families with expanded access to the West Orange Trail Network. On May 12th, 2026, the FHWO board approved the City's grant request. The grant agreement includes the following terms and requirements:FHWO will issue the $100,000 grant payment once the City has expended its matching $100,000 toward Phase 1 construction.
Phase 1 must be completed within three years.
The City will support the Healthy West Orange initiative and, where possible, display the Healthy West Orange logo and provide links to the movement (https://healthywestorange.org/) and the Healthy West Orange Trails Connection (https://fhwo.org/hwo-trails-connection) on its website.
The City will incorporate permanent and prominent Healthy West Orange naming and branding on all trail assets funded through the grant and include Healthy West Orange information in related programming and educational materials.
Additionally, the City is engaged in good‑faith negotiations with CSX Transportation to acquire the remaining parcels needed for construction of the Ocoee Downtown Rail Trail.

description:
The Ocoee WWTF Electrical Upgrade & Expansion increases the existing Wastewater Treatment Facility’s electrical and control infrastructure to support future required treatment system improvements and the continued expansion of the City’s Central Sewer System. This upgrade supports the long-term operational reliability of the wastewater treatment plant’s electrical and monitoring systems. During construction, additional conduit, electrical, and instrumentation/control requirements were identified that were not included in the original scope of the upgrade but are necessary for full implementation of the upgraded systems. These improvements are essential to support communication pathways for new equipment, provide spare conduit capacity, and complete infrastructure needed for the revised PLC-based control architecture. The scope of these changes includes the following:
Driveway Open Cut, Additional Signal Wiring, and Spare Conduits for Plant Monitoring Equipment:Installation of additional wiring, new conduit installation, and signal extensions including open cutting of the driveway to support the transition to the new PLC E‑1 control system, intercepting and extending existing signal wires,
Installation of new shielded cables,
Removal of outdated components and associated improvements required for the system switchover.
Installation of Additional Conduits:
Placement of new conduits, including core drilling and sealing of existing structures, to ensure proper communication and power routing between process buildings and PLC equipment.
Change Order No. 4 is required to complete these infrastructure improvements and ensure proper integration of the upgraded systems. The change order results in a net increase of $54,602.73 to the contract and does not modify the project completion timeframe.
title: Approval of Change Order No. 4 for ITB #24-008 Ocoee WWTF Electrical Upgrade & Expansion - Rebid Project. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The Lakewood Avenue Gravity Sewer Expansion Project Phases 1 & 2, (ITB 26‑004) extends the City’s wastewater collection system and upgrades to the existing system to support the expansion of the City’s wastewater collection system and comply with the Wekiwa and Rock Springs Basin Management Action Plan nutrient reduction requirements. As construction has progressed, several unforeseen field conditions and required system improvements were identified that were not included in the original contract scope but are essential to properly complete the project.
Utility staff have worked closely with the Contractor, J. Malever Construction Company, to compile the remaining work items necessary to address these conditions, resolve conflicts with existing infrastructure, and ensure all components meet current City standards. The scope of the additional work includes the following:
Removal and Replacement of Sewer Force Main Air Release Valves (ARVs)Replacement of four ARVs within the project area that were found to be non‑compliant with current engineering standards, including removal of existing equipment and installation of new ARV assemblies and cabinets. These valves are old and are not fully functioning.
Excavation and Removal of Unknown Steel Casing
Exposure and removal of an unforeseen 12‑inch cast iron/steel casing discovered during construction, which conflicted with installation of the new 12‑inch gravity sewer main.
Relocation of Installed 6‑Inch Water Main
Revise alignment of 6-inch watermain and valve location for watermain on Mobile Lane due to conflict with existing storm system.
Change Order No. 2 is necessary to complete these corrective and unanticipated tasks, ensure proper installation of all new infrastructure, and maintain compliance with City standards. This change order requires a contract modification authorizing the Contractor to perform the additional work, resulting in a total project cost increase of $90,725.00.
title: Approval of Change Order No. 2 for ITB #26-004 Lakewood Avenue Gravity Sewer Expansion Project – Phase 1 & 2. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The City of Ocoee’s Wastewater Treatment Permit requires that the City maintain a Sanitary Sewer Collections System Action Plan to prevent sewer overflows and wastewater leakages that may endanger public health and the environment. As part of this plan, the City is required to conduct pipe condition assessments on 10% of the gravity sanitary sewer system annually for the next 10 years starting in Fiscal Year 25/26. The FY 26/27 assessment is year 2 of the 10-year assessment.
The information collected by the RedZone sewer camera will be used in conjunction with other infrastructure performance indicators to identify, plan for, and complete repairs, replacements, maintenance activities, expansions, and upgrades to the sewer system. An annual report documenting findings and actions taken to address issues must be submitted to the Department of Environmental Protection by June 30, annually. This approach creates a long-term repair plan designed to improve the capital planning process by matching available funds and manpower to required projects and assisting staff with planning for grant opportunities. RedZone Robotics was approved by the City Commission in FY 25/26 as a sole source vendor for gravity sewer inspections.
RedZone Robotics specializes in wastewater infrastructure condition assessments using autonomous robots specially designed to overcome challenging underground pipe conditions. RedZone Robotics is the sole owner developer, and distributor of RedZone Robotics equipment, and their software includes AI predictive tools to better prioritize repair and replacements. GPS coordinates recorded during the assessment also provide the pipe's center line and manholes for GIS mapping.
The RedZone robot is the only product that requires fewer manhole access points, minimizing impacts on traffic flow in the area and limiting the need for extensive Maintenance of Traffic (MOT). The approved City of Ocoee Budget for Fiscal Year 26/27 includes a $120,000 budget for the condition assessment of 10% of the gravity sewer system (41,883 feet of linear pipe and 206 manholes). The Utilities Department has received a quote to inspect the second 10% of the total gravity system for a total cost of $94,493.86, which is $25,506.14 below the budgeted amount.
title: Approval of RedZone Robotics to Complete the First Stage of Gravity System Condition Assessment. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The property is located at 859 Hammocks Drive, assigned parcel ID number 21-22-28-8613-00-960, and is lot 96 in the Hammocks subdivision. Additionally, the property is located in commission district 2.
Per the Hammocks subdivision plat and the property survey for the lot, there is a utility easement on all four sides of the lot, including the subject 5-foot utility easement in the rear yard of the property. The applicants have replaced an existing retaining wall in the rear yard that encroaches into a 5-foot utility easement area. The applicant did not seek a permit to replace the retaining wall due to the cost of the work not exceeding the monetary threshold of $7,500.00 per FL Statutes.
Section 5-1B of Article V of the Land Development Code (LDC) states, "The zoning regulations are not intended to interfere with, abrogate, or annul any lawful easements, covenants, or other agreements between parties; provided, however, that where this Code imposes greater restrictions upon the use of buildings or premises than are imposed or required by other resolutions, rules, regulations, or by lawful easements, covenants, or agreements, the provisions of this Code shall prevail." As a result, the applicants are seeking city approval to vacate the 5-foot utility easement.
Letters were sent to the utility providers, and no objections to the requested vacation have been received. The provider letters and property survey are attached.
title: Public Hearing and Approval of Resolution for 859 Hammocks Drive - Staples Property Easement Vacate Request Project No. VAC-26-042. (Planner II Belizaire)

description:
Public Works Administration and Fleet staff continually evaluate industry practices and technologies to improve efficiency, accountability, and compliance in managing the City’s vehicle and equipment fleet. Following a review of available fleet management solutions, staff recommends contracting with Fleetio for fleet management software and implementation services.
Fleetio provides a centralized, cloud-based platform for managing the City’s vehicles, and equipment for maintenance, inspections, fuel, expenses, assignments, and fleet performance. The system will allow City staff to maintain a centralized asset inventory, schedule preventive maintenance, create and track work orders, conduct electronic inspections, monitor fuel transactions, assign vehicles, and maintain service and expense records throughout each asset’s lifecycle.
The platform’s reporting and dashboard tools provide visibility into maintenance costs, downtime, fuel consumption, utilization, inspection compliance, and total cost of ownership. Mobile inspection capabilities allow staff to document defects and initiate follow-up maintenance, while automated service reminders support preventive maintenance based on mileage, hours, or time intervals. Fuel transactions can be imported from fuel-card providers or entered through the mobile application, providing additional insight into fuel usage, operating costs, and unusual activity.
The City currently uses RTA Fleet Management, with the existing agreement scheduled to expire on March 31, 2027. In response to increasing fleet management, maintenance, inspection, reporting, and asset lifecycle requirements, staff evaluated available platforms. Fleetio was identified as meeting the City’s needs for asset management, preventive maintenance, inspections, fuel tracking, reporting, ease of use, and integration capabilities.
Fleetio supports integrations with fuel cards, telematics, and GPS systems and offers implementation services including data migration, system configuration, implementation planning, training, and best-practice guidance. Fleetio states that most customers can be operational within approximately 90 days, depending on fleet size and requirements.
Under GSA Cooperative Purchasing, Fleetio’s proposal includes a three-year contract at a cost of $52,920 for FY 2027, including implementation, data migration, training, etc. Subsequent annual subscription costs are estimated at $52,920 for FY 2028 and $52,920 for FY 2029, subject to the proposed agreement.
Implementing Fleetio will provide the City with a centralized fleet management system that replaces manual and paper-based processes with digital workflows and accessible fleet data. The system will improve tracking of maintenance, fuel, inspections, operating expenses, asset utilization, and lifecycle costs while providing reporting to support budgeting and future fleet replacement decisions.
title: Approval of Fleetio Fleet Management Software Program. (Deputy Public Works Director Rigwood)

Staff notified the City Manager and FDOT of the extent of the damage and received authorization to perform all necessary repairs to reopen the roadway as quickly and safely as possible.

description:
The Ocoee Police Department has historically donated State Forfeiture Funds to support programs or organizations that partner with the Department in its crime prevention/public safety mission and wishes to continue. The services these organizations provide to the Ocoee Police Department and the community cannot be duplicated within the Department. The Ocoee Police Department recommends donating funds to the following programs:
Crimeline ($2,500.00) provides crime-solving to the law enforcement agencies within Central Florida and provides rewards for members of the public.
Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) ($2,500.00), whose mission is to end drunk driving, support victims of these crimes, and prevent underage drinking.
Aspire Behavioral Health Care ($2,500.00) (also known as Central Florida Crisis Intervention Team) trains members of law enforcement on how to deal with people in mental health crises.
Children’s Safety Village ($2,500.00) aims to make Central Florida the safest community for children by providing various safety programs, including car seat check-ups, safety workshops, and sports clinics.
These donations comply with Florida State Statute 932.7055, which states that “Such funds may be used only for school resource officers, crime prevention, safe neighborhood, drug abuse education, or drug prevention programs or such other law enforcement purposes as the board of county commissioners or governing body of the municipality deems appropriate.
title: Approval to Donate State Forfeiture Funds to Organizations Supporting Law Enforcement. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has approved $300,000 through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), Watershed Planning Program (WPP), for the City of Ocoee to develop Watershed Master Plans for the McCormick East and West Basins as well as Lake Bennet Basin. The City will be a sub-recipient of this funding through the Florida Division of Emergency Management’s (FDEM) Mitigation Bureau.
This planning project serves to improve the City’s flood resiliency by guiding staff efforts to improve the safety of the community through increased flood protection during severe storms. Watershed Master Plans are creditable under the Community Rating System (CRS), which establishes community eligibility for discounts on flood insurance for National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) policyholders, and are required for a CRS class rating of 4 or better. These activities align with the City’s Envision 2045 Comprehensive Plan and the County’s Local Mitigation Strategy (LMS) Working Group’s goals.
Public Works recommends approval of the Watershed Master Plan project awarded under the FEMA’s Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) Watershed Planning Program (WPP).
title: Approval of Projects Awarded Funding under the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) Watershed Planning Program (WPP). (Public Works Director Krug)

Public Works is seeking and recommends approval from the City Commission to reallocate unused extra funds from the Clarke Road Corridor Lighting project to fund this relocation effort.

description:
The approved Ocoee American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) project list includes funds to construct a new reclaimed storage tank and pump station at the City’s Wastewater Treatment Plant. This project was revised to provide the infrastructure necessary to accept, store, and re-pump 1.0 million gallons per day (MGD) of reclaimed water from Orange County into the City’s reclaim distribution system following new rate classification requirements implemented by Orange County.
The City is taking steps to qualify for lower reclaimed water rates under the updated rate classifications implemented by Orange County, the first of which was implemented by the work under Change Order #1 with the addition of a supplementary potable water supply pipe to this new tank.
Change Order No. 4 includes:
Installation of post restraints on the existing potable water line to accommodate the new air gap potable water piping connection.
Installation of a permanent Insertion Valve on Leslie Ann Lane to properly isolate the existing water main during construction and future maintenance activities.
Removal of two trees located near the Reclaimed Water Tank’s Electrical Building that pose a safety and structural risk to the building and to the adjacent property.
These items are required to complete the potable water connection and protect the reclaim tank and pump house infrastructure. This change requires a contract modification, increasing the total project cost by $89,732.93.

description:
On January 1, 2025, a Code Violation (2024-03865) was issued to the Preserve at Crown Point Homeowners Association, which is located in Commission District 1. The violation was regarding multiple trees that had been removed from the HOA's private right-of-way (ROW) without a permit. Staff from Development Services began coordinating with the president of the homeowner's association (HOA) on how to correct the violation. The HOA provided an amendment to the community's declaration, and section 3B of the amendment states the following:
Section 11.8 of the Declaration, entitled "Limited Common Area," is hereby amended with the following additions and deletions:
11.8 Limited Common Area. Each Owner shall be responsible for the costs, charges and expenses incurred in connection with maintenance of the irrigation facilities, sidewalk, driveway and certain landscaping, including maintenance, repair and/or replacement of sod located immediately adjacent to such Owner's Lot between such Owner's Lot and the private Common Area roadway (each, an Owner's "Limited Common Area"). Every Owner shall be required to irrigate the grass and landscaping located in such Owner's Limited Common Area in a routine and ordinary manner and shall ensure that sufficient irrigation occurs during all periods when the Owner is absent from the Home. Further, each Owner is required to timely repair, maintain and/or replace the driveways, walkways, sidewalks, including without limitation brick pavers, and other paved and concrete surfaces comprising part of a Lot and the Owner's Limited Common Area. The Association: Each Owner, at their sole cost and expense, shall be responsible for the maintenance, pruning and replacement of any trees located within the Limited Common Areas, in accordance with the Association's rules and regulations and applicable governmental requirements. The Association shall have no responsibility for such trees. No tree installed by the Declarant in Limited Common Areas shall be felled, removed, or cut down unless such tree represents an immediate hazard to the Home or other improvements on the Lot, or to persons occupying or utilizing THE PRESERVE AT CROWN POINT. If any such tree dies, or is removed in accordance with this Section 11.8, then such tree shall be replaced at the expense of and by the Association as an Operating Expense, and each Owner shall pay an equal share of such costs of the replacement.
The HOA informed staff that the intention of this amendment was to allow individual property owners to remove street trees in front of the residences, and the HOA did not have plans currently to remove the street trees. Staff informed the HOA that regardless of the change in the declaration, the HOA was still responsible for ensuring compliance for trees in the private ROW that is owned by the HOA.
Staff directed the HOA to follow the process for tree removals in subdivisions in accordance with § 45-13.(F)(2), Commission Review of Applications for Tree Removal in Communities and Subdivisions, City of Ocoee Code of Ordinances. This process requires the applicant to submit an application under the Large-Scale Site Plan process, which requires a public hearing with the Planning and Zoning Commission and subsequently, the City Commission.
On July 1, 2026, the HOA submitted an application in accordance with the Large-Scale Site Plan process. The application proposes to remove 144 street trees on ten (10) parcels that make up the internal, private ROW of the subdivision. The applicant also submitted an assessment from an ISA-certified arborist discussing the street trees. The application from the HOA requests the removal of 144 street trees throughout the subdivision. The need and justification for the removal listed in the application is as follows:
"The removal of the oak trees is necessary to prevent future sidewalk damage, maintain the visibility of stop signs and intersections, and avoid obstruction of street lighting. This action will help improve safety and maintenance costs."
In discussions with staff, the HOA has agreed to provide approximately 54 replacement trees to mitigate the removal of the 144 street trees. These 54 replacement trees will be planted along the subdivision's existing multi-use trail. Staff is recommending that 90 additional street trees be planted in the private ROW to fully mitigate the 144 street trees that are proposed for removal. Staff is currently in the process of drafting an agreement between the City and HOA to codify the requirements for the replacement trees and the process for homeowners to apply for the removal of the street trees.
title: Public Hearing for Preserve at Crown Point Street Tree Removal Preliminary-Final Large-Scale Subdivision Plan; Project No. LS-2026-006. AT THE REQUEST OF THE APPLICANT, THIS ITEM IS BEING WITHDRAWN. (Community Development Administrator McFarlane)

attachments.name: Septic to Sewer Final Assessment Resolution

description:
The 2017 Downtown Master Plan identified the lack of central sewer as a major barrier to redevelopment. Concurrently to this study, state-led Wekiva Basin management studies determined that septic tanks are a significant contributor to nutrient loading in Starke Lake. To support downtown redevelopment and comply with state-mandated nutrient reduction requirements, the City has been extending sewer in the downtown area over the past several years. In 2014, it was determined that 39 parcels were not yet connected to available sewer. Connection is required by state statute.
The City applied for and was awarded a Florida Springs Grant that funds 100% of the on-property construction costs needed to connect to sewer. The grant does not, however, fund the City’s one-time sewer capital fee.
On April 7, 2026, the City Commission approved three payment options for the sewer capital fee: Standard cash payment at time of connection
Interest free 24 month payment on the utility bill (statutorily required)
A 10-year non-ad valorem assessment under the City’s home rule authority and Section 197.3632, Florida Statutes
Nineteen property owners have opted for the 10-year non-ad valorem assessment program.
The sewer capital fee for all parcels was calculated using the Equivalent Residential Unit (ERU) methodology in Chapter 173 of the City Code, based on a fee of $7,811 per ERU. The non-ad valorem assessment consists of the sewer capital fee, a 3% interest rate, and a $120 recording cost per property. The total estimated sewer assessment is $194,968.21.
title: Public Hearing for Adoption of the Septic-To-Sewer Final Assessment Resolution. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The City currently charges fire protection service assessments within its incorporated boundaries pursuant to a methodology established in a study conducted by Anser Advisory Consulting, LLC, dated May 2025. The Amended and Restated Final Assessment Resolution was passed and adopted on August 5th, 2025. Section 2.08 of the City’s Fire Protection Assessment Ordinance, adopted as Ordinance No. 2013-010 on August 6, 2013, sets forth the procedure for determining the Fire Protection Assessment for each subsequent fiscal year.
On May 19, 2026, the City Commission was given a presentation on the Fire Service Assessment Fee Program, with the option of selecting one of two new methodologies (Historical & Demand-Availability) and staff discussed various rates based on the Fire Department's 5-Year assessable budget. The City Commission voted 4-0 to authorize staff to update the City's existing Fire Services Special Assessment Program from the Fire Protection Unit methodology to the Demand and Availability methodology and to set June 16, 2026, as the hearing date to adopt the initial assessment resolution. The Initial Rate Assessment Resolution was approved at the June 16, 2026, City Commission Meeting establishing a maximum Fire Service Assessment funding level equal to 70% of the five-year average assessable Fire Budget and set August 18, 2026, as the hearing to adopt the final assessment resolution.
The Amended and Restated Final Assessment Resolution for approval provides for formally adopting the Demand-Availability assessment methodology, sets the FY 2026-27 assessment rate at 45% of the five-year average assessable Fire Budget generating an estimated net revenue of $8,445,222. This rate will assess each Residential property as follows: $86.03/dwelling unit (demand) + $297.87/dwelling unit (availability) = $383.90/dwelling unit total and for nonresidential, the assessment rate is factored as: i) Demand rate — a category-specific charge, calculated by $/sq ft and ii) Availability rate — a single value of 297.87per EDU (2,423 sf per edu). The resolution also establishes a maximum assessment rate at 70% of the five-year average assessable Fire Budget, generating an estimated net revenue of $13,139,397. It should be noted that the city typically realizes approximately 95% of estimated net revenue.
Under the Demand-Availability assessment methodology, the Demand Component (time spent in response to fire protection calls), residential structures are assessed a flat per dwelling unit rate with nonresidential assessed a per square foot rate. For the Availability Component (time available to respond to primary structure fire incidents), residential structures are assigned a flat Equivalent Dwelling Unit (EDU) rate with nonresidential also assigned an EDU rate based on building square footage. The assessment rates in the resolution are provided in the tables below:

description:
Members of the Citizen Advisory Council for Ocoee Fire Department (CACOFD) serve three-year terms. The Resolution creating the Board allows no more than nine (9) members and currently, the board has nine (9) members. The terms of Members Warren Channell, Kaitlyn Ochoa, Michael Fletcher, and Jim Washington expire in November 2026. description:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) has announced a Notice of Funding Availability under the Volkswagen (VW) Settlement Program, providing up to $12 million statewide for the replacement of eligible Class 8 emergency service vehicles. The program provides qualifying municipalities with an opportunity to receive up to $800,000 per eligible replacement vehicle.
The Ocoee Fire Department currently maintains a 2006 fire engine that has exceeded its anticipated service life. Due to its age, continued maintenance requirements, and the need to maintain a reliable emergency response fleet, the Department is seeking funding assistance to replace this apparatus with a new fire engine.
The existing 2006 fire engine meets the program's model-year requirement for replacement of diesel-powered vehicles manufactured in 2009 or earlier, subject to verification of the remaining eligibility requirements. As a condition of the grant, the existing apparatus must be permanently removed from service and scrapped in accordance with the program guidelines.
The estimated funding breakdown is as follows:FDEP Volkswagen Settlement Grant$800,000 City of Ocoee Contribution $400,000 Total Estimated Project Cost$1,200,000
If awarded the maximum grant amount, the City would be responsible for the remaining estimated $400,000. Should the grant award be less than the maximum available amount, the City's financial obligation would increase accordingly.
Submission of the grant application does not obligate the City to purchase the apparatus or commit matching funds at this time. If awarded, the Fire Department will return to the City Commission for authorization to accept the grant, approve the required City funding, and proceed with the purchase in accordance with applicable procurement requirements.
Justification: Replacing the 2006 fire engine will improve the Department's operational readiness, reduce the maintenance challenges associated with aging apparatus, and ensure the continued availability of reliable fire suppression equipment.
Additionally, the grant provides an opportunity to offset a substantial portion of the cost of a necessary capital equipment replacement while supporting the state's efforts to reduce diesel emissions through the retirement of older vehicles.
The grant application deadline is December 4, 2026, at 5:00 PM EST.
title: Authorization to Apply for the Florida Department of Environmental Protection Volkswagen Settlement Grant – Fire Engine Replacement. (Deputy Fire Chief Van Camp)

description:
The property at 611 N. Lakewood Avenue, owned by Rental Home Holdings LLC, is subject to ongoing code enforcement proceedings for unsafe structural conditions and accumulated junk and debris (Code Enforcement Case # 2025-01222). These violations were cited under Section 108-35 of the City Code, which addresses nuisance conditions and structural hazards that require corrective action to protect public health, safety, and welfare.
On June 24, 2025, during the code enforcement hearing, Code Enforcement Officer Rodriguez advised the Board that the property remained noncompliant and requested an Order of Compliance requiring corrective action by August 23, 2025. The Board unanimously determined that the property had been in violation since April 23, 2025, and ordered compliance by August 23, 2025. The Board also authorized daily fines of $100 per violation for continued noncompliance and authorized the City to abate the property and assess associated costs if it became vacant. During the hearing, the owner's representative and real estate broker, Erich Spivey, indicated that contractors had been hired to address the violations and requested additional time to achieve compliance.
The Code Enforcement Board again reviewed the property on March 19, 2026. Code Enforcement Officer Loeffler reported that the property remained noncompliant, continued to constitute an unsafe structure, and contained accumulated junk and debris. After considering the evidence, the Code Enforcement Board unanimously approved a motion authorizing the City to abate the property through demolition, with associated costs assessed against the property. On July 21, 2026, the City Commission approved demolition of the unsafe structure at 611 N. Lakewood Avenue, Ocoee, Florida 34787. The authorization resulted from repeated opportunities given to the property owner to correct the outstanding violations and the property owner's continued failure to bring the property into compliance. The City subsequently incurred $8,857.00 in asbestos remediation expenses associated with the property.
On October 20, 2026, after the City Commission authorized demolition. Attorney Jeffrey Donner of Donner Law Firm requested reconsideration of the demolition order on behalf of the property owner. Attorney Donner asked the Commission to review the owner's rehabilitation proposal and suspend demolition while the owner develops a rehabilitation agreement. The property manager, Erich Spivey, addressed the City Commission and explained the owner's efforts to bring the property into compliance. He also asked the Commission to lift the stop-work order to allow rehabilitation activities.
During a subsequent Commission discussion, City Manager Shadrix asked City Attorney Geller to provide an overview of the case and suggested returning the matter to the City Commission as a formal agenda item. City Attorney Geller provided a history of the enforcement proceedings and advised that deadlines established by the Code Enforcement Board, including applicable appeal periods, had expired. Attorney Geller also provided the current liens on the property as follows: Outstanding Code Enforcement Lien of $42,495.20, Asbestos Remediation Expenses $8,857.00, Total Identified Amount $51,352.20. During the discussion, Mr. Spivey indicated he could pay the full outstanding amount of $51,352.20. Mayor Johnson directed the matter to be returned to the City Commission for consideration at its November 3, 2026, meeting.
Attached is a Settlement Agreement drafted by the City Attorney which memorializes terms between the City and property (Parties) owner relating to the outstanding code enforcement and demolition of the property. The Parties agree to the following:
Item (a): Owner will deposit $51,352.20 into the City Attorney's escrow account, which covers the Outstanding Code Enforcement Lien of $42,495.20 and Asbestos Remediation Expenses of $8,857.00.
Item (b): The City shall cancel all demolition work and lift the Stop-Work Order on the roof permit.
Item (c): The City gives 60 days from the effective date of the agreement to correct violations.
Item (d): Once corrections have been made, the city will receive the full payment from escrow and no later than five (5) days will record a Satisfaction of Lien in the public records of Orange County.
title: Approval of Settlement Agreement between the City of Ocoee and Rental Home Holdings LLC for 611 N. Lakewood Avenue. (Police Chief Ogburn)

description:
The City of Ocoee operates 69 wastewater lift stations located throughout the City. These facilities serve a critical function in conveying raw wastewater through the collection system to the City of Ocoee Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP). The structural integrity of each lift station is essential to maintaining reliable wastewater service and protecting public health and the environment.
Over time, protective liners and associated piping within lift stations deteriorate due to constant exposure to corrosive wastewater gases and conditions. Failed, deteriorated, or missing liners can accelerate corrosion of the underlying concrete structure, resulting in structural damage, wastewater leakage, environmental concerns, increased maintenance costs, and in severe cases, facility failure or collapse.
Pricing for RCM utilities services for lift station rehabilitation is available through the City of Zephyrhills General Construction Continuing Services Agreement No. 41-25-13, which was competitively solicited through RFP No. 2025-004 and awarded on July 14, 2025. The agreement provides for general construction services on an as-needed basis through July 13, 2028.
The approved Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Utilities Department budget includes $75,000 for the planned relining and repiping of Lift Station 14 and $95,000 for the planned relining and repiping of Lift Station 30. The existing liners and piping systems at both facilities have reached or are approaching the end of their useful service lives. Performing these improvements at this time will help preserve the structural integrity of the lift stations, reduce the risk of equipment and structural failures, and ensure the continued reliable operation of the City's wastewater collection system.
title: Approval of the Relining and Repiping of Lift Stations 14 and 30 Utilizing the City of Zephyrhills General Construction Continuing Services Agreement No. 41-25-13. (Utilities Director Bolling)

description:
The property is located at 109 Coquina Key Drive within Commission District 3. It is zoned RT-1 (Mobile Home Subdivision District) and is assigned parcel ID number 18-22-28-7126-04-090.
The subject property was platted in 1978 as part of the Pioneer Key Park Section—Two mobile home subdivision. The lot is a substandard lot of record because it does not meet the minimum 7,000-square-foot lot area for the RT-1 zoning district. Although the lot does not meet the minimum lot area, it has retained the same configuration since being platted. Therefore, construction is permitted subject to meeting all other applicable minimum zoning requirements, including building setbacks.
Provided below are the minimum zoning requirements for the RT-1 zoning district from Table 5-2: Minimum Zoning Descriptions on Permitted Uses of Article V of the Land Development Code (LDC).

The applicant is requesting a variance to Section 5-14A and Table 5-2 of Article V of the LDC, to reduce the minimum rear building setback from 20 feet to 13 feet for the purpose of installing a double-wide 56' x 26' 8" mobile home on the lot. Per Article IV, Section 4-9A, approval of a variance requires that the applicant demonstrate compliance with four (4) criteria, as follows:
1. That special conditions and circumstances exist which are peculiar to the land, structures, or required subdivision improvements involved and which are not applicable to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements;
2. That a literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties with similar conditions;
3. That the special conditions and circumstances do not result from the actions of the applicant;
4. That the granting of the variance requested will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by these regulations to other lands, structures, or required subdivision improvements under similar conditions. No pre-existing conditions of neighboring lands which are contrary to these regulations shall be considered grounds for the issuance of a variance.
Staff Analysis: Staff finds that, based on the circumstances and conditions of the existing lot, there is sufficient demonstration that the four (4) variance evaluation criteria are met. Staff analysis is summarized below:
Criteria 1: Special Circumstances & Conditions: Special circumstances and conditions exist that are unique to the subject property due to its substandard size and unusual configuration. Unlike other typical RT-1 (Mobile Home Subdivision District) lots within Pioneer Key Park Section-Two, which are generally deeper than they are wide, the subject parcel's dimensions limit the available buildable area and restrict the placement of a double-wide mobile home in compliance with current setback requirements.
Criteria 2: Literal Interpretation of Code: The literal interpretation of the provisions of these regulations would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other similarly situated properties. Strict application of the required front and rear setbacks would reduce the lot's buildable area to approximately 16 feet in width. As a result, the remaining buildable area would be insufficient to accommodate a 26-foot double-wide mobile home, thereby limiting the reasonable use of the property in a manner enjoyed by neighboring lots with a similar mobile home size.
Criteria 3: Actions of the Application: The circumstances necessitating the variance were not created by the applicant, as the parcel has maintained its original configuration since it was platted in 1978. Due to the lot's substandard lot size and atypical configuration, which differ from those of a typical RT-1 lot within the subdivision that is generally deeper than it is wide, the proposed mobile home cannot reasonably be placed on the property while complying with the required 20-foot front and rear setbacks.
Criteria 4: Conference of Special Privilege: Approval of the requested variance would not grant the applicant a special privilege to other similarly situated properties. Within Pioneer Key Park Section Two, there are numerous existing mobile homes that were established in accordance with zoning regulations in effect prior to 1992. Due to the usual configuration of the subject lot, the requested setback reduction is necessary to allow the reasonable placement of a double-wide mobile home. Approval would enable the property owner to utilize the parcel in a manner comparable to other developed lots within Pioneer Key Park Section Two and would provide the same benefit afforded to neighboring lots, rather than creating a preferential advantage.
Staff supports the variance as there is sufficient justification to support the request.
title: Public Hearing for 109 Coquina Key Drive - Harper Family Revocable Trust Property Variance Request - Project No. VR-26-03. (Planner I Scarbrough)
